abstract: Advances in brain theory need two complementary approaches: Analytical investigations by in situ measurements and as well synthetic modelling supported by computer simulations to generate suggestive hypothesis on purposeful structures in the neural tissue. In this paper research of the second line is described: Starting from a neurophysiologically inspired model of stimulusresponse (S-R) and/or associative memorization and a psychologically motivated ministructure for basic control tasks, pre-conditions and conditions are studied for cooperation of such units in a hierarchical organisation, as can be assumed to be the general layout of macrostructures in the brain.
originalAbstract: Advances in brain theory need two complementary approaches: Analytical investigations by in situ measurements and as well synthetic modelling supported by computer simulations to generate suggestive hypothesis on purposeful structures in the neural tissue. In this paper research of the second line is described: Starting from a neurophysiologically inspired model of stimulusresponse (S-R) and/or associative memorization and a psychologically motivated ministructure for basic control tasks, pre-conditions and conditions are studied for cooperation of such units in a hierarchical organisation, as can be assumed to be the general layout of macrostructures in the brain.

paragraphs: This paper studies how small units for associative memory and basic control can cooperate in a hierarchy. It takes a synthetic approach to brain theory: construct a model and use computer simulation to develop hypotheses about purposeful neural organization. The authors present this as complementary to direct measurements of nervous tissue.

The starting point combines a neurophysiologically inspired model of stimulus–response or associative memory with a psychologically motivated structure for elementary control tasks. These components connect remembering associations with producing organized responses. The research then shifts from the behavior of an individual unit to the conditions needed for several units to work together.

The main question is what prerequisites allow cooperation when these units occupy different parts of a hierarchical organization. A hierarchy is treated as a plausible broad layout for brain macrostructure. The approach matters because useful behavior at the level of one memory or controller does not by itself explain coordinated behavior across a larger organization. The paper uses constructed models to investigate that relationship.
summary.tldr: The paper uses synthetic modeling to study the conditions under which associative-memory and basic-control units can cooperate in a hierarchy.

title: Hierarchical Learning Control - An Approach with Neuron-Like Associative Memories

abstract: Parallelizable optimization techniques are applied to the problem of learning in feedforward neural networks. In addition to having supe(cid:173) rior convergence properties, optimization techniques such as the Polak(cid:173) Ribiere method are also significantly more efficient than the Back(cid:173) propagation algorithm. These results are based on experiments per(cid:173) formed on small boolean learning problems and the noisy real-valued learning problem of hand-written character recognition.

In addition to having supe(cid:173) rior convergence properties, optimization techniques such as the Polak(cid:173) Ribiere method are also significantly more efficient than the Back(cid:173) propagation algorithm. These results are based on experiments per(cid:173) formed on small boolean learning problems and the noisy real-valued learning problem of hand-written character recognition.

paragraphs: This paper applies parallelizable optimization methods to learning in feedforward neural networks. The central concern is the procedure used to find suitable connection weights. By changing that procedure, the authors seek more efficient training and better convergence while keeping feedforward-network learning as the underlying problem.

The methods include Polak–Ribiere optimization, which the paper compares with the backpropagation algorithm. The experiments cover small Boolean learning problems and handwritten character recognition with noisy, real-valued data. These tasks place the comparison in both discrete problems and a recognition setting with inputs that vary continuously and contain noise.

The reported findings favor the optimization techniques in both convergence behavior and efficiency. This suggests that the choice of weight-search method can materially affect how readily a network learns, beyond the choice of network itself. Parallelizability is also part of the proposed approach, making the organization of computation relevant to the training method. The evidence stated in the abstract concerns the Boolean and handwritten-character tasks used in the experiments.
summary.tldr: Parallelizable optimization methods, including Polak–Ribiere, improve training efficiency and convergence over backpropagation in the reported experiments.

title: Efficient Parallel Learning Algorithms for Neural Networks

paragraphs: This paper proposes an unsupervised learning method that treats a neural network as a nonlinear dynamical system. The focus is its velocity field in phase space: a description of how the network's state changes at each location. Learning shapes this motion using the examples supplied to the network.

Each example serves as an interpolation point where a desired velocity is specified. Those velocities are selected so that the resulting trajectories converge toward an attracting set within the subspace occupied by the cluster of examples. The examples thus help define where the dynamics should lead, connecting the structure of the data with the network's evolving state.

A learning procedure then finds synaptic interconnections that produce the selected field. The theory is illustrated with examples. The contribution is a way to formulate unsupervised learning through the design of state-space motion: the learned network embodies a flow toward a data-associated attracting set. This makes the geometry and convergence of the dynamics part of the learned representation.
summary.tldr: An unsupervised learning method shapes neural dynamics so that trajectories converge toward an attracting set associated with the example cluster.

title: Unsupervised Learning in Neurodynamics Using the Phase Velocity Field Approach

abstract: Coherent oscillatory activity in large networks of biological or artifi(cid:173) cial neural units may be a useful mechanism for coding information pertaining to a single perceptual object or for detailing regularities within a data set. We consider the dynamics of a large array of simple coupled oscillators under a variety of connection schemes. Of particular interest is the rapid and robust phase-locking that results from a "sparse" scheme where each oscillator is strongly coupled to a tiny, randomly selected, subset of its neighbors.
originalAbstract: Coherent oscillatory activity in large networks of biological or artifi(cid:173) cial neural units may be a useful mechanism for coding information pertaining to a single perceptual object or for detailing regularities within a data set. We consider the dynamics of a large array of simple coupled oscillators under a variety of connection schemes. Of particular interest is the rapid and robust phase-locking that results from a "sparse" scheme where each oscillator is strongly coupled to a tiny, randomly selected, subset of its neighbors.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how a large array of simple oscillators develops coordinated activity. Its motivation is that coherent oscillation could help represent information belonging to one perceptual object or reveal regularities in a dataset. In this view, the timing relationships among units provide a possible way to associate information across a network.

The authors examine the dynamics under several connection schemes. Their highlighted scheme is sparse: each oscillator has strong connections to only a very small, randomly selected subset of its neighbors. The relevant design choice is therefore both how many connections each oscillator has and how strongly those selected connections act.

This sparse arrangement produces rapid and robust phase-locking, meaning that the oscillators establish stable relationships between their cycles. The result matters because coordinated timing emerges with few selected connections per unit. The reported finding concerns the dynamics of the oscillator array; coding a perceptual object or describing data regularities supplies the proposed motivation for seeking that coordinated behavior.
summary.tldr: Strong connections to a tiny random subset of neighbors produce rapid, robust phase-locking in a large oscillator array.

title: Phase-coupling in Two-Dimensional Networks of Interacting Oscillators

abstract: I exhibit a systematic way to derive neural nets for vision problems. It involves formulating a vision problem as Bayesian inference or decision on a comprehensive model of the visual domain given by a probabilistic grammar.
originalAbstract: I exhibit a systematic way to derive neural nets for vision problems. It involves formulating a vision problem as Bayesian inference or decision on a comprehensive model of the visual domain given by a probabilistic grammar.
title: Visual Grammars and Their Neural Nets

abstract: Neurons learning under an unsupervised Hebbian learning rule can perform a nonlinear generalization of principal component analysis. This relationship between nonlinear PCA and nonlinear neurons is reviewed. The stable fixed points of the neuron learning dynamics correspond to the maxima of the statist,ic optimized under non(cid:173) linear PCA. However, in order to predict. what the neuron learns, knowledge of the basins of attractions of the neuron dynamics is required. Here the correspondence between nonlinear PCA and neural networks breaks down. This is shown for a simple model. Methods of statistical mechanics can be used to find the optima of the objective function of non-linear PCA. This determines what the neurons can learn. In order to find how the solutions are parti(cid:173) tioned amoung the neurons, however, one must solve the dynamics.

In order to find how the solutions are parti(cid:173) tioned amoung the neurons, however, one must solve the dynamics.

paragraphs: The paper examines the relationship between unsupervised Hebbian learning and nonlinear principal component analysis. In this relationship, neurons adapt according to learning dynamics whose stable fixed points correspond to maxima of a statistical objective. Identifying those maxima describes the representations that the neurons could potentially learn.

The authors show why this objective-based description is insufficient to predict the actual learning outcome. That prediction also depends on basins of attraction: the sets of starting conditions whose dynamics lead to particular solutions. A simple model demonstrates where the correspondence between nonlinear PCA and the neural learning process stops providing a complete explanation.

Methods from statistical mechanics can identify the optima of the nonlinear PCA objective, establishing possible destinations for learning. Determining how those solutions are distributed among neurons requires solving the dynamics as well. The contribution separates two questions that can otherwise be conflated: which representations satisfy the objective, and which representations the learning process actually selects.
summary.tldr: Nonlinear PCA identifies possible Hebbian learning outcomes, but predicting which neurons reach which outcomes requires analyzing their dynamics.

title: Non-Linear Statistical Analysis and Self-Organizing Hebbian Networks

abstract: This paper introduces GNARL, an evolutionary program which induces recurrent neural networks that are structurally unconstrained. In contrast to constructive and destructive algorithms, GNARL employs a popula(cid:173) tion of networks and uses a fitness function's unsupervised feedback to guide search through network space. Annealing is used in generating both gaussian weight changes and structural modifications. Applying GNARL to a complex search and collection task demonstrates that the system is capable of inducing networks with complex internal dynamics.
originalAbstract: This paper introduces GNARL, an evolutionary program which induces recurrent neural networks that are structurally unconstrained. In contrast to constructive and destructive algorithms, GNARL employs a popula(cid:173) tion of networks and uses a fitness function's unsupervised feedback to guide search through network space. Annealing is used in generating both gaussian weight changes and structural modifications. Applying GNARL to a complex search and collection task demonstrates that the system is capable of inducing networks with complex internal dynamics.

paragraphs: This paper introduces GNARL, an evolutionary program for discovering recurrent neural networks without fixing their structure in advance. The search concerns both how a network is connected and how it behaves. Because recurrent networks have internal dynamics, changing their structure can change the patterns of activity through which they perform a task.

GNARL maintains a population of networks and uses unsupervised feedback from a fitness function to guide the search. This differs from procedures organized around progressively adding or removing network components. Its modifications include Gaussian changes to connection weights and changes to structure, with annealing used in generating both kinds of variation.

The authors apply the program to a complex search-and-collection task. The resulting demonstration shows that it can induce networks with complex internal dynamics. This supports the central premise that evolutionary search over structure and weights can produce recurrent behavior suited to a demanding task. The reported contribution combines an unconstrained structural search method with evidence that the method can discover dynamically rich networks.
summary.tldr: GNARL evolves recurrent network structures and weights, producing complex internal dynamics for a search-and-collection task.

title: Structural and Behavioral Evolution of Recurrent Networks

paragraphs: The repeating rise and fall of a sound's amplitude carries timing information relevant to pitch. This paper presents a silicon model that uses synchronized neuronal spikes to extract a sound's fundamental frequency. Its organizing idea is that coordinated spike timing can make the periodic structure of an acoustic signal available to a physical circuit.

The biological motivation comes from neurons called choppers in the mammalian cochlear nucleus. These cells synchronize especially well with particular rates of amplitude modulation, depending on their own intrinsic chopping frequency. The model draws on this relationship between a cell's internal rhythm and the timing of changes in the incoming sound.

The implementation combines an artificial cochlea, an inner hair cell circuit, and a spiking neuron circuit. Together, these components form a hardware model connecting auditory input processing with spike-based timing. The contribution is a concrete circuit approach to a biologically motivated pitch-processing step: detecting modulation periodicity through synchrony. It places the temporal behavior of the neurons at the center of the computation.
summary.tldr: A silicon auditory model uses synchronized spikes, inspired by cochlear-nucleus chopper cells, to extract a sound's fundamental frequency.

title: A Silicon Model of Amplitude Modulation Detection in the Auditory Brainstem

abstract: A new algorithm for Support Vector regression is described. For a priori chosen 1/, it automatically adjusts a flexible tube of minimal radius to the data such that at most a fraction 1/ of the data points lie outside. More(cid:173) over, it is shown how to use parametric tube shapes with non-constant radius. The algorithm is analysed theoretically and experimentally.
originalAbstract: A new algorithm for Support Vector regression is described. For a priori chosen 1/, it automatically adjusts a flexible tube of minimal radius to the data such that at most a fraction 1/ of the data points lie outside. More(cid:173) over, it is shown how to use parametric tube shapes with non-constant radius. The algorithm is analysed theoretically and experimentally.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a support vector regression algorithm that adapts the width of a tube around its predictions. The tube describes a band within which data points are accommodated. Its central design choice is to let the user specify an allowed fraction of points outside that band, while the algorithm adjusts the radius.

For the chosen fraction, the method finds a flexible tube of minimum radius subject to the stated bound on outside points. This connects the fitted tolerance directly to the data and to an interpretable user-selected constraint. The resulting learning problem jointly concerns the regression fit and how tightly its surrounding band can enclose the observations.

The authors also show how to use parametric tube shapes whose radius is not constant. This extends the construction beyond a band with the same width everywhere. The algorithm receives both theoretical and experimental analysis. Its contribution is a regression formulation that learns the tube size automatically while allowing structured variation in its shape.
summary.tldr: A support vector regression algorithm learns a minimal-width prediction tube from a user-chosen bound on the fraction of points outside it.

title: Shrinking the Tube: A New Support Vector Regression Algorithm

abstract: Nonlinear Support Vector Machines (SVMs) are investigated for visual sex classification with low resolution "thumbnail" faces (21- by-12 pixels) processed from 1,755 images from the FE RET face database. The performance of SVMs is shown to be superior to traditional pattern classifiers (Linear, Quadratic, Fisher Linear Dis(cid:173) criminant, Nearest-Neighbor) as well as more modern techniques such as Radial Basis Function (RBF) classifiers and large ensemble(cid:173) RBF networks. Furthermore, the SVM performance (3.4% error) is currently the best result reported in the open literature.

The performance of SVMs is shown to be superior to traditional pattern classifiers (Linear, Quadratic, Fisher Linear Dis(cid:173) criminant, Nearest-Neighbor) as well as more modern techniques such as Radial Basis Function (RBF) classifiers and large ensemble(cid:173) RBF networks. Furthermore, the SVM performance (3.4% error) is currently the best result reported in the open literature.

paragraphs: The paper investigates nonlinear support vector machines for the visual sex-classification task defined in its face dataset. The inputs are very small face images: thumbnails measuring 21 by 12 pixels, processed from 1,755 images in the FERET database. This focuses the study on how much useful classification information remains in low-resolution facial imagery.

The authors compare support vector machines with several established pattern classifiers. These include linear and quadratic classifiers, Fisher linear discriminant, and nearest-neighbor methods, along with radial basis function classifiers and large ensembles of radial basis function networks. The comparison tests the nonlinear support vector approach against multiple alternative ways of classifying the same kind of visual input.

The reported support vector machine error is 3.4%, and the abstract states that its performance exceeds the compared methods. It also describes the result as the best reported in the open literature at the time of the paper. The finding is an empirical result for the studied image-classification setting, showing strong performance despite the small size of the input images.
summary.tldr: Nonlinear SVMs achieve a reported 3.4% error on sex classification from low-resolution FERET face images, outperforming the compared classifiers.

title: Sex with Support Vector Machines

abstract: In this communication we present a new algorithm for solving Support Vector Classifiers (SVC) with large training data sets. The new algorithm is based on an Iterative Re-Weighted Least Squares procedure which is used to optimize the SVc. Moreover, a novel sample selection strategy for the working set is presented, which randomly chooses the working set among the training samples that do not fulfill the stopping criteria. The validity of both proposals, the optimization procedure and sample selection strategy, is shown by means of computer experiments using well-known data sets.
originalAbstract: In this communication we present a new algorithm for solving Support Vector Classifiers (SVC) with large training data sets. The new algorithm is based on an Iterative Re-Weighted Least Squares procedure which is used to optimize the SVc. Moreover, a novel sample selection strategy for the working set is presented, which randomly chooses the working set among the training samples that do not fulfill the stopping criteria. The validity of both proposals, the optimization procedure and sample selection strategy, is shown by means of computer experiments using well-known data sets.

paragraphs: The paper presents an algorithm for training support vector classifiers on large datasets. Its contribution addresses two parts of the training process: the optimization procedure used to solve the classifier and the selection of examples included in a working set. Both choices concern how the training computation is organized.

The optimization procedure uses iterative reweighted least squares. This means that training proceeds through least-squares calculations whose weights change across iterations. Alongside this procedure, the authors introduce a randomized working-set strategy. It draws its examples from the training samples that do not satisfy the stopping criteria, directing selection toward samples for which the relevant conditions remain unmet.

Computer experiments on well-known datasets support the validity of both proposals. The abstract presents these experiments as evidence for the optimization procedure and the sample-selection strategy. The approach matters because it treats large-scale support vector training as a combination of numerical optimization and selective attention to training examples, with an explicit rule connecting the working set to stopping conditions.
summary.tldr: The proposed support vector training method combines iterative reweighted least squares with randomized selection among samples that fail stopping criteria.

title: Fast Training of Support Vector Classifiers

abstract: We present methods for learning and tracking human motion in video. We estimate a statistical model of typical activities from a large set of 3D periodic human motion data by segmenting these data automatically into "cycles". Then the mean and the princi(cid:173) pal components of the cycles are computed using a new algorithm that accounts for missing information and enforces smooth tran(cid:173) sitions between cycles. The learned temporal model provides a prior probability distribution over human motions that can be used in a Bayesian framework for tracking human subjects in complex monocular video sequences and recovering their 3D motion.
originalAbstract: We present methods for learning and tracking human motion in video. We estimate a statistical model of typical activities from a large set of 3D periodic human motion data by segmenting these data automatically into "cycles". Then the mean and the princi(cid:173) pal components of the cycles are computed using a new algorithm that accounts for missing information and enforces smooth tran(cid:173) sitions between cycles. The learned temporal model provides a prior probability distribution over human motions that can be used in a Bayesian framework for tracking human subjects in complex monocular video sequences and recovering their 3D motion.

paragraphs: This paper learns a statistical description of repeating human movements and uses it to support tracking in video. The training material is a large collection of three-dimensional periodic motion. The method automatically divides these recordings into cycles, making repeated portions of an activity the units from which the motion model is built.

The authors then compute an average cycle and principal components describing variation among cycles. Their algorithm accounts for missing information and enforces smooth transitions between cycles. These features connect the statistical representation to the temporal structure of motion: the learned description must accommodate incomplete observations while allowing successive cycles to join smoothly.

The resulting temporal model supplies prior probabilities over possible human motions. Within a Bayesian tracking framework, that prior can guide interpretation of complex video recorded by a single camera and support recovery of three-dimensional movement. The approach matters because information learned from repeated 3D activities becomes a structured source of guidance for interpreting motion in monocular images.
summary.tldr: A learned model of smooth motion cycles supplies a Bayesian prior for tracking people and recovering 3D movement from single-camera video.

title: Learning and Tracking Cyclic Human Motion

abstract: Mutual Boosting is a method aimed at incorporating contextual information to augment object detection. When multiple detectors of objects and parts are trained in parallel using AdaBoost [1], object detectors might use the remaining intermediate detectors to enrich the weak learner set. This method generalizes the efficient features suggested by Viola and Jones thus enabling information inference between parts and objects in a compositional hierarchy. In our experiments eye-, nose-, mouth- and face detectors are trained using the Mutual Boosting framework. Results show the method outperforms applications overlooking contextual information. We suggest that achieving contextual integration is a step toward human-like detection capabilities.

When multiple detectors of objects and parts are trained in parallel using AdaBoost [1], object detectors might use the remaining intermediate detectors to enrich the weak learner set. This method generalizes the efficient features suggested by Viola and Jones thus enabling information inference between parts and objects in a compositional hierarchy. In our experiments eye-, nose-, mouth- and face detectors are trained using the Mutual Boosting framework. Results show the method outperforms applications overlooking contextual information. paragraphs: Mutual Boosting aims to improve object detection by allowing detectors to use contextual information from related objects and parts. The paper's example involves eyes, noses, mouths, and faces, where evidence for individual components and evidence for the whole object can inform one another.

The method trains multiple detectors in parallel using AdaBoost. During training, a detector can use the other intermediate detectors to expand its available set of weak learners. This generalizes the efficient features associated with Viola and Jones and enables information to pass between parts and objects in a compositional hierarchy. Context becomes part of the detector's learned evidence.

Experiments train the facial-part and face detectors within this framework. The reported results outperform applications that overlook contextual information, supporting the value of exchanging information among related detection tasks. The authors suggest that contextual integration is a step toward human-like detection capabilities. That broader interpretation accompanies the demonstrated improvement, rather than establishing that the system matches human detection.
summary.tldr: Mutual Boosting improves detection by letting jointly trained object and part detectors use one another as contextual evidence.

title: Mutual Boosting for Contextual Inference

abstract: A graph-based prior is proposed for parametric semi-supervised classification. The prior utilizes both labelled and unlabelled data; it also integrates features from multiple views of a given sample (e.g., multiple sensors), thus implementing a Bayesian form of co-training. An EM algorithm for training the classifier automatically adjusts the tradeoff between the contributions of: (a) the labelled data; (b) the unlabelled data; and (c) the co-training information. Active label query selection is performed using a mutual information based criterion that explicitly uses the unlabelled data and the co-training information. Encouraging results are presented on public benchmarks and on measured data from single and multiple sensors.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a graph-based prior for a parametric classifier that learns from both labeled and unlabeled examples. It also incorporates multiple views of the same sample, such as information from different sensors. Combining these views within a Bayesian formulation provides a form of co-training.

Training uses an expectation-maximization algorithm that automatically adjusts the balance among three contributions: labeled examples, unlabeled examples, and information from co-training. This matters because the framework must bring together different sources of evidence. Their relative contributions are adjusted during learning as part of the classifier's training procedure.

The method also selects examples for label queries using a mutual-information criterion. That selection explicitly considers the unlabeled data and the information supplied by multiple views, connecting active querying to the same evidence used in training. The authors report encouraging results on public benchmarks and measurements from single and multiple sensors. The contribution combines semi-supervised learning, multiple-view integration, and active label selection within one probabilistic approach.
summary.tldr: A graph-based Bayesian classifier combines labeled data, unlabeled data, multiple views, and information-based label querying.

title: On Semi-Supervised Classification

abstract: Most nervous systems encode information about stimuli in the responding activity of large neuronal networks. This activity often manifests itself as dynamically coordinated sequences of action potentials. Since multiple electrode recordings are now a standard tool in neuroscience research, it is important to have a measure of such network-wide behavioral coordination and information sharing, applicable to multiple neural spike train data. We propose a new statistic, informational coherence, which measures how much better one unit can be predicted by knowing the dynamical state of another. We argue informational coherence is a measure of association and shared information which is superior to traditional pairwise measures of synchronization and correlation. To find the dynamical states, we use a recently-introduced algorithm which reconstructs effective state spaces from stochastic time series. We then extend the pairwise measure to a multivariate analysis of the network by estimating the network multi-information. We illustrate our method by testing it on a detailed model of the transition from gamma to beta rhythms.

paragraphs: The paper develops a measure of coordination in neuronal spike trains. Neural populations can represent stimuli through changing sequences of activity, so the authors seek a statistic that captures information sharing in those dynamics. Their proposed informational coherence asks how much better one unit can be predicted when the dynamical state of another is known.

To obtain those dynamical states, the method uses an algorithm that reconstructs effective state spaces from stochastic time series. This makes the inferred state of each unit central to the comparison. The authors argue that informational coherence provides a better measure of association and shared information than traditional pairwise synchronization and correlation measures.

The approach also extends beyond pairs by estimating network multi-information, allowing a multivariate analysis of shared activity. The authors illustrate the method on a detailed model of a transition from gamma to beta rhythms. This application demonstrates how the proposed analysis can be used to study changing network coordination, with the abstract presenting the broader superiority claim as an argument by the authors.
summary.tldr: Informational coherence measures neural coordination through improved prediction from another unit's dynamical state and extends to network-wide information sharing.

title: Measuring Shared Information and Coordinated Activity in Neuronal Networks

abstract: Independent component analysis (ICA) is a powerful method to decouple signals. Most of the algorithms performing ICA do not consider the temporal correlations of the signal, but only higher moments of its amplitude distribution. Moreover, they require some preprocessing of the data (whitening) so as to remove second order correlations. In this paper, we are interested in understanding the neural mechanism responsible for solving ICA. We present an online learning rule that exploits delayed correlations in the input. This rule performs ICA by detecting joint variations in the firing rates of pre- and postsynaptic neurons, similar to a local rate-based Hebbian learning rule.

Moreover, they require some preprocessing of the data (whitening) so as to remove second order correlations. This rule performs ICA by detecting joint variations in the firing rates of pre- and postsynaptic neurons, similar to a local rate-based Hebbian learning rule.

paragraphs: Independent component analysis aims to separate signals that have been mixed together. The paper approaches this task through a question about neural computation: what learning mechanism could allow neurons to perform such separation? The authors contrast their approach with algorithms that mainly use higher-order properties of signal amplitudes while ignoring temporal correlations.

Their proposed online rule instead exploits delayed correlations in the inputs. It detects joint changes in the firing rates of a neuron sending a signal and a neuron receiving it. The resulting update resembles a local, rate-based Hebbian learning rule, linking the signal-separation computation to activity available at a connection between neurons.

The stated contribution is that this rule performs independent component analysis using temporal information in an online learning setting. The abstract also identifies whitening, which removes second-order correlations, as preprocessing required by many existing approaches. The paper’s central explanatory shift is toward delayed relationships and local firing-rate changes as ingredients of an ICA mechanism, rather than relying solely on the distribution of instantaneous signal amplitudes.
summary.tldr: An online learning rule performs independent component analysis by exploiting delayed input correlations and local changes in neural firing rates.

title: An online Hebbian learning rule that performs Independent Component Analysis

abstract: Extensive labeled data for image annotation systems, which learn to assign class labels to image regions, is difficult to obtain. We explore a hybrid model framework for utilizing partially labeled data that integrates a generative topic model for image appearance with discriminative label prediction. We propose three alternative formulations for imposing a spatial smoothness prior on the image labels. Tests of the new models and some baseline approaches on two real image datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of incorporating the latent structure.
originalAbstract: Extensive labeled data for image annotation systems, which learn to assign class labels to image regions, is difficult to obtain. We explore a hybrid model framework for utilizing partially labeled data that integrates a generative topic model for image appearance with discriminative label prediction. We propose three alternative formulations for imposing a spatial smoothness prior on the image labels. Tests of the new models and some baseline approaches on two real image datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of incorporating the latent structure.

paragraphs: Image annotation systems assign category labels to regions within images, but obtaining extensive region-level labels is difficult. This paper explores how to learn from partially labeled data. The challenge is to use information in image appearance while also learning the relationship between that appearance and the labels that are available.

The proposed framework combines a generative topic model of image appearance with discriminative label prediction. The topic model represents latent structure in the visual data, while the discriminative component connects the representation to annotation. The authors also develop three alternative ways to impose a spatial smoothness prior, expressing a preference for labels that are spatially consistent.

Tests compare the new models and baseline approaches on two real image datasets. The results support the effectiveness of incorporating latent structure into the annotation model. The contribution is thus a hybrid framework for incomplete supervision, together with alternative treatments of spatial consistency and empirical evidence that hidden structure in image appearance can help label prediction.
summary.tldr: Hybrid generative and discriminative models use latent image structure to support region annotation from partially labeled data.

title: Learning Hybrid Models for Image Annotation with Partially Labeled Data

abstract: By adding a spatial regularization kernel to a standard loss function formulation of the boosting problem, we develop a framework for spatially informed boosting. From this regularized loss framework we derive an efficient boosting algorithm that uses additional weights/priors on the base classifiers. We prove that the proposed algorithm exhibits a ``grouping effect, which encourages the selection of all spatially local, discriminative base classifiers. The algorithms primary advantage is in applications where the trained classifier is used to identify the spatial pattern of discriminative information, e.g. the voxel selection problem in fMRI. We demonstrate the algorithms performance on various data sets.

From this regularized loss framework we derive an efficient boosting algorithm that uses additional weights/priors on the base classifiers. We prove that the proposed algorithm exhibits a ``grouping effect, which encourages the selection of all spatially local, discriminative base classifiers. The algorithms primary advantage is in applications where the trained classifier is used to identify the spatial pattern of discriminative information, e.g. the voxel selection problem in fMRI. We demonstrate the algorithms performance on various data sets.

paragraphs: The paper adapts boosting to problems where the spatial arrangement of predictive information matters. It adds a spatial regularization kernel to the usual loss formulation, so the learning objective incorporates spatial relationships. This is particularly useful when a trained classifier is also used to locate informative regions in the data.

From that objective, the authors derive an efficient boosting algorithm with additional weights or priors on the base classifiers. They prove a grouping effect: the algorithm encourages selection of spatially local base classifiers that carry discriminative information. The result concerns an encouragement toward joint selection, allowing nearby informative components to appear together in the learned classifier.

The stated primary application is recovering the spatial pattern of discriminative information, with voxel selection in fMRI as an example. In such a setting, the arrangement of selected components is itself part of what the researcher wants to understand. The authors demonstrate performance on several datasets, supporting the use of spatial structure within the boosting framework.
summary.tldr: Spatially regularized boosting encourages nearby informative base classifiers to be selected together, helping reveal discriminative spatial patterns.

title: Boosting with Spatial Regularization

abstract: While loopy Belief Propagation (LBP) has been utilized in a wide variety of applications with empirical success, it comes with few theoretical guarantees. Especially, if the interactions of random variables in a graphical model are strong, the behaviors of the algorithm can be difficult to analyze due to underlying phase transitions. In this paper, we develop a novel approach to the uniqueness problem of the LBP fixed point; our new “necessary and sufficient” condition is stated in terms of graphs and signs, where the sign denotes the types (attractive/repulsive) of the interaction (i.e., compatibility function) on the edge. In all previous works, uniqueness is guaranteed only in the situations where the strength of the interactions are “sufficiently” small in certain senses. In contrast, our condition covers arbitrary strong interactions on the specified class of signed graphs. The result of this paper is based on the recent theoretical advance in the LBP algorithm; the connection with the graph zeta function.

paragraphs: Loopy belief propagation is widely used for inference in graphical models, but its empirical success exceeds the available theoretical guarantees. Strong interactions between variables make its behavior especially difficult to analyze because of underlying phase transitions. This paper focuses on whether the algorithm has a unique fixed point, a state that remains unchanged by its updates.

The authors derive a necessary-and-sufficient condition expressed through graph structure and interaction signs. Each sign identifies an interaction as attractive or repulsive. This shifts attention toward the arrangement and types of relationships in the graph. Earlier uniqueness guarantees, as characterized in the abstract, required interaction strengths to be sufficiently small in particular senses.

For the specified class of signed graphs, the new condition covers arbitrarily strong interactions. That scope is essential: the result does not assert uniqueness for every graph with strong interactions. The proof builds on a connection between belief propagation and the graph zeta function. Its significance is a structural characterization of fixed-point uniqueness that extends beyond weak-interaction guarantees within the covered graph class.
summary.tldr: A graph-and-sign condition characterizes belief-propagation fixed-point uniqueness and covers arbitrarily strong interactions within a specified signed-graph class.

title: Uniqueness of Belief Propagation on Signed Graphs

abstract: This paper describes a new acoustic model based on variational Gaussian process dynamical system (VGPDS) for phoneme classification. The proposed model overcomes the limitations of the classical HMM in modeling the real speech data, by adopting a nonlinear and nonparametric model. In our model, the GP prior on the dynamics function enables representing the complex dynamic structure of speech, while the GP prior on the emission function successfully models the global dependency over the observations. Additionally, we introduce variance constraint to the original VGPDS for mitigating sparse approximation error of the kernel matrix. The effectiveness of the proposed model is demonstrated with extensive experimental results including parameter estimation, classification performance on the synthetic and benchmark datasets.

Additionally, we introduce variance constraint to the original VGPDS for mitigating sparse approximation error of the kernel matrix. The effectiveness of the proposed model is demonstrated with extensive experimental results including parameter estimation, classification performance on the synthetic and benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: This paper develops an acoustic model for phoneme classification using a variational Gaussian process dynamical system. Its motivation is to address limitations of classical hidden Markov models in representing real speech. The proposed model uses nonlinear, nonparametric components to capture a richer account of how speech evolves and how observations relate.

Two Gaussian process priors serve separate purposes. The prior over the dynamics function represents complex temporal structure in speech. The prior over the emission function models global dependencies among observations. Together, they provide flexibility both in the evolving internal process and in the relationship between that process and the observed acoustic data.

The authors also add a variance constraint to the original variational model to mitigate error from a sparse approximation of the kernel matrix. This addresses the approximation used within the modeling procedure alongside the choice of model itself. Experiments covering parameter estimation and classification on synthetic and benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
summary.tldr: A constrained Gaussian process dynamical model captures nonlinear speech structure and mitigates sparse approximation error for phoneme classification.

title: Phoneme Classification using Constrained Variational Gaussian Process Dynamical System

abstract: Recently, [Valiant and Valiant] showed that a class of distributional properties, which includes such practically relevant properties as entropy, the number of distinct elements, and distance metrics between pairs of distributions, can be estimated given a SUBLINEAR sized sample. Specifically, given a sample consisting of independent draws from any distribution over at most n distinct elements, these properties can be estimated accurately using a sample of size O(n / log n). We propose a novel modification of this approach and show: 1) theoretically, our estimator is optimal (to constant factors, over worst-case instances), and 2) in practice, it performs exceptionally well for a variety of estimation tasks, on a variety of natural distributions, for a wide range of parameters. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the key step in this approach is to first use the sample to characterize the unseen" portion of the distribution. This goes beyond such tools as the Good-Turing frequency estimation scheme, which estimates the total probability mass of the unobserved portion of the distribution: we seek to estimate the "shape"of the unobserved portion of the distribution. This approach is robust, general, and theoretically principled; we expect that it may be fruitfully used as a component within larger machine learning and data analysis systems. "

paragraphs: A sample can leave many possible outcomes unseen, yet still contain enough information to estimate properties of the underlying distribution. The paper builds on results showing that entropy, distinct-element counts, and certain distribution distances can be estimated from independent samples of size O(n/log n) for distributions over at most n elements.

Its modification focuses on reconstructing the shape of the unseen portion of the distribution. Estimating only the total probability assigned to unobserved outcomes does not describe how that probability is distributed among them. The proposed approach seeks this richer characterization as a basis for estimating distributional properties.

The authors prove that their estimator is optimal up to constant factors on worst-case instances. They also report strong practical performance across multiple estimation tasks, natural distributions, and parameter settings. The theoretical result concerns worst-case efficiency, while the experiments show usefulness across the tested conditions. The authors further suggest that estimating unseen structure could become a component of larger learning and analysis systems; this is presented as a potential application.
summary.tldr: Estimating the shape of unobserved probability mass yields property estimators that are worst-case optimal up to constants and perform strongly in experiments.

title: Estimating the Unseen: Improved Estimators for Entropy and other Properties

abstract: We consider the design of strategies for \emph{market making} in a market like a stock, commodity, or currency exchange. In order to obtain profit guarantees for a market maker one typically requires very particular stochastic assumptions on the sequence of price fluctuations of the asset in question. We propose a class of spread-based market making strategies whose performance can be controlled even under worst-case (adversarial) settings. We prove structural properties of these strategies which allows us to design a master algorithm which obtains low regret relative to the best such strategy in hindsight. We run a set of experiments showing favorable performance on real-world price data.

paragraphs: A market maker needs a trading strategy that can cope with changing asset prices. Guarantees about profit often depend on specific probabilistic assumptions about how those prices fluctuate. This paper develops a class of strategies based on trading spreads whose performance can instead be controlled in a worst-case setting, where price movements may be adversarial.

The authors prove structural properties of this strategy class and use them to build a master algorithm. Its guarantee concerns regret: how much performance it loses relative to the best strategy from that class, chosen after seeing the price sequence. This provides a way to adapt across available strategies while retaining a meaningful retrospective comparison.

Experiments on real price data show favorable performance. The theoretical and empirical contributions address complementary questions: whether adaptation can be controlled under adverse price sequences, and whether the approach works favorably on observed data. The guarantee is relative to the specified strategy class; it does not establish unconditional profitability.
summary.tldr: An online market-making algorithm achieves low regret against a class of spread-based strategies, with favorable results on real price data.

title: Adaptive Market Making via Online Learning

abstract: The learning with privileged information setting has recently attracted a lot of attention within the machine learning community, as it allows the integration of additional knowledge into the training process of a classifier, even when this comes in the form of a data modality that is not available at test time. Here, we show that privileged information can naturally be treated as noise in the latent function of a Gaussian process classifier (GPC). That is, in contrast to the standard GPC setting, the latent function is not just a nuisance but a feature: it becomes a natural measure of confidence about the training data by modulating the slope of the GPC probit likelihood function. Extensive experiments on public datasets show that the proposed GPC method using privileged noise, called GPC+, improves over a standard GPC without privileged knowledge, and also over the current state-of-the-art SVM-based method, SVM+. Moreover, we show that advanced neural networks and deep learning methods can be compressed as privileged information.

paragraphs: The paper studies classification with privileged information: additional knowledge available during training but unavailable when making predictions on new examples. The challenge is to make that information useful without requiring the same input modality at test time. The authors address this within a Gaussian process classifier by representing privileged information as noise in its latent function.

This noise has an informative role. It changes the slope of the classifier's probit likelihood, allowing the model to express confidence about individual training data through that modulation. The proposed GPC+ method thus uses extra training knowledge to influence how observations are interpreted within the probabilistic classifier.

Extensive experiments on public datasets show improvements over a standard Gaussian process classifier without privileged information and over SVM+, the state-of-the-art SVM-based method identified in the abstract. The authors also show that information from advanced neural networks and deep learning methods can be compressed into privileged information. This broadens the kinds of training-only knowledge that can contribute to the classifier through the proposed noise-based formulation.
summary.tldr: GPC+ encodes training-only privileged information as informative noise, improving Gaussian process classification in the reported experiments.

title: Mind the Nuisance: Gaussian Process Classification using Privileged Noise

abstract: The Generic Viewpoint Assumption (GVA) states that the position of the viewer or the light in a scene is not special. Thus, any estimated parameters from an observation should be stable under small perturbations such as object, viewpoint or light positions. The GVA has been analyzed and quantified in previous works, but has not been put to practical use in actual vision tasks. In this paper, we show how to utilize the GVA to estimate shape and illumination from a single shading image, without the use of other priors. We propose a novel linearized Spherical Harmonics (SH) shading model which enables us to obtain a computationally efficient form of the GVA term. Together with a data term, we build a model whose unknowns are shape and SH illumination. The model parameters are estimated using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers embedded in a multi-scale estimation framework. In this prior-free framework, we obtain competitive shape and illumination estimation results under a variety of models and lighting conditions, requiring fewer assumptions than competing methods.

paragraphs: The paper estimates object shape and illumination from a single shading image using the Generic Viewpoint Assumption. This assumption says that the viewer or light is not in a special position. Accordingly, an estimated explanation of the image should remain stable under small changes in object, viewpoint, or light position.

The authors turn this stability principle into a practical estimation term. They introduce a linearized spherical harmonics shading model that makes the term computationally efficient. Combining it with a term measuring agreement with the image yields a model whose unknowns are shape and spherical harmonics illumination. An alternating direction method of multipliers solves the estimation problem within a multiscale framework.

The approach uses the viewpoint assumption without adding other priors. Experiments report competitive shape and illumination estimates across a variety of models and lighting conditions, with fewer assumptions than competing methods. The contribution is a concrete route from a previously analyzed stability principle to a working vision method that estimates both sources of shading variation together.
summary.tldr: A practical formulation of the Generic Viewpoint Assumption enables joint shape and illumination estimation from one shading image without additional priors.

title: Shape and Illumination from Shading using the Generic Viewpoint Assumption

abstract: We study the restless bandit problem where arms are associated with stationary $\varphi$-mixing processes and where rewards are therefore dependent: the question that arises from this setting is that of carefully recovering some independence by `ignoring' the values of some rewards. As we shall see, the bandit problem we tackle requires us to address the exploration/exploitation/independence trade-off, which we do by considering the idea of a {\em waiting arm} in the new Remix-UCB algorithm, a generalization of Improved-UCB for the problem at hand, that we introduce. We provide a regret analysis for this bandit strategy; two noticeable features of Remix-UCB are that i) it reduces to the regular Improved-UCB when the $\varphi$-mixing coefficients are all $0$, i.e. when the i.i.d scenario is recovered, and ii) when $\varphi(n)=O(n^{-\alpha})$, it is able to ensure a controlled regret of order $\Ot\left( \Delta_*^{(\alpha- 2)/\alpha} \log^{1/\alpha} T\right),$ where $\Delta_*$ encodes the distance between the best arm and the best suboptimal arm, even in the case when $\alpha<1$, i.e. the case when the $\varphi$-mixing coefficients {\em are not} summable.

We provide a regret analysis for this bandit strategy; two noticeable features of Remix-UCB are that i) it reduces to the regular Improved-UCB when the $\varphi$-mixing coefficients are all $0$, i.e. when the i.i.d scenario is recovered, and ii) when $\varphi(n)=O(n^{-\alpha})$, it is able to ensure a controlled regret of order $\Ot\left( \Delta_*^{(\alpha- 2)/\alpha} \log^{1/\alpha} T\right),$ where $\Delta_*$ encodes the distance between the best arm and the best suboptimal arm, even in the case when $\alpha<1$, i.e. the case when the $\varphi$-mixing coefficients {\em are not} summable.

paragraphs: This paper studies restless bandits whose arms produce rewards through stationary φ-mixing processes. Rewards are dependent across time, so collecting another observation does not necessarily provide the independence that ordinary bandit reasoning relies on. The learning problem therefore includes managing dependence alongside choosing which arms to explore and exploit.

The proposed Remix-UCB algorithm introduces a waiting arm and deliberately ignores some reward values to recover useful independence. It generalizes Improved-UCB to this dependent setting. Waiting becomes part of the decision process because the value of an observation depends partly on its temporal relationship to other observations.

The authors provide a regret analysis with two notable properties. When all mixing coefficients are zero, the method reduces to Improved-UCB in the independent setting. When dependence decays as φ(n) = O(n^−α), the analysis gives controlled regret depending on the horizon, decay rate, and gap between the best and next-best arms. The result also covers α below one, where the mixing coefficients are not summable.
summary.tldr: Remix-UCB uses waiting to manage dependent bandit rewards and provides regret guarantees even for some slowly mixing processes.

title: Cornering Stationary and Restless Mixing Bandits with Remix-UCB

abstract: Deep structured output learning shows great promise in tasks like semantic image segmentation. We proffer a new, efficient deep structured model learning scheme, in which we show how deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) can be used to directly estimate the messages in message passing inference for structured prediction with Conditional Random Fields CRFs). With such CNN message estimators, we obviate the need to learn or evaluate potential functions for message calculation. This confers significant efficiency for learning, since otherwise when performing structured learning for a CRF with CNN potentials it is necessary to undertake expensive inference for every stochastic gradient iteration. The network output dimension of message estimators is the same as the number of classes, rather than exponentially growing in the order of the potentials. Hence it is more scalable for cases that a large number of classes are involved. We apply our method to semantic image segmentation and achieve impressive performance, which demonstrates the effectiveness and usefulness of our CNN message learning method.

We proffer a new, efficient deep structured model learning scheme, in which we show how deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) can be used to directly estimate the messages in message passing inference for structured prediction with Conditional Random Fields CRFs). With such CNN message estimators, we obviate the need to learn or evaluate potential functions for message calculation. This confers significant efficiency for learning, since otherwise when performing structured learning for a CRF with CNN potentials it is necessary to undertake expensive inference for every stochastic gradient iteration. The network output dimension of message estimators is the same as the number of classes, rather than exponentially growing in the order of the potentials. Hence it is more scalable for cases that a large number of classes are involved. We apply our method to semantic image segmentation and achieve impressive performance, which demonstrates the effectiveness and usefulness of our CNN message learning method.

paragraphs: Structured image prediction involves relationships among output labels, making inference an important part of learning. In conditional random fields with neural potential functions, training can require expensive inference at every stochastic gradient step. This paper changes what the neural network learns in order to reduce that computational burden.

The proposed convolutional networks estimate the messages used by message-passing inference directly. Consequently, the method does not need to learn or evaluate potential functions for calculating those messages. It places the learned component at the level of the information exchanged during inference, avoiding an intermediate calculation that would otherwise make structured training expensive.

The message estimator's output dimension equals the number of classes, rather than growing exponentially with potential order. This provides a scaling advantage when many classes are involved. The authors apply the method to semantic image segmentation and report strong performance. The findings support direct message estimation as a useful way to combine deep learning with structured prediction while reducing the cost of the learning procedure.
summary.tldr: Convolutional networks directly estimate inference messages, reducing the computational burden of learning structured image predictions.

title: Deeply Learning the Messages in Message Passing Inference

abstract: Deep distributed decision trees and tree ensembles have grown in importance due to the need to model increasingly large datasets. However, PLANET, the standard distributed tree learning algorithm implemented in systems such as \xgboost and Spark MLlib, scales poorly as data dimensionality and tree depths grow. We present Yggdrasil, a new distributed tree learning method that outperforms existing methods by up to 24x. Unlike PLANET, Yggdrasil is based on vertical partitioning of the data (i.e., partitioning by feature), along with a set of optimized data structures to reduce the CPU and communication costs of training. Yggdrasil (1) trains directly on compressed data for compressible features and labels; (2) introduces efficient data structures for training on uncompressed data; and (3) minimizes communication between nodes by using sparse bitvectors. Moreover, while PLANET approximates split points through feature binning, Yggdrasil does not require binning, and we analytically characterize the impact of this approximation. We evaluate Yggdrasil against the MNIST 8M dataset and a high-dimensional dataset at Yahoo; for both, Yggdrasil is faster by up to an order of magnitude.

These are reported upper-end improvements in the evaluated comparisons. summary.tldr: Yggdrasil accelerates distributed deep-tree training through feature-based partitioning, optimized storage, and lower communication costs.

title: Yggdrasil: An Optimized System for Training Deep Decision Trees at Scale

abstract: A single color image can contain many cues informative towards different aspects of local geometric structure. We approach the problem of monocular depth estimation by using a neural network to produce a mid-level representation that summarizes these cues. This network is trained to characterize local scene geometry by predicting, at every image location, depth derivatives of different orders, orientations and scales. However, instead of a single estimate for each derivative, the network outputs probability distributions that allow it to express confidence about some coefficients, and ambiguity about others. Scene depth is then estimated by harmonizing this overcomplete set of network predictions, using a globalization procedure that finds a single consistent depth map that best matches all the local derivative distributions. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through evaluation on the NYU v2 depth data set.

paragraphs: Estimating depth from a single color image requires combining visual clues about local scene geometry. Some clues may strongly suggest a surface shape, while others admit several interpretations. This paper builds a representation that preserves such local information and uncertainty before constructing the final depth map.

A neural network predicts depth derivatives at every image location, covering multiple orders, orientations, and scales. These derivatives describe aspects of how depth varies across the image. For each quantity, the network predicts a probability distribution instead of one fixed value. It can therefore express confidence in some geometric details while leaving others ambiguous.

A subsequent globalization procedure finds one coherent depth map that best agrees with the collection of local distributions. The predictions are overcomplete: they offer overlapping descriptions that must be reconciled into a single scene estimate. This separates gathering local geometric evidence from enforcing consistency across the image. Evaluation on the NYU v2 depth dataset demonstrates the effectiveness of the approach, supporting the use of uncertain local predictions as an intermediate representation for monocular depth estimation.
summary.tldr: The method combines probabilistic predictions of local depth changes into one globally consistent depth map.

title: Depth from a Single Image by Harmonizing Overcomplete Local Network Predictions

abstract: In this paper, we revisit the Empirical Risk Minimization problem in the non-interactive local model of differential privacy. In the case of constant or low dimensions ($p\ll n$), we first show that if the loss function is $(\infty, T)$-smooth, we can avoid a dependence of the sample complexity, to achieve error $\alpha$, on the exponential of the dimensionality $p$ with base $1/\alpha$ ({\em i.e.,} $\alpha^{-p}$), which answers a question in \cite{smith2017interaction}. Our approach is based on polynomial approximation. Then, we propose player-efficient algorithms with $1$-bit communication complexity and $O(1)$ computation cost for each player. The error bound is asymptotically the same as the original one. With some additional assumptions, we also give an efficient algorithm for the server. In the case of high dimensions ($n\ll p$), we show that if the loss function is a convex generalized linear function, the error can be bounded by using the Gaussian width of the constrained set, instead of $p$, which improves the one in \cite{smith2017interaction}.

paragraphs: This paper studies empirical risk minimization when each participant privately reports information without interactive rounds. The central issue is how sample requirements and computation depend on dimension, accuracy, and the structure of the loss. The authors treat low-dimensional and high-dimensional regimes separately.

For constant or low dimension and an infinitely smooth loss with the stated smoothness condition, polynomial approximation avoids a sample-complexity dependence of the form alpha to the power minus p. They also obtain participant-efficient algorithms requiring one bit of communication and constant computation per participant, with asymptotically matching error bounds. Efficient server computation needs additional assumptions.

In high dimensions, convex generalized linear losses permit error bounds involving the Gaussian width of the constraint set instead of ambient dimension p. These are assumption-dependent theoretical improvements. The abstract does not claim the same guarantees for arbitrary losses or arbitrary constraint sets, and it provides no empirical benchmark results.
summary.tldr: Polynomial approximation improves noninteractive private learning under smoothness and structural assumptions.

title: Empirical Risk Minimization in Non-interactive Local Differential Privacy Revisited

abstract: (This is a theory paper) In this paper, we consider first-order methods for solving stochastic non-convex optimization problems. The key building block of the proposed algorithms is first-order procedures to extract negative curvature from the Hessian matrix through a principled sequence starting from noise, which are referred to {\it NEgative-curvature-Originated-from-Noise or NEON} and are of independent interest. Based on this building block, we design purely first-order stochastic algorithms for escaping from non-degenerate saddle points with a much better time complexity (almost linear time in the problem's dimensionality). In particular, we develop a general framework of {\it first-order stochastic algorithms} with a second-order convergence guarantee based on our new technique and existing algorithms that may only converge to a first-order stationary point. For finding a nearly {\it second-order stationary point} $\x$ such that $\|\nabla F(\x)\|\leq \epsilon$ and $\nabla^2 F(\x)\geq -\sqrt{\epsilon}I$ (in high probability), the best time complexity of the presented algorithms is $\widetilde O(d/\epsilon^{3.5})$, where $F(\cdot)$ denotes the objective function and $d$ is the dimensionality of the problem. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first theoretical result of first-order stochastic algorithms with an almost linear time in terms of problem's dimensionality for finding second-order stationary points, which is even competitive with existing stochastic algorithms hinging on the second-order information.

paragraphs: In nonconvex optimization, a small gradient does not necessarily indicate a useful stopping point: a saddle point can also have little first-order signal. This theory paper develops stochastic algorithms that use first-order information to escape non-degenerate saddle points and obtain a stronger, second-order form of stationarity.

The central construction, NEON, starts from noise and follows a principled sequence of first-order operations to extract negative curvature associated with the Hessian. Negative curvature identifies a direction relevant to leaving a saddle. The authors use this construction in a general framework that upgrades existing algorithms whose guarantees may stop at first-order stationary points.

With high probability, the resulting methods can find a point whose gradient norm is at most epsilon and whose Hessian has no eigenvalue below negative square root of epsilon. The best stated time complexity is Õ(d/epsilon^3.5), nearly linear in dimension d. The authors describe this as the first such dimensional dependence for first-order stochastic methods, and as competitive with stochastic methods that use second-order information.
summary.tldr: NEON extracts negative-curvature information through first-order operations, enabling stochastic saddle escape with nearly linear dependence on dimension.

title: First-order Stochastic Algorithms for Escaping From Saddle Points in Almost Linear Time

abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have shown great capability of solving various artificial intelligence tasks. However, the increasing model size has raised challenges in employing them in resource-limited applications. In this work, we propose to compress deep models by using channel-wise convolutions, which replace dense connections among feature maps with sparse ones in CNNs. Based on this novel operation, we build light-weight CNNs known as ChannelNets. ChannelNets use three instances of channel-wise convolutions; namely group channel-wise convolutions, depth-wise separable channel-wise convolutions, and the convolutional classification layer. Compared to prior CNNs designed for mobile devices, ChannelNets achieve a significant reduction in terms of the number of parameters and computational cost without loss in accuracy. Notably, our work represents the first attempt to compress the fully-connected classification layer, which usually accounts for about 25% of total parameters in compact CNNs. Experimental results on the ImageNet dataset demonstrate that ChannelNets achieve consistently better performance compared to prior methods.

paragraphs: ChannelNets address the difficulty of using large convolutional neural networks in applications with limited resources. The paper targets connections among feature maps, replacing dense connectivity with sparse connectivity through channel-wise convolutions. The intended benefit is to reduce both stored parameters and computation while retaining useful recognition capability.

The resulting architectures use three forms of this operation: group channel-wise convolutions, depth-wise separable channel-wise convolutions, and a convolutional classification layer. The final component extends compression to the classification stage. The authors highlight this as their first attempt to compress a fully connected classification layer, a component they say typically holds about a quarter of the parameters in compact CNNs.

On ImageNet, the authors report consistently better performance than prior methods. They also report substantial parameter and computational reductions compared with earlier CNNs designed for mobile devices, without an accuracy loss. The findings support sparse connections across feature maps as a useful design choice for compact networks, including a classification stage that remains a substantial part of an already small model.
summary.tldr: ChannelNets use sparse connections among feature maps to reduce CNN parameters and computation while preserving accuracy in the reported comparisons.

title: ChannelNets: Compact and Efficient Convolutional Neural Networks via Channel-Wise Convolutions

abstract: In theory, importance sampling speeds up stochastic gradient algorithms for supervised learning by prioritizing training examples. In practice, the cost of computing importances greatly limits the impact of importance sampling. We propose a robust, approximate importance sampling procedure (RAIS) for stochastic gradient de- scent. By approximating the ideal sampling distribution using robust optimization, RAIS provides much of the benefit of exact importance sampling with drastically reduced overhead. Empirically, we find RAIS-SGD and standard SGD follow similar learning curves, but RAIS moves faster through these paths, achieving speed-ups of at least 20% and sometimes much more.

In practice, the cost of computing importances greatly limits the impact of importance sampling. We propose a robust, approximate importance sampling procedure (RAIS) for stochastic gradient de- scent. By approximating the ideal sampling distribution using robust optimization, RAIS provides much of the benefit of exact importance sampling with drastically reduced overhead. paragraphs: Importance sampling can accelerate supervised learning by giving some training examples higher sampling priority. The theoretical benefit comes with a practical expense: determining those priorities can itself require substantial computation. This paper focuses on that overhead, which can prevent a better sampling strategy from delivering a useful reduction in total training time.

The proposed procedure, robust approximate importance sampling, or RAIS, approximates the ideal sampling distribution using robust optimization. It is designed for stochastic gradient descent. The objective is to retain much of exact importance sampling's benefit while greatly reducing the work required to decide which examples to sample.

Empirically, RAIS-SGD and standard SGD trace similar learning curves, but RAIS progresses through them more quickly. The authors report speedups of at least 20% in their experiments, with larger gains in some cases. The result highlights an implementation-sensitive aspect of learning algorithms: a theoretically advantageous sampling rule becomes useful when its own computational cost is sufficiently small. Here, approximation is the mechanism that makes that tradeoff favorable.
summary.tldr: RAIS approximates importance sampling cheaply enough to accelerate SGD, with reported experimental speedups of at least 20%.

title: Training Deep Models Faster with Robust, Approximate Importance Sampling

abstract: We present a new technique for deep reinforcement learning that automatically detects moving objects and uses the relevant information for action selection. The detection of moving objects is done in an unsupervised way by exploiting structure from motion. Instead of directly learning a policy from raw images, the agent first learns to detect and segment moving objects by exploiting flow information in video sequences. The learned representation is then used to focus the policy of the agent on the moving objects. Over time, the agent identifies which objects are critical for decision making and gradually builds a policy based on relevant moving objects. This approach, which we call Motion-Oriented REinforcement Learning (MOREL), is demonstrated on a suite of Atari games where the ability to detect moving objects reduces the amount of interaction needed with the environment to obtain a good policy. Furthermore, the resulting policy is more interpretable than policies that directly map images to actions or values with a black box neural network. We can gain insight into the policy by inspecting the segmentation and motion of each object detected by the agent. This allows practitioners to confirm whether a policy is making decisions based on sensible information. Our code is available at https://github.com/vik-goel/MOREL.
