paragraphs: Motion-Oriented Reinforcement Learning, or MOREL, gives an agent a representation of moving objects before it learns how to act from visual observations. The method detects and segments objects without supervision by using motion structure and flow information in video. Those object representations then guide the policy's attention during action selection.

As learning proceeds, the agent identifies which moving objects matter for decisions and gradually builds a policy around them. This separates the discovery of useful visual structure from the task of choosing actions. The approach makes moving objects an explicit part of the information the policy uses.

Experiments on a suite of Atari games show that detecting moving objects reduces the environmental interaction needed to obtain a good policy. The resulting policies are also more interpretable than direct black-box mappings from images to actions or values. Inspecting each detected object's segmentation and motion gives practitioners a way to examine whether the policy relies on sensible information. The reported benefits therefore include both learning efficiency and visibility into the policy's visual basis.
summary.tldr: MOREL learns moving-object representations from video to reduce reinforcement-learning interaction needs and make visual policies easier to inspect.

title: Unsupervised Video Object Segmentation for Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of learning probabilistic logical rules for inductive and interpretable link prediction. Despite the importance of inductive link prediction, most previous works focused on transductive link prediction and cannot manage previously unseen entities. Moreover, they are black-box models that are not easily explainable for humans. We propose DRUM, a scalable and differentiable approach for mining first-order logical rules from knowledge graphs that resolves these problems. We motivate our method by making a connection between learning confidence scores for each rule and low-rank tensor approximation. DRUM uses bidirectional RNNs to share useful information across the tasks of learning rules for different relations. We also empirically demonstrate the efficiency of DRUM over existing rule mining methods for inductive link prediction on a variety of benchmark datasets.

Despite the importance of inductive link prediction, most previous works focused on transductive link prediction and cannot manage previously unseen entities. Moreover, they are black-box models that are not easily explainable for humans. We propose DRUM, a scalable and differentiable approach for mining first-order logical rules from knowledge graphs that resolves these problems. We motivate our method by making a connection between learning confidence scores for each rule and low-rank tensor approximation. paragraphs: Predicting missing links in a knowledge graph becomes especially challenging when predictions involve entities absent during training. The paper targets this inductive setting while also seeking explanations people can understand. It contrasts that goal with approaches built around already observed entities and representations whose predictions are difficult to explain.

DRUM learns probabilistic first-order logical rules from the graph through a scalable, differentiable procedure. The rules provide an interpretable basis for link prediction, with confidence scores expressing how strongly they are supported. The method is motivated by a connection between learning those scores and low-rank tensor approximation. Bidirectional recurrent neural networks share useful information between the tasks of learning rules for different relations.

This shared learning structure lets the approach connect relation-specific rule discovery within one framework. The authors report empirical efficiency advantages over existing rule-mining methods for inductive link prediction across several benchmark datasets. The contribution brings together rule-based interpretability, support for previously unseen entities, and differentiable learning, showing how logical prediction rules can be learned with information shared across relations.
summary.tldr: DRUM learns interpretable probabilistic rules for predicting knowledge-graph links involving previously unseen entities.

title: DRUM: End-To-End Differentiable Rule Mining On Knowledge Graphs

abstract: We augment recurrent neural networks with an external memory mechanism that builds upon recent progress in metalearning. We conceptualize this memory as a rapidly adaptable function that we parameterize as a deep neural network. Reading from the neural memory function amounts to pushing an input (the key vector) through the function to produce an output (the value vector). Writing to memory means changing the function; specifically, updating the parameters of the neural network to encode desired information. We leverage training and algorithmic techniques from metalearning to update the neural memory function in one shot. The proposed memory-augmented model achieves strong performance on a variety of learning problems, from supervised question answering to reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: This paper augments recurrent neural networks with an external memory represented by another deep neural network. The memory is conceived as a function that can adapt quickly. Its stored information is expressed through the function’s parameters, making changes to that function the central operation for recording new information.

Reading and writing have concrete meanings in this design. To read, the model passes a key vector through the memory network and receives a value vector. To write, it updates the memory network’s parameters so that the desired information is encoded. The authors use training and algorithmic techniques from metalearning to make this neural memory update possible in one shot.

The resulting memory-augmented model achieves strong performance across learning problems ranging from supervised question answering to reinforcement learning. These results support the usefulness of rapidly adaptable functions as external memory mechanisms. The conceptual contribution is to connect memory access with neural function evaluation and memory storage with learned parameter adaptation, bringing metalearning directly into how a recurrent model retains information.
summary.tldr: A metalearned neural network serves as external memory, reading through function evaluation and writing through rapid parameter updates.

title: Metalearned Neural Memory

abstract: The problem of adversarial robustness has been studied extensively for neural networks. However, for boosted decision trees and decision stumps there are almost no results, even though they are widely used in practice (e.g. XGBoost) due to their accuracy, interpretability, and efficiency. We show in this paper that for boosted decision stumps the \textit{exact} min-max robust loss and test error for an $l_\infty$-attack can be computed in $O(T\log T)$ time per input, where $T$ is the number of decision stumps and the optimal update step of the ensemble can be done in $O(n^2\,T\log T)$, where $n$ is the number of data points. For boosted trees we show how to efficiently calculate and optimize an upper bound on the robust loss, which leads to state-of-the-art robust test error for boosted trees on MNIST (12.5\% for $\epsilon_\infty=0.3$), FMNIST (23.2\% for $\epsilon_\infty=0.1$), and CIFAR-10 (74.7\% for $\epsilon_\infty=8/255$). Moreover, the robust test error rates we achieve are competitive to the ones of provably robust convolutional networks. The code of all our experiments is available at \url{http://github.com/max-andr/provably-robust-boosting}.

paragraphs: This paper develops adversarial robustness methods for boosted decision stumps and trees. It considers attacks bounded in the l-infinity norm, which constrain the change to each input coordinate. The goal is to evaluate and train models against worst-case allowed changes, extending formal robustness analysis to model families widely used for their accuracy, interpretability, and efficiency.

For an ensemble of T decision stumps, the authors show that the exact worst-case robust loss and test error can be computed in O(T log T) time per input. They also compute an optimal ensemble update in O(n² T log T), where n is the number of data points. For boosted trees, the method instead efficiently calculates and optimizes an upper bound on robust loss.

The tree method achieves reported state-of-the-art robust test errors of 12.5% on MNIST at radius 0.3, 23.2% on FMNIST at 0.1, and 74.7% on CIFAR-10 at 8/255. The authors describe these rates as competitive with provably robust convolutional networks. The distinction between exact calculations for stumps and upper bounds for trees is central to understanding the guarantees.
summary.tldr: Efficient exact robustness calculations for boosted stumps and robust-loss bounds for boosted trees enable provably robust boosting methods.

title: Provably robust boosted decision stumps and trees against adversarial attacks

abstract: Recent results in the literature indicate that a residual network (ResNet) composed of a single residual block outperforms linear predictors, in the sense that all local minima in its optimization landscape are at least as good as the best linear predictor. However, these results are limited to a single residual block (i.e., shallow ResNets), instead of the deep ResNets composed of multiple residual blocks. We take a step towards extending this result to deep ResNets. We start by two motivating examples. First, we show that there exist datasets for which all local minima of a fully-connected ReLU network are no better than the best linear predictor, whereas a ResNet has strictly better local minima. Second, we show that even at the global minimum, the representation obtained from the residual block outputs of a 2-block ResNet do not necessarily improve monotonically over subsequent blocks, which highlights a fundamental difficulty in analyzing deep ResNets. Our main theorem on deep ResNets shows under simple geometric conditions that, any critical point in the optimization landscape is either (i) at least as good as the best linear predictor; or (ii) the Hessian at this critical point has a strictly negative eigenvalue. Notably, our theorem shows that a chain of multiple skip-connections can improve the optimization landscape, whereas existing results study direct skip-connections to the last hidden layer or output layer. Finally, we complement our results by showing benign properties of the "near-identity regions" of deep ResNets, showing depth-independent upper bounds for the risk attained at critical points as well as the Rademacher complexity.
originalAbstract: Recent results in the literature indicate that a residual network (ResNet) composed of a single residual block outperforms linear predictors, in the sense that all local minima in its optimization landscape are at least as good as the best linear predictor. However, these results are limited to a single residual block (i.e., shallow ResNets), instead of the deep ResNets composed of multiple residual blocks. We take a step towards extending this result to deep ResNets. We start by two motivating examples. First, we show that there exist datasets for which all local minima of a fully-connected ReLU network are no better than the best linear predictor, whereas a ResNet has strictly better local minima. Second, we show that even at the global minimum, the representation obtained from the residual block outputs of a 2-block ResNet do not necessarily improve monotonically over subsequent blocks, which highlights a fundamental difficulty in analyzing deep ResNets. Our main theorem on deep ResNets shows under simple geometric conditions that, any critical point in the optimization landscape is either (i) at least as good as the best linear predictor; or (ii) the Hessian at this critical point has a strictly negative eigenvalue. Notably, our theorem shows that a chain of multiple skip-connections can improve the optimization landscape, whereas existing results study direct skip-connections to the last hidden layer or output layer. Finally, we complement our results by showing benign properties of the "near-identity regions" of deep ResNets, showing depth-independent upper bounds for the risk attained at critical points as well as the Rademacher complexity.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether guarantees comparing shallow residual networks with linear predictors extend to networks with multiple residual blocks. It first gives examples showing both the promise and difficulty of that extension. A ResNet can have strictly better local minima than a fully connected ReLU network on some datasets, yet successive residual blocks need not produce monotonically improving representations, even at a global optimum.

The main theorem establishes a conditional guarantee for deep ResNets. Under specified geometric conditions, every critical point either performs at least as well as the best linear predictor or has a Hessian with a strictly negative eigenvalue. The latter identifies a direction of negative curvature, distinguishing such a point from an ordinary local minimum.

The result explains how a chain of skip connections can improve the optimization landscape. It does not assert that every deep ResNet strictly outperforms linear prediction. The authors also analyze regions where residual transformations are near the identity, obtaining depth-independent upper bounds on critical-point risk and Rademacher complexity.
summary.tldr: Under geometric conditions, deep ResNet critical points either match the best linear predictor or possess a direction of negative curvature.

title: Are deep ResNets provably better than linear predictors?

abstract: We propose a practical inexact augmented Lagrangian method (iALM) for nonconvex problems with nonlinear constraints. We characterize the total computational complexity of our method subject to a verifiable geometric condition, which is closely related to the Polyak-Lojasiewicz and Mangasarian-Fromowitz conditions. In particular, when a first-order solver is used for the inner iterates, we prove that iALM finds a first-order stationary point with $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/\epsilon^3)$ calls to the first-order oracle. {If, in addition, the problem is smooth and} a second-order solver is used for the inner iterates, iALM finds a second-order stationary point with $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/\epsilon^5)$ calls to the second-order oracle. These complexity results match the known theoretical results in the literature. We also provide strong numerical evidence on large-scale machine learning problems, including the Burer-Monteiro factorization of semidefinite programs, and a novel nonconvex relaxation of the standard basis pursuit template. For these examples, we also show how to verify our geometric condition.

These bounds match known theoretical results, while the numerical evidence addresses large-scale machine learning problems. Examples include Burer–Monteiro factorizations of semidefinite programs and a new nonconvex relaxation of basis pursuit. The authors also show how to check the geometric condition for these examples, connecting the assumptions behind the analysis to the problems used to demonstrate the method.
summary.tldr: An inexact augmented Lagrangian framework matches known stationarity complexity bounds under a verifiable geometric condition and shows strong numerical results.

title: An Inexact Augmented Lagrangian Framework for Nonconvex Optimization with Nonlinear Constraints

abstract: We propose a novel, conceptually simple and general framework for instance segmentation on 3D point clouds. Our method, called 3D-BoNet, follows the simple design philosophy of per-point multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). The framework directly regresses 3D bounding boxes for all instances in a point cloud, while simultaneously predicting a point-level mask for each instance. It consists of a backbone network followed by two parallel network branches for 1) bounding box regression and 2) point mask prediction. 3D-BoNet is single-stage, anchor-free and end-to-end trainable. Moreover, it is remarkably computationally efficient as, unlike existing approaches, it does not require any post-processing steps such as non-maximum suppression, feature sampling, clustering or voting. Extensive experiments show that our approach surpasses existing work on both ScanNet and S3DIS datasets while being approximately 10x more computationally efficient. Comprehensive ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of our design.

paragraphs: Instance segmentation on a 3D point cloud requires distinguishing individual objects and assigning points to them. The proposed 3D-BoNet framework tackles both object extent and point membership directly. It predicts a three-dimensional bounding box for every instance while also producing a point-level mask for each instance.

The architecture follows a design based on per-point multilayer perceptrons. A shared backbone feeds two parallel branches: one regresses bounding boxes, and the other predicts masks. The system is single-stage, uses no anchors, and can be trained end to end. It also avoids post-processing operations such as non-maximum suppression, feature sampling, clustering, and voting.

Experiments on ScanNet and S3DIS show that 3D-BoNet surpasses the existing work considered while being approximately ten times more computationally efficient. Ablation studies additionally support the effectiveness of its design. These findings show that directly learning boxes and masks together can provide an effective and computationally economical framework for the evaluated point-cloud segmentation tasks.
summary.tldr: 3D-BoNet jointly predicts object boxes and point masks, surpassing compared methods on two datasets with approximately tenfold computational efficiency.

title: Learning Object Bounding Boxes for 3D Instance Segmentation on Point Clouds

abstract: Learning to optimize has emerged as a powerful framework for various optimization and machine learning tasks. Current such "meta-optimizers" often learn in the space of continuous optimization algorithms that are point-based and uncertainty-unaware. To overcome the limitations, we propose a meta-optimizer that learns in the algorithmic space of both point-based and population-based optimization algorithms. The meta-optimizer targets at a meta-loss function consisting of both cumulative regret and entropy. Specifically, we learn and interpret the update formula through a population of LSTMs embedded with sample- and feature-level attentions. Meanwhile, we estimate the posterior directly over the global optimum and use an uncertainty measure to help guide the learning process. Empirical results over non-convex test functions and the protein-docking application demonstrate that this new meta-optimizer outperforms existing competitors. The codes are publicly available at: https://github.com/Shen-Lab/LOIS

paragraphs: Learning to optimize treats an optimization procedure itself as something that can be trained. This paper expands that idea beyond methods organized around individual search points and without explicit uncertainty awareness. Its meta-optimizer learns within an algorithmic space that includes both point-based and population-based approaches, allowing a group of candidate solutions to inform the search.

The update rule is represented through a population of LSTM networks equipped with attention across samples and features. Training uses a meta-loss containing cumulative regret and entropy. The method also estimates a posterior distribution directly over the global optimum and uses an uncertainty measure to guide learning, making uncertainty part of the optimization process.

Experiments on non-convex test functions and a protein-docking application show the proposed meta-optimizer outperforming the competitors considered. These findings support combining learned update rules, population information, and uncertainty estimates in the evaluated tasks. The contribution is an expanded framework for learning how to search, with attention and posterior estimation supplying information beyond a single candidate's position.
summary.tldr: A learned swarm optimizer combines attention-equipped LSTMs with uncertainty over the global optimum and outperforms tested competitors.

title: Learning to Optimize in Swarms

abstract: Learning with sparse rewards remains a significant challenge in reinforcement learning (RL), especially when the aim is to train a policy capable of achieving multiple different goals. To date, the most successful approaches for dealing with multi-goal, sparse reward environments have been model-free RL algorithms. In this work we propose PlanGAN, a model-based algorithm specifically designed for solving multi-goal tasks in environments with sparse rewards. Our method builds on the fact that any trajectory of experience collected by an agent contains useful information about how to achieve the goals observed during that trajectory. We use this to train an ensemble of conditional generative models (GANs) to generate plausible trajectories that lead the agent from its current state towards a specified goal. We then combine these imagined trajectories into a novel planning algorithm in order to achieve the desired goal as efficiently as possible. The performance of PlanGAN has been tested on a number of robotic navigation/manipulation tasks in comparison with a range of model-free reinforcement learning baselines, including Hindsight Experience Replay. Our studies indicate that PlanGAN can achieve comparable performance whilst being around 4-8 times more sample efficient.

paragraphs: Sparse rewards give a learning agent little direct feedback, especially when it must learn to reach several different goals. PlanGAN addresses this with a model-based approach to planning. Its starting observation is that a collected trajectory still teaches the agent how to reach the goals encountered along that trajectory, even when reward feedback is limited.

The method trains an ensemble of conditional generative adversarial models to produce plausible trajectories from the agent's current state toward a specified goal. A planning algorithm then combines these imagined trajectories to select behavior aimed at reaching that goal efficiently. The learned models therefore supply possible paths through experience that the planner can use.

The authors evaluate PlanGAN on robotic navigation and manipulation tasks against several model-free reinforcement learning baselines, including Hindsight Experience Replay. Their studies indicate comparable performance with roughly four to eight times greater sample efficiency. The result suggests that generating goal-directed trajectories can make collected experience more useful for planning in the evaluated sparse-reward settings.
summary.tldr: PlanGAN plans with generated goal-directed trajectories, achieving comparable reported performance with roughly four to eight times greater sample efficiency.

title: PlanGAN: Model-based Planning With Sparse Rewards and Multiple Goals

abstract: In this paper, we develop a simple and fast online algorithm for solving a class of binary integer linear programs (LPs) arisen in the general resource allocation problem. The algorithm requires only one single pass through the input data and is free of doing any matrix inversion. It can be viewed as both an approximate algorithm for solving binary integer LPs and a fast algorithm for solving online LP problems. The algorithm is inspired by an equivalent form of the dual problem of the relaxed LP and it essentially performs (one-pass) projected stochastic subgradient descent in the dual space. We analyze the algorithm under two different models, stochastic input and random permutation, with minimal technical assumptions on the input data. The algorithm achieves $O\left(m \sqrt{n}\right)$ expected regret under the stochastic input model and $O\left((m+\log n)\sqrt{n}\right)$ expected regret under the random permutation model, and it achieves $O(m \sqrt{n})$ expected constraint violation under both models, where $n$ is the number of decision variables and $m$ is the number of constraints. In addition, we employ the notion of permutational Rademacher complexity and derive regret bounds for two earlier online LP algorithms for comparison. Both algorithms improve the regret bound with a factor of $\sqrt{m}$ by paying more computational cost. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to convert the possibly infeasible solution to a feasible one through a randomized procedure. Numerical experiments illustrate the general applicability and effectiveness of the algorithms.

The paper also analyzes two earlier online algorithms, finding improved regret dependence by a factor of √m at greater computational cost. Numerical experiments demonstrate applicability and effectiveness, highlighting the tradeoff between a particularly cheap single pass and stronger regret bounds.
summary.tldr: A single-pass dual optimization algorithm provides fast resource allocation with regret and constraint-violation bounds under two input models.

title: Simple and Fast Algorithm for Binary Integer and Online Linear Programming

abstract: We introduce Data Diversification: a simple but effective strategy to boost neural machine translation (NMT) performance. It diversifies the training data by using the predictions of multiple forward and backward models and then merging them with the original dataset on which the final NMT model is trained. Our method is applicable to all NMT models. It does not require extra monolingual data like back-translation, nor does it add more computations and parameters like ensembles of models. Our method achieves state-of-the-art BLEU scores of 30.7 and 43.7 in the WMT'14 English-German and English-French translation tasks, respectively. It also substantially improves on 8 other translation tasks: 4 IWSLT tasks (English-German and English-French) and 4 low-resource translation tasks (English-Nepali and English-Sinhala). We demonstrate that our method is more effective than knowledge distillation and dual learning, it exhibits strong correlation with ensembles of models, and it trades perplexity off for better BLEU score.

paragraphs: Data Diversification improves neural machine translation by changing the training data available to the final model. Multiple models translating in forward and backward directions generate predictions, which are combined with the original dataset. A final translation model then learns from this expanded collection of translation examples.

The approach is presented as applicable to all neural machine translation models. It does not require the additional monolingual data used by back-translation, and the final model avoids the extra parameters and computation associated with running an ensemble. The multiple models contribute through preparation of the training data, allowing their predictions to influence a single final translator.

The authors report BLEU scores of 30.7 and 43.7 on the WMT'14 English–German and English–French tasks, described as state of the art. They also report substantial gains on eight other tasks, including low-resource translation. Their comparisons favor diversification over knowledge distillation and dual learning. A reported tradeoff between perplexity and BLEU shows that improving translation scores need not coincide with improving the model's probabilistic fit.
summary.tldr: Training on original data combined with predictions from multiple translation models improves translation quality without requiring an ensemble at inference.

title: Data Diversification: A Simple Strategy For Neural Machine Translation

abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (RL) has shown great potential in various control tasks in terms of both sample-efficiency and final performance. However, learning a generalizable dynamics model robust to changes in dynamics remains a challenge since the target transition dynamics follow a multi-modal distribution. In this paper, we present a new model-based RL algorithm, coined trajectory-wise multiple choice learning, that learns a multi-headed dynamics model for dynamics generalization. The main idea is updating the most accurate prediction head to specialize each head in certain environments with similar dynamics, i.e., clustering environments. Moreover, we incorporate context learning, which encodes dynamics-specific information from past experiences into the context latent vector, enabling the model to perform online adaptation to unseen environments. Finally, to utilize the specialized prediction heads more effectively, we propose an adaptive planning method, which selects the most accurate prediction head over a recent experience. Our method exhibits superior zero-shot generalization performance across a variety of control tasks, compared to state-of-the-art RL methods. Source code and videos are available at https://sites.google.com/view/trajectory-mcl.

paragraphs: A dynamics model trained for one environment may fail when the transition behavior changes. This paper treats that variation as multimodal and introduces trajectory-wise multiple choice learning, a model-based reinforcement-learning method with several prediction heads.

Training updates the head that predicts a trajectory most accurately, encouraging different heads to specialize in environments with similar dynamics. A learned context vector summarizes dynamics-specific information from past experience, allowing online adaptation to unseen environments. During planning, the system selects the head that best predicts recent experience.

Evaluations across multiple control tasks show stronger zero-shot generalization than state-of-the-art reinforcement-learning comparisons. The abstract does not supply task names or numerical gains. Its contribution is the combination of dynamics specialization, contextual adaptation, and adaptive planning; the reported generalization does not imply accurate prediction under every possible change in environment dynamics.
summary.tldr: Specialized dynamics heads and context adaptation improve model-based control under changing dynamics.

title: Trajectory-wise Multiple Choice Learning for Dynamics Generalization in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Geometric methods rely on tensors that can be encoded using a symbolic formula and data arrays, such as kernel and distance matrices. We present an extension for standard machine learning frameworks that provides comprehensive support for this abstraction on CPUs and GPUs: our toolbox combines a versatile, transparent user interface with fast runtimes and low memory usage. Unlike general purpose acceleration frameworks such as XLA, our library turns generic Python code into binaries whose performances are competitive with state-of-the-art geometric libraries - such as FAISS for nearest neighbor search - with the added benefit of flexibility. We perform an extensive evaluation on a broad class of problems: Gaussian modelling, K-nearest neighbors search, geometric deep learning, non-Euclidean embeddings and optimal transport theory. In practice, for geometric problems that involve 1k to 1M samples in dimension 1 to 100, our library speeds up baseline GPU implementations by up to two orders of magnitude.

paragraphs: Many geometric learning computations use matrices whose entries are determined by a formula and input data, such as distances between points or kernel values. This paper builds a toolbox around that symbolic representation. It extends standard machine learning frameworks with support for these computations on both CPUs and GPUs, emphasizing fast execution and low memory use.

The interface turns generic Python code into compiled binaries while retaining flexibility across geometric operations. The authors report performance competitive with specialized geometric libraries, including FAISS for nearest-neighbor search. The significance is that a common programming abstraction can support varied computations without giving up the speed associated with tools built for particular tasks.

The evaluation covers Gaussian modeling, nearest-neighbor search, geometric deep learning, non-Euclidean embeddings, and optimal transport. For the tested geometric problems involving one thousand to one million samples and dimensions from one to one hundred, speedups over baseline GPU implementations reach two orders of magnitude. That is a reported maximum within the evaluated range, rather than a uniform improvement for every workload.
summary.tldr: A symbolic-matrix toolbox makes varied geometric computations fast and memory-efficient, with reported GPU speedups reaching two orders of magnitude.

title: Fast geometric learning with symbolic matrices

abstract: We develop a distributed second order optimization algorithm that is communication-efficient as well as robust against Byzantine failures of the worker machines. We propose an iterative approximate Newton-type algorithm, where the worker machines communicate \emph{only once} per iteration with the central machine. This is in sharp contrast with the state-of-the-art distributed second order algorithms like GIANT \cite{giant}, DINGO\cite{dingo}, where the worker machines send (functions of) local gradient and Hessian sequentially; thus ending up communicating twice with the central machine per iteration. Furthermore, we employ a simple norm based thresholding rule to filter-out the Byzantine worker machines. We establish the linear-quadratic rate of convergence of our proposed algorithm and establish that the communication savings and Byzantine resilience attributes only correspond to a small statistical error rate for arbitrary convex loss functions. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that addresses the issue of Byzantine resilience in second order distributed optimization. Furthermore, we validate our theoretical results with extensive experiments on synthetically generated and benchmark LIBSVM \cite{libsvm} data-set and demonstrate convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Distributed second-order optimization uses information from worker machines to update a model at a central machine. Communication can become a significant part of that process, and Byzantine worker failures introduce unreliable contributions. This paper develops an approximate Newton-type algorithm that addresses communication efficiency and resilience to those failures together.

Workers communicate with the central machine only once per iteration. The compared methods, GIANT and DINGO, require two sequential communications involving local gradient and Hessian information. The proposed algorithm also uses a simple threshold based on norms to filter Byzantine workers, incorporating a robustness mechanism into the distributed optimization procedure.

The authors establish a linear-quadratic convergence rate and show that communication savings and Byzantine resilience incur only a small statistical error rate for arbitrary convex loss functions. Experiments on synthetic data and a benchmark LIBSVM dataset support the theoretical analysis. The contribution demonstrates that reducing communication and handling faulty workers can be combined within a second-order method while retaining the stated convergence behavior and statistical accuracy.
summary.tldr: An approximate distributed Newton method combines one communication per iteration with Byzantine-worker filtering and theoretical convergence guarantees.

title: Distributed Newton Can Communicate Less and Resist Byzantine Workers

abstract: Second-order information, in the form of Hessian- or Inverse-Hessian-vector products, is a fundamental tool for solving optimization problems. Recently, there has been significant interest in utilizing this information in the context of deep neural networks; however, relatively little is known about the quality of existing approximations in this context. Our work considers this question, examines the accuracy of existing approaches, and proposes a method called WoodFisher to compute a faithful and efficient estimate of the inverse Hessian. Our main application is to neural network compression, where we build on the classic Optimal Brain Damage/Surgeon framework. We demonstrate that WoodFisher significantly outperforms popular state-of-the-art methods for one-shot pruning. Further, even when iterative, gradual pruning is allowed, our method results in a gain in test accuracy over the state-of-the-art approaches for popular image classification datasets such as ImageNet ILSVRC. Further, we show how our method can be extended to take into account first-order information, and illustrate its ability to automatically set layer-wise pruning thresholds, or perform compression in the limited-data regime.

This paper examines their quality and introduces WoodFisher as a faithful, efficient estimate of the inverse Hessian.

The compression method builds on the Optimal Brain Damage and Optimal Brain Surgeon framework. It uses the curvature approximation to guide pruning, and the authors also extend the approach to incorporate first-order information. Additional capabilities include choosing layer-specific pruning thresholds and operating with limited data.

WoodFisher substantially outperforms popular alternatives for one-shot pruning. It also improves test accuracy over state-of-the-art approaches when iterative gradual pruning is allowed, including on ImageNet ILSVRC. The abstract does not give sparsity levels or exact accuracy gains, so the comparative findings should be understood within the evaluated compression configurations rather than as an unconditional pruning guarantee.
summary.tldr: WoodFisher uses an efficient inverse-Hessian estimate to guide neural-network pruning.

title: WoodFisher: Efficient Second-Order Approximation for Neural Network Compression

abstract: Adapting large-scale pretrained language models to downstream tasks via fine-tuning is the standard method for achieving state-of-the-art performance on NLP benchmarks. However, fine-tuning all weights of models with millions or billions of parameters is sample-inefficient, unstable in low-resource settings, and wasteful as it requires storing a separate copy of the model for each task. Recent work has developed parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, but these approaches either still require a relatively large number of parameters or underperform standard fine-tuning. In this work, we propose Compacter, a method for fine-tuning large-scale language models with a better trade-off between task performance and the number of trainable parameters than prior work. Compacter accomplishes this by building on top of ideas from adapters, low-rank optimization, and parameterized hypercomplex multiplication layers.Specifically, Compacter inserts task-specific weight matrices into a pretrained model's weights, which are computed efficiently as a sum of Kronecker products between shared ``slow'' weights and ``fast'' rank-one matrices defined per Compacter layer. By only training 0.047% of a pretrained model's parameters, Compacter performs on par with standard fine-tuning on GLUE and outperforms standard fine-tuning on SuperGLUE and low-resource settings. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/rabeehk/compacter.

The abstract also identifies instability and poor sample efficiency when training data are scarce. Compacter addresses these costs by adding compact, task-specific weight structures to the pretrained model.

They also report better performance on SuperGLUE and in low-resource settings. summary.tldr: Compacter uses compact structured adapters to match or exceed standard fine-tuning in reported evaluations while training just 0.047% of model parameters.

title: Compacter: Efficient Low-Rank Hypercomplex Adapter Layers

abstract: We study the model-based reward-free reinforcement learning with linear function approximation for episodic Markov decision processes (MDPs). In this setting, the agent works in two phases. In the exploration phase, the agent interacts with the environment and collects samples without the reward. In the planning phase, the agent is given a specific reward function and uses samples collected from the exploration phase to learn a good policy. We propose a new provably efficient algorithm, called UCRL-RFE under the Linear Mixture MDP assumption, where the transition probability kernel of the MDP can be parameterized by a linear function over certain feature mappings defined on the triplet of state, action, and next state. We show that to obtain an $\epsilon$-optimal policy for arbitrary reward function, UCRL-RFE needs to sample at most $\tilde O(H^5d^2\epsilon^{-2})$ episodes during the exploration phase. Here, $H$ is the length of the episode, $d$ is the dimension of the feature mapping. We also propose a variant of UCRL-RFE using Bernstein-type bonus and show that it needs to sample at most $\tilde O(H^4d(H + d)\epsilon^{-2})$ to achieve an $\epsilon$-optimal policy. By constructing a special class of linear Mixture MDPs, we also prove that for any reward-free algorithm, it needs to sample at least $\tilde \Omega(H^2d\epsilon^{-2})$ episodes to obtain an $\epsilon$-optimal policy. Our upper bound matches the lower bound in terms of the dependence on $\epsilon$ and the dependence on $d$ if $H \ge d$.

These results characterize part of the exploration cost under the stated transition-model assumption without claiming that every dependence is optimal.
summary.tldr: UCRL-RFE provides sample-efficiency guarantees for exploring linear-mixture environments before a reward function is specified.

title: Reward-Free Model-Based Reinforcement Learning with Linear Function Approximation

abstract: Massive deployment of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in high-stake applications generates a strong demand for explanations that are robust to noise and align well with human intuition. Most existing methods generate explanations by identifying a subgraph of an input graph that has a strong correlation with the prediction. These explanations are not robust to noise because independently optimizing the correlation for a single input can easily overfit noise. Moreover, they are not counterfactual because removing an identified subgraph from an input graph does not necessarily change the prediction result. In this paper, we propose a novel method to generate robust counterfactual explanations on GNNs by explicitly modelling the common decision logic of GNNs on similar input graphs. Our explanations are naturally robust to noise because they are produced from the common decision boundaries of a GNN that govern the predictions of many similar input graphs. The explanations are also counterfactual because removing the set of edges identified by an explanation from the input graph changes the prediction significantly. Exhaustive experiments on many public datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our method.

paragraphs: Many graph-neural-network explanations identify a subgraph that is strongly associated with a prediction. It seeks explanations that are both resistant to noise and counterfactual in their effect on the model.

The proposed method models decision logic shared across similar input graphs. Its explanations draw on common decision boundaries governing many predictions, rather than an independently optimized correlation for one graph. Each explanation identifies edges whose removal significantly changes the prediction. This connects the highlighted graph structure to a concrete intervention on the model's input.

The authors attribute the explanations' noise robustness to their grounding in shared decision boundaries. They report superior performance through extensive experiments on public datasets. The contribution brings together two goals: identifying a meaningful change to a particular prediction and using behavior across similar graphs to avoid explanations driven by noise in that single example.
summary.tldr: The method explains graph-network predictions through edge removals derived from decision logic shared across similar graphs.

title: Robust Counterfactual Explanations on Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Recently, transformation-based self-supervised learning has been applied to generative adversarial networks (GANs) to mitigate catastrophic forgetting in the discriminator by introducing a stationary learning environment. However, the separate self-supervised tasks in existing self-supervised GANs cause a goal inconsistent with generative modeling due to the fact that their self-supervised classifiers are agnostic to the generator distribution. To address this problem, we propose a novel self-supervised GAN that unifies the GAN task with the self-supervised task by augmenting the GAN labels (real or fake) via self-supervision of data transformation. Specifically, the original discriminator and self-supervised classifier are unified into a label-augmented discriminator that predicts the augmented labels to be aware of both the generator distribution and the data distribution under every transformation, and then provide the discrepancy between them to optimize the generator. Theoretically, we prove that the optimal generator could converge to replicate the real data distribution. Empirically, we show that the proposed method significantly outperforms previous self-supervised and data augmentation GANs on both generative modeling and representation learning across benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Self-supervised tasks can help a GAN discriminator avoid forgetting, but a separate transformation-prediction task may not align with the generator's goal. This paper attributes that mismatch to self-supervised classifiers that do not account for the generator's distribution. It proposes making transformation learning part of the real-versus-fake discrimination task itself.

The method augments GAN labels with information about data transformations. A single label-augmented discriminator replaces the separate discriminator and self-supervised classifier. It considers both generated and real distributions under each transformation, then supplies their discrepancy as a signal for optimizing the generator. This makes the additional supervision directly relevant to distinguishing generated samples from real data.

The theoretical result shows that the optimal generator could converge to reproduce the real data distribution. That is a statement about the formulation's possible optimum, rather than a guarantee for every training run. Empirically, the method significantly outperforms previous self-supervised and data-augmentation GANs on generative modeling and representation learning benchmarks. The results support integrating the auxiliary task with the adversarial objective.
summary.tldr: Augmenting real/fake labels with transformation information aligns GAN self-supervision with generation and improves reported modeling and representation results.

title: Self-Supervised GANs with Label Augmentation

abstract: Many representative graph neural networks, $e.g.$, GPR-GNN and ChebNet, approximate graph convolutions with graph spectral filters. However, existing work either applies predefined filter weights or learns them without necessary constraints, which may lead to oversimplified or ill-posed filters. To overcome these issues, we propose $\textit{BernNet}$, a novel graph neural network with theoretical support that provides a simple but effective scheme for designing and learning arbitrary graph spectral filters. In particular, for any filter over the normalized Laplacian spectrum of a graph, our BernNet estimates it by an order-$K$ Bernstein polynomial approximation and designs its spectral property by setting the coefficients of the Bernstein basis. Moreover, we can learn the coefficients (and the corresponding filter weights) based on observed graphs and their associated signals and thus achieve the BernNet specialized for the data. Our experiments demonstrate that BernNet can learn arbitrary spectral filters, including complicated band-rejection and comb filters, and it achieves superior performance in real-world graph modeling tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/ivam-he/BernNet.

paragraphs: Graph spectral filters control how a graph neural network processes different components of signals on a graph. Existing approaches can be restrictive when their filter weights are fixed, or produce poorly formed filters when weights are learned without suitable constraints. BernNet introduces a theoretically supported way to design and learn more flexible filters.

Its central tool is an order-K Bernstein polynomial approximation over the spectrum of the normalized graph Laplacian. The coefficients of the Bernstein basis determine the filter's spectral behavior. They can be set to design a desired response or learned from observed graphs and their associated signals, adapting the filter to the data.

Experiments show that BernNet can learn complicated filter shapes, including band-rejection and comb filters, and report superior performance on real-world graph modeling tasks. The contribution is a common framework for deliberate filter design and data-driven learning. Its ability to represent arbitrary filters is expressed through polynomial approximation, rather than a claim that every filter is reproduced exactly at any fixed order.
summary.tldr: BernNet uses Bernstein polynomial approximations to design or learn flexible graph spectral filters, including complex responses demonstrated experimentally.

title: BernNet: Learning Arbitrary Graph Spectral Filters via Bernstein Approximation

abstract: 3D point cloud data is increasingly used in safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving. Thus, the robustness of 3D deep learning models against adversarial attacks becomes a major consideration. In this paper, we systematically study the impact of various self-supervised learning proxy tasks on different architectures and threat models for 3D point clouds with adversarial training. Specifically, we study MLP-based (PointNet), convolution-based (DGCNN), and transformer-based (PCT) 3D architectures. Through extensive experimentation, we demonstrate that appropriate applications of self-supervision can significantly enhance the robustness in 3D point cloud recognition, achieving considerable improvements compared to the standard adversarial training baseline. Our analysis reveals that local feature learning is desirable for adversarial robustness in point clouds since it limits the adversarial propagation between the point-level input perturbations and the model's final output. This insight also explains the success of DGCNN and the jigsaw proxy task in achieving stronger 3D adversarial robustness.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether self-supervised learning can strengthen adversarially trained systems that recognize 3D point clouds. Robustness matters for applications such as autonomous driving, where altered input points can affect recognition. The study examines how auxiliary learning tasks interact with the architecture and the type of adversarial threat.

The experiments cover PointNet, DGCNN, and PCT, representing multilayer-perceptron, convolutional, and transformer approaches. Rather than treating self-supervision as uniformly beneficial, the authors study different proxy tasks and their applications. They find that appropriate choices substantially improve robustness compared with standard adversarial training in the evaluated settings.

Their analysis points to learning local features as a useful ingredient. Local processing can limit how perturbations at individual input points propagate toward the final prediction. This explanation also helps account for the stronger robustness obtained with DGCNN and the jigsaw proxy task. The findings therefore offer both an empirical improvement and an explanation for why particular combinations of architecture and self-supervision work well.
summary.tldr: Appropriately chosen self-supervised tasks improve adversarially trained point-cloud recognition, with local feature learning helping limit perturbation propagation.

title: Adversarially Robust 3D Point Cloud Recognition Using Self-Supervisions

abstract: This paper is on video recognition using Transformers. Very recent attempts in this area have demonstrated promising results in terms of recognition accuracy, yet they have been also shown to induce, in many cases, significant computational overheads due to the additional modelling of the temporal information. In this work, we propose a Video Transformer model the complexity of which scales linearly with the number of frames in the video sequence and hence induces no overhead compared to an image-based Transformer model. To achieve this, our model makes two approximations to the full space-time attention used in Video Transformers: (a) It restricts time attention to a local temporal window and capitalizes on the Transformer's depth to obtain full temporal coverage of the video sequence. (b) It uses efficient space-time mixing to attend jointly spatial and temporal locations without inducing any additional cost on top of a spatial-only attention model. We also show how to integrate 2 very lightweight mechanisms for global temporal-only attention which provide additional accuracy improvements at minimal computational cost. We demonstrate that our model produces very high recognition accuracy on the most popular video recognition datasets while at the same time being significantly more efficient than other Video Transformer models.

paragraphs: Video transformers must model relationships across both image locations and time, which can make them computationally expensive. This paper proposes a video recognition architecture whose complexity grows linearly with the number of frames. It achieves that scaling by approximating full space-time attention in two complementary ways.

First, each attention operation considers only a local temporal window, while successive network layers provide coverage across the video sequence. Second, efficient space-time mixing lets the model attend jointly to spatial and temporal locations without additional cost over a spatial-only attention model. The authors also integrate two lightweight mechanisms for global temporal-only attention, gaining additional accuracy at a small computational cost.

The design combines local temporal processing, depth, and efficient mixing to capture video information without the overhead of unrestricted space-time attention. Experiments on popular video recognition datasets report very high recognition accuracy and substantially greater efficiency than other video transformer models. The stated computational advantage concerns how temporal information is incorporated while keeping scaling linear in video length.
summary.tldr: Local temporal attention and efficient space-time mixing deliver strong video recognition while keeping computational complexity linear in the number of frames.

title: Space-time Mixing Attention for Video Transformer

abstract: We consider a nonlinear inverse problem $\mathbf{y}= f(\mathbf{Ax})$, where observations $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^m$ are the componentwise nonlinear transformation of $\mathbf{Ax} \in \mathbb{R}^m$, $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is the signal of interest and $\mathbf{A}$ is a known linear mapping. By properly specifying the nonlinear processing function, this model can be particularized to many signal processing problems, including compressed sensing and phase retrieval. Our main goal in this paper is to understand the impact of sensing matrices, or more specifically the spectrum of sensing matrices, on the difficulty of recovering $\mathbf{x}$ from $\mathbf{y}$. Towards this goal, we study the performance of one of the most successful recovery methods, i.e. the expectation propagation algorithm (EP). We define a notion for the spikiness of the spectrum of $\mathbf{A}$ and show the importance of this measure in the performance of the EP. Whether the spikiness of the spectrum can hurt or help the recovery performance of EP depends on $f$. We define certain quantities based on the function $f$ that enables us to describe the impact of the spikiness of the spectrum on EP recovery. Based on our framework, we are able to show that for instance, in phase-retrieval problems, matrices with spikier spectrums are better for EP, while in 1-bit compressed sensing problems, less spiky (flatter) spectrums offer better recoveries. Our results unify and substantially generalize the existing results that compare sub-Gaussian and orthogonal matrices, and provide a platform toward designing optimal sensing systems.

paragraphs: This paper studies recovery of an unknown signal from measurements formed by applying a known linear map followed by a componentwise nonlinear function. Different choices of that function describe different sensing problems. The central question is how the spectrum of the sensing matrix affects recovery, with the analysis focused on the expectation propagation algorithm.

The authors define a measure of spectral spikiness and quantities derived from the nonlinear observation function. Together, these describe whether a more uneven spectrum helps or harms expectation propagation. The observation function is therefore essential to interpreting the spectrum: the same broad spectral preference does not apply across all sensing problems.

The analysis gives contrasting examples. Spikier spectra improve expectation propagation recovery in phase retrieval, whereas flatter spectra offer better recovery in one-bit compressed sensing. The framework unifies and substantially extends earlier comparisons between sub-Gaussian and orthogonal matrices. Its practical significance is a basis for designing sensing systems around both their measurement nonlinearity and their recovery algorithm, rather than choosing a matrix spectrum in isolation.
summary.tldr: The effect of sensing-matrix spectral spikiness on expectation propagation recovery depends on the nonlinear observation function.

title: Analysis of Sensing Spectral for Signal Recovery under a Generalized Linear Model

abstract: Adversarial attacks on graphs have posed a major threat to the robustness of graph machine learning (GML) models. Naturally, there is an ever-escalating arms race between attackers and defenders. However, the strategies behind both sides are often not fairly compared under the same and realistic conditions. To bridge this gap, we present the Graph Robustness Benchmark (GRB) with the goal of providing a scalable, unified, modular, and reproducible evaluation for the adversarial robustness of GML models. GRB standardizes the process of attacks and defenses by 1) developing scalable and diverse datasets, 2) modularizing the attack and defense implementations, and 3) unifying the evaluation protocol in refined scenarios. By leveraging the modular GRB pipeline, the end-users can focus on the development of robust GML models with automated data processing and experimental evaluations. To support open and reproducible research on graph adversarial learning, GRB also hosts public leaderboards for different scenarios. As a starting point, we provide various baseline experiments to benchmark the state-of-the-art techniques. GRB is an open-source benchmark and all datasets, code, and leaderboards are available at https://cogdl.ai/grb/home.

The authors identify a problem with the surrounding arms race: competing methods are often evaluated under different or unrealistic conditions. GRB aims to make those comparisons more unified, reproducible, and scalable.

The benchmark combines diverse datasets, modular attack and defense implementations, and a common evaluation protocol across defined scenarios. Its modular organization lets researchers develop components within a shared pipeline. Automated data processing and experimental evaluation reduce the amount of surrounding infrastructure needed to study a new robust graph model.

The authors provide baseline experiments with existing techniques and public leaderboards for different scenarios. These establish starting points for comparison and support open research. The main contribution is an evaluation framework that makes experimental conditions more consistent, giving subsequent attack and defense results a clearer basis for comparison within the scenarios the benchmark defines.
summary.tldr: GRB standardizes datasets, attack and defense implementations, and evaluation scenarios for reproducible comparisons of graph model robustness.

title: Graph Robustness Benchmark: Benchmarking the Adversarial Robustness of Graph Machine Learning

abstract: We propose a novel normal estimation method called HSurf-Net, which can accurately predict normals from point clouds with noise and density variations. Previous methods focus on learning point weights to fit neighborhoods into a geometric surface approximated by a polynomial function with a predefined order, based on which normals are estimated. However, fitting surfaces explicitly from raw point clouds suffers from overfitting or underfitting issues caused by inappropriate polynomial orders and outliers, which significantly limits the performance of existing methods. To address these issues, we introduce hyper surface fitting to implicitly learn hyper surfaces, which are represented by multi-layer perceptron (MLP) layers that take point features as input and output surface patterns in a high dimensional feature space. We introduce a novel space transformation module, which consists of a sequence of local aggregation layers and global shift layers, to learn an optimal feature space, and a relative position encoding module to effectively convert point clouds into the learned feature space. Our model learns hyper surfaces from the noise-less features and directly predicts normal vectors. We jointly optimize the MLP weights and module parameters in a data-driven manner to make the model adaptively find the most suitable surface pattern for various points. Experimental results show that our HSurf-Net achieves the state-of-the-art performance on the synthetic shape dataset, the real-world indoor and outdoor scene datasets. The code, data and pretrained models are publicly available.

We introduce a novel space transformation module, which consists of a sequence of local aggregation layers and global shift layers, to learn an optimal feature space, and a relative position encoding module to effectively convert point clouds into the learned feature space. We jointly optimize the MLP weights and module parameters in a data-driven manner to make the model adaptively find the most suitable surface pattern for various points. Experimental results show that our HSurf-Net achieves the state-of-the-art performance on the synthetic shape dataset, the real-world indoor and outdoor scene datasets. The code, data and pretrained models are publicly available.

paragraphs: HSurf-Net estimates surface normals from three-dimensional point clouds affected by noise and uneven sampling density. Earlier approaches fit local geometric surfaces using polynomials of a predefined order. The paper identifies a weakness in that choice: an unsuitable polynomial order or outlying points can make the fitted surface too simple or too sensitive to the observations.

The proposed method learns surface patterns implicitly in a higher-dimensional feature space. Multilayer perceptrons represent these patterns, while a space transformation module combines local aggregation and global shifts to learn the feature space. Relative position encoding maps the points into that space. The model then predicts normal vectors directly from the learned surface features.

The surface representation and transformation modules are optimized together, allowing the model to adapt its surface patterns to different points. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on synthetic shapes and real indoor and outdoor scenes. These results support replacing a fixed polynomial surface choice with a learned representation when estimating normals under the noise and density variations considered in the paper.
summary.tldr: HSurf-Net learns implicit surface patterns in feature space to estimate point-cloud normals under noise and density variation.

title: HSurf-Net: Normal Estimation for 3D Point Clouds by Learning Hyper Surfaces

abstract: Many generative models synthesize data by transforming a standard Gaussian random variable using a deterministic neural network. Among these models are the Variational Autoencoders and the Generative Adversarial Networks. In this work, we call them "push-forward" models and study their expressivity. We formally demonstrate that the Lipschitz constant of these generative networks has to be large in order to fit multimodal distributions. More precisely, we show that the total variation distance and the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the generated and the data distribution are bounded from below by a constant depending on the mode separation and the Lipschitz constant. Since constraining the Lipschitz constants of neural networks is a common way to stabilize generative models, there is a provable trade-off between the ability of push-forward models to approximate multimodal distributions and the stability of their training. We validate our findings on one-dimensional and image datasets and empirically show that the recently introduced diffusion models do not suffer of such limitation.

paragraphs: Many generative models create samples by passing a standard Gaussian random input through a deterministic neural network. This paper studies how well these push-forward models can represent distributions with multiple separated modes. Such modes correspond to distinct concentrations of data, so fitting them requires reproducing both the concentrations and their separation.

The authors prove that accurate fitting requires a sufficiently large Lipschitz constant, which measures how strongly the network can amplify changes in its input. They derive lower bounds on distribution mismatch, measured by total variation distance and Kullback-Leibler divergence, that depend on both mode separation and this constant. These bounds connect a restriction on the generating network directly to limits on the distributions it can approximate.

This matters because restricting Lipschitz constants is commonly used to stabilize generative training. The results establish a trade-off between that stabilization strategy and the ability to fit multimodal data. Experiments on one-dimensional and image datasets support the analysis. The authors also empirically find that diffusion models avoid this limitation in their evaluations; that observation is distinct from the formal bounds proved for the studied push-forward models.
summary.tldr: Push-forward generators face a provable trade-off between Lipschitz-based stabilization and accurately representing separated modes.

title: Can Push-forward Generative Models Fit Multimodal Distributions?

abstract: Multi-Task Learning (MTL) is a powerful learning paradigm to improve generalization performance via knowledge sharing. However, existing studies find that MTL could sometimes hurt generalization, especially when two tasks are less correlated. One possible reason that hurts generalization is spurious correlation, i.e., some knowledge is spurious and not causally related to task labels, but the model could mistakenly utilize them and thus fail when such correlation changes. In MTL setup, there exist several unique challenges of spurious correlation. First, the risk of having non-causal knowledge is higher, as the shared MTL model needs to encode all knowledge from different tasks, and causal knowledge for one task could be potentially spurious to the other. Second, the confounder between task labels brings in a different type of spurious correlation to MTL. Given such label-label confounders, we theoretically and empirically show that MTL is prone to taking non-causal knowledge from other tasks. To solve this problem, we propose Multi-Task Causal Representation Learning (MT-CRL) framework. MT-CRL aims to represent multi-task knowledge via disentangled neural modules, and learn which module is causally related to each task via MTL-specific invariant regularization. Experiments show that MT-CRL could enhance MTL model's performance by 5.5% on average over Multi-MNIST, MovieLens, Taskonomy, CityScape, and NYUv2, and show it could indeed alleviate spurious correlation problem.

A feature that genuinely helps determine one task’s label may be merely correlated with another task’s label, so sharing it can create an unreliable shortcut for the second task.

The authors also examine confounders linking task labels. Given such confounders, they show theoretically and empirically that multi-task models are prone to using noncausal knowledge from other tasks. The findings support more selective sharing: the framework aims to retain the benefits of shared knowledge while distinguishing which pieces are appropriate for each task. Its causal interpretation is tied to the problem structure studied in the paper.
summary.tldr: MT-CRL separates shared knowledge into modules and regularizes their use to reduce harmful spurious correlations across tasks.

title: Improving Multi-Task Generalization via Regularizing Spurious Correlation

abstract: Neural networks trained with ERM (empirical risk minimization) sometimes learn unintended decision rules, in particular when their training data is biased, i.e., when training labels are strongly correlated with undesirable features. To prevent a network from learning such features, recent methods augment training data such that examples displaying spurious correlations (i.e., bias-aligned examples) become a minority, whereas the other, bias-conflicting examples become prevalent. However, these approaches are sometimes difficult to train and scale to real-world data because they rely on generative models or disentangled representations. We propose an alternative based on mixup, a popular augmentation that creates convex combinations of training examples. Our method, coined SelecMix, applies mixup to contradicting pairs of examples, defined as showing either (i) the same label but dissimilar biased features, or (ii) different labels but similar biased features. Identifying such pairs requires comparing examples with respect to unknown biased features. For this, we utilize an auxiliary contrastive model with the popular heuristic that biased features are learned preferentially during training. Experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the method, in particular when label noise complicates the identification of bias-conflicting examples.

paragraphs: When labels strongly correlate with undesirable features, a neural network may learn a shortcut instead of the intended decision rule. SelecMix addresses this by constructing augmented examples that challenge those correlations. It builds on mixup, which forms weighted combinations of training examples, and focuses on choosing informative pairs to combine.

The method selects pairs that contradict a biased association in one of two ways: matching labels with dissimilar biased features, or different labels with similar biased features. Because those features are unknown, SelecMix uses an auxiliary contrastive model to compare examples. This relies on the heuristic that networks tend to learn biased features preferentially during training.

Benchmark experiments show that the approach is effective, particularly when noisy labels make bias-conflicting examples harder to identify. Pair selection is therefore the main mechanism connecting augmentation to debiasing: the mixed examples are chosen to weaken the unwanted label-feature relationship. The method offers an alternative to augmentation approaches that depend on generative models or disentangled representations, while retaining a specific heuristic for locating the relevant biased features.
summary.tldr: SelecMix reduces reliance on spurious correlations by mixing carefully selected example pairs that contradict biased label-feature associations.

title: SelecMix: Debiased Learning by Contradicting-pair Sampling

abstract: Learning new task-specific skills from a few trials is a fundamental challenge for artificial intelligence. Meta reinforcement learning (meta-RL) tackles this problem by learning transferable policies that support few-shot adaptation to unseen tasks. Despite recent advances in meta-RL, most existing methods require the access to the environmental reward function of new tasks to infer the task objective, which is not realistic in many practical applications. To bridge this gap, we study the problem of few-shot adaptation in the context of human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning. We develop a meta-RL algorithm that enables fast policy adaptation with preference-based feedback. The agent can adapt to new tasks by querying human's preference between behavior trajectories instead of using per-step numeric rewards. By extending techniques from information theory, our approach can design query sequences to maximize the information gain from human interactions while tolerating the inherent error of non-expert human oracle. In experiments, we extensively evaluate our method, Adaptation with Noisy OracLE (ANOLE), on a variety of meta-RL benchmark tasks and demonstrate substantial improvement over baseline algorithms in terms of both feedback efficiency and error tolerance.

paragraphs: Meta reinforcement learning aims to prepare an agent to learn a new task from only a few trials. Many existing approaches still need access to the new task's reward function to determine what behavior is desirable. This paper studies adaptation when people instead communicate the objective through preferences between complete behavior trajectories.

The proposed method, ANOLE, lets an agent adapt by asking which of two trajectories a human prefers. This replaces the need for numeric rewards at every step during adaptation. The method extends information-theoretic techniques to choose sequences of questions that maximize information gained from human interactions while tolerating mistakes from a nonexpert respondent.

This makes query selection part of the adaptation process: each interaction is chosen to help clarify the task objective. Across a variety of meta reinforcement learning benchmarks, the authors report substantial improvements over baseline algorithms in both feedback efficiency and error tolerance. The findings support preference feedback as a practical signal for rapid adaptation, including when that feedback is imperfect.
summary.tldr: ANOLE adapts policies to new tasks using informative human preference queries while tolerating errors in the feedback.

title: Efficient Meta Reinforcement Learning for Preference-based Fast Adaptation

abstract: Unsupervised object-centric learning aims to represent the modular, compositional, and causal structure of a scene as a set of object representations and thereby promises to resolve many critical limitations of traditional single-vector representations such as poor systematic generalization. Although there have been many remarkable advances in recent years, one of the most critical problems in this direction has been that previous methods work only with simple and synthetic scenes but not with complex and naturalistic images or videos. In this paper, we propose STEVE, an unsupervised model for object-centric learning in videos. Our proposed model makes a significant advancement by demonstrating its effectiveness on various complex and naturalistic videos unprecedented in this line of research. Interestingly, this is achieved by neither adding complexity to the model architecture nor introducing a new objective or weak supervision. Rather, it is achieved by a surprisingly simple architecture that uses a transformer-based image decoder conditioned on slots and the learning objective is simply to reconstruct the observation. Our experiment results on various complex and naturalistic videos show significant improvements compared to the previous state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Object-centric learning represents a scene through separate object representations, aiming to reflect its compositional structure. This direction promises advantages over compressing a whole scene into one vector, but previous methods struggled beyond simple synthetic scenes. The paper introduces STEVE to extend unsupervised object-centric learning to complex and naturalistic videos.

STEVE uses a transformer-based image decoder conditioned on slots, which provide the object-oriented representation. Its training objective is simply to reconstruct the observation. The reported advance comes from this architectural arrangement without adding weak supervision, introducing a new objective, or increasing architectural complexity. This makes the reconstruction setup itself central to the result.

Experiments on various complex and naturalistic videos show significant improvements over previous state-of-the-art methods. The findings demonstrate that a comparatively simple unsupervised design can work on visual material that had been difficult for earlier object-centric approaches. They establish progress in learning object representations from richer videos, while the broader promises of object-centric representation remain motivations for the research rather than additional outcomes established here.
summary.tldr: STEVE uses a slot-conditioned transformer decoder and reconstruction training to improve unsupervised object-centric learning on complex, naturalistic videos.

title: Simple Unsupervised Object-Centric Learning for Complex and Naturalistic Videos

abstract: Despite the non-convex optimization landscape, over-parametrized shallow networks are able to achieve global convergence under gradient descent. The picture can be radically different for narrow networks, which tend to get stuck in badly-generalizing local minima. Here we investigate the cross-over between these two regimes in the high-dimensional setting, and in particular investigate the connection between the so-called mean-field/hydrodynamic regime and the seminal approach of Saad \& Solla. Focusing on the case of Gaussian data, we study the interplay between the learning rate, the time scale, and the number of hidden units in the high-dimensional dynamics of stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Our work builds on a deterministic description of SGD in high-dimensions from statistical physics, which we extend and for which we provide rigorous convergence rates.
