paragraphs: This paper investigates the transition between two different training behaviours in shallow neural networks. Overparameterised networks can achieve global convergence under gradient descent despite nonconvex objectives, whereas narrow networks tend to become trapped in local minima that generalise poorly. The authors study how these regimes connect in a high-dimensional setting.

The analysis focuses on Gaussian data and the interaction among learning rate, training time scale, and the number of hidden units during stochastic gradient descent. Considering these quantities together helps frame the crossover as a question about training dynamics, rather than network width in isolation. The work also examines the connection between the mean-field or hydrodynamic regime and the earlier Saad–Solla approach.

The authors extend a deterministic description of high-dimensional stochastic gradient descent drawn from statistical physics and provide rigorous convergence rates for that description. The contribution is a theoretical account linking different regimes of shallow-network learning. Its stated Gaussian-data focus is part of the setting in which the analysis is developed, so the results should be understood within that scope.
summary.tldr: The paper analyses how width, learning rate, and time scale shape high-dimensional SGD dynamics in shallow networks with Gaussian data.

title: Phase diagram of Stochastic Gradient Descent in high-dimensional two-layer neural networks

abstract: Information-directed sampling (IDS) has revealed its potential as a data-efficient algorithm for reinforcement learning (RL). However, theoretical understanding of IDS for Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) is still limited. We develop novel information-theoretic tools to bound the information ratio and cumulative information gain about the learning target. Our theoretical results shed light on the importance of choosing the learning target such that the practitioners can balance the computation and regret bounds. As a consequence, we derive prior-free Bayesian regret bounds for vanilla-IDS which learns the whole environment under tabular finite-horizon MDPs. In addition, we propose a computationally-efficient regularized-IDS that maximizes an additive form rather than the ratio form and show that it enjoys the same regret bound as vanilla-IDS. With the aid of rate-distortion theory, we improve the regret bound by learning a surrogate, less informative environment. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to linear MDPs and prove similar regret bounds for Thompson sampling as a by-product.

paragraphs: Information-directed sampling chooses actions using a tradeoff between learning and performance. This paper develops theoretical tools for understanding that tradeoff in reinforcement learning. A central question is what the algorithm should try to learn: the entire environment or a simpler target containing less information.

The authors bound an information ratio and the cumulative information gained about the chosen target. For tabular, finite-horizon Markov decision processes, this yields prior-free Bayesian regret bounds for vanilla IDS that learns the whole environment. This shows how choosing the learning target can affect both computational demands and theoretical performance guarantees. The analysis also extends to linear Markov decision processes and yields related regret bounds for Thompson sampling. The contribution is a broader theoretical account of information-directed exploration and the value of selecting what information to acquire.
summary.tldr: New regret analyses show how information-directed reinforcement learning can benefit from simpler objectives and carefully chosen learning targets.

title: Regret Bounds for Information-Directed Reinforcement Learning

abstract: A fundamental challenge in deep metric learning is the generalization capability of the feature embedding network model since the embedding network learned on training classes need to be evaluated on new test classes. To address this challenge, in this paper, we introduce a new method called coded residual transform (CRT) for deep metric learning to significantly improve its generalization capability. Specifically, we learn a set of diversified prototype features, project the feature map onto each prototype, and then encode its features using their projection residuals weighted by their correlation coefficients with each prototype. The proposed CRT method has the following two unique characteristics. First, it represents and encodes the feature map from a set of complimentary perspectives based on projections onto diversified prototypes. Second, unlike existing transformer-based feature representation approaches which encode the original values of features based on global correlation analysis, the proposed coded residual transform encodes the relative differences between the original features and their projected prototypes. Embedding space density and spectral decay analysis show that this multi perspective projection onto diversified prototypes and coded residual representation are able to achieve significantly improved generalization capability in metric learning. Finally, to further enhance the generalization performance, we propose to enforce the consistency on their feature similarity matrices between coded residual transforms with different sizes of projection prototypes and embedding dimensions. Our extensive experimental results and ablation studies demonstrate that the proposed CRT method outperform the state-of-the-art deep metric learning methods by large margins and improving upon the current best method by up to 4.28% on the CUB dataset.

paragraphs: Deep metric learning trains a network to represent examples in a space where their relationships can be compared. A central difficulty is that evaluation uses classes absent from training. Coded residual transform, or CRT, aims to make these learned representations transfer more effectively to those new classes.

CRT learns diverse prototype features and projects a feature map onto each prototype. It represents the features through the residual differences from these projections, weighted by their correlations with the prototypes. Each prototype supplies another perspective, so the representation captures relative differences across multiple reference points. The method also encourages consistency between feature-similarity matrices produced with different prototype counts and embedding dimensions.

Analyses of embedding-space density and spectral decay support the claimed improvement in generalization. Experiments and ablations report substantial gains over existing deep metric learning methods, including an improvement of up to 4.28% over the current best method on CUB. The findings support residual-based, multi-perspective encoding as a way to improve transfer to unseen classes in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: CRT improves metric-learning generalization by encoding features as weighted differences from multiple learned prototypes.

title: Coded Residual Transform for Generalizable Deep Metric Learning

abstract: The majority of methods for crafting adversarial attacks have focused on scenes with a single dominant object (e.g., images from ImageNet). On the other hand, natural scenes include multiple dominant objects that are semantically related. Thus, it is crucial to explore designing attack strategies that look beyond learning on single-object scenes or attack single-object victim classifiers. Due to their inherent property of strong transferability of perturbations to unknown models, this paper presents the first approach of using generative models for adversarial attacks on multi-object scenes. In order to represent the relationships between different objects in the input scene, we leverage upon the open-sourced pre-trained vision-language model CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training), with the motivation to exploit the encoded semantics in the language space along with the visual space. We call this attack approach Generative Adversarial Multi-object Attacks (GAMA). GAMA demonstrates the utility of the CLIP model as an attacker's tool to train formidable perturbation generators for multi-object scenes. Using the joint image-text features to train the generator, we show that GAMA can craft potent transferable perturbations in order to fool victim classifiers in various attack settings. For example, GAMA triggers ~16% more misclassification than state-of-the-art generative approaches in black-box settings where both the classifier architecture and data distribution of the attacker are different from the victim. Our code is available here: https://abhishekaich27.github.io/gama.html

These findings demonstrate that the semantic information available in a vision-language model can strengthen attacks on the evaluated multi-object scenes.
summary.tldr: GAMA uses CLIP's image-text features to train transferable adversarial perturbations for scenes containing multiple related objects.

title: GAMA: Generative Adversarial Multi-Object Scene Attacks

abstract: Addressing decision-making problems using sequence modeling to predict future trajectories shows promising results in recent years.In this paper, we take a step further to leverage the sequence predictive method in wider areas such as long-term planning, vision-based control, and multi-task decision-making.To this end, we propose a method to utilize a diffusion-based generative sequence model to plan a series of milestones in a latent space and to have an agent to follow the milestones to accomplish a given task.The proposed method can learn control-relevant, low-dimensional latent representations of milestones, which makes it possible to efficiently perform long-term planning and vision-based control.Furthermore, our approach exploits generation flexibility of the diffusion model, which makes it possible to plan diverse trajectories for multi-task decision-making.We demonstrate the proposed method across offline reinforcement learning (RL) benchmarks and an visual manipulation environment.The results show that our approach outperforms offline RL methods in solving long-horizon, sparse-reward tasks and multi-task problems,while also achieving the state-of-the-art performance on the most challenging vision-based manipulation benchmark.

paragraphs: Predicting sequences of future behavior offers a way to make decisions, but long-term planning and visual control require representations that remain manageable over extended tasks. This paper proposes planning a series of milestones in a learned latent space. An agent then follows those milestones to accomplish the requested task.

A diffusion-based generative sequence model produces the milestone plan. The method learns low-dimensional milestone representations that retain information relevant to control, making long-term planning and vision-based control more efficient. The diffusion model's flexibility also allows it to generate diverse trajectories, supporting decision-making across multiple tasks rather than relying on one fixed form of future behavior.

The authors evaluate the method on offline reinforcement learning benchmarks and a visual manipulation environment. They report better results than offline reinforcement learning methods on long-horizon tasks with sparse rewards and on multi-task problems. They also report state-of-the-art performance on the most challenging vision-based manipulation benchmark they consider. These findings support combining compact control representations with generative planning for demanding sequential decisions.
summary.tldr: A diffusion model plans compact latent milestones that an agent follows, improving reported results on long-horizon, multi-task, and visual control benchmarks.

title: Diffused Task-Agnostic Milestone Planner

abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are hard to deploy on edge devices due to its high computation and storage complexities. As a common practice for model compression, network pruning consists of two major categories: unstructured and structured pruning, where unstructured pruning constantly performs better. However, unstructured pruning presents a structured pattern at high pruning rates, which limits its performance. To this end, we propose a Rank-based PruninG (RPG) method to maintain the ranks of sparse weights in an adversarial manner. In each step, we minimize the low-rank approximation error for the weight matrices using singular value decomposition, and maximize their distance by pushing the weight matrices away from its low rank approximation. This rank-based optimization objective guides sparse weights towards a high-rank topology. The proposed method is conducted in a gradual pruning fashion to stabilize the change of rank during training. Experimental results on various datasets and different tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm in high sparsity. The proposed RPG outperforms the state-of-the-art performance by 1.13\% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet in ResNet-50 with 98\% sparsity. The codes are available at https://github.com/huawei-noah/Efficient-Computing/tree/master/Pruning/RPG and https://gitee.com/mindspore/models/tree/master/research/cv/RPG.

paragraphs: Pruning reduces the storage and computation demands of convolutional networks by removing weights. This paper focuses on a problem that appears when unstructured pruning becomes very aggressive: the remaining weights develop structured patterns that limit performance. The proposed Rank-based PruninG method, RPG, addresses this by encouraging sparse weight matrices to retain higher rank during training.

RPG uses an adversarial interaction between a weight matrix and its low-rank approximation. Each step first uses singular value decomposition to minimize the approximation error, then pushes the weight matrix away from that approximation. This opposing process encourages a higher-rank arrangement among the surviving weights. Pruning proceeds gradually to stabilize how rank changes as training continues.

Experiments across datasets and tasks support the method's effectiveness at high sparsity. For ResNet-50 on ImageNet with 98% sparsity, the authors report a 1.13% top-1 accuracy improvement over the state of the art. The result highlights the importance of the structure retained by sparse weights, beyond simply counting how many parameters remain after pruning.
summary.tldr: RPG improves highly sparse networks by gradually pruning while adversarially pushing weight matrices away from low-rank approximations.

title: Towards Higher Ranks via Adversarial Weight Pruning

abstract: 3D reconstruction and novel view rendering can greatly benefit from geometric priors when the input views are not sufficient in terms of coverage and inter-view baselines. Deep learning of geometric priors from 2D images requires each image to be represented in a $2D$ canonical frame and the prior to be learned in a given or learned $3D$ canonical frame. In this paper, given only the relative poses of the cameras, we show how to learn priors from multiple views equivariant to coordinate frame transformations by proposing an $SE(3)$-equivariant convolution and transformer in the space of rays in 3D. We model the ray space as a homogeneous space of $SE(3)$ and introduce the $SE(3)$-equivariant convolution in ray space. Depending on the output domain of the convolution, we present convolution-based $SE(3)$-equivariant maps from ray space to ray space and to $\mathbb{R}^3$. Our mathematical framework allows us to go beyond convolution to $SE(3)$-equivariant attention in the ray space. We showcase how to tailor and adapt the equivariant convolution and transformer in the tasks of equivariant $3D$ reconstruction and equivariant neural rendering from multiple views. We demonstrate $SE(3)$-equivariance by obtaining robust results in roto-translated datasets without performing transformation augmentation.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a scene or rendering new views from limited images benefits from learned geometric structure. This paper develops a way to learn that structure using only relative camera poses while remaining consistent under changes of coordinate frame. Its key setting is the space of rays in 3D, rather than a fixed canonical frame for the scene.

The authors model ray space mathematically under SE(3), the transformations consisting of 3D rotations and translations. They construct equivariant convolutions that map ray-based information either to other rays or to 3D locations. Equivariance means the outputs transform consistently when the coordinate frame changes. The framework also supports equivariant attention, enabling a transformer in ray space.

The paper adapts these operations to multiview 3D reconstruction and neural rendering. Experiments on rotated and translated datasets show robust results without transformation augmentation. These findings demonstrate the value of incorporating coordinate-frame consistency directly into the model's operations, with relative camera poses supplying the geometric relationships needed by the proposed approach.
summary.tldr: Ray-space convolutions and attention build rotation-and-translation equivariance into multiview reconstruction and neural rendering.

title: $SE(3)$ Equivariant Convolution and Transformer in Ray Space

abstract: Given the recent impressive accomplishments of language models (LMs) for code generation, we explore the use of LMs as general adaptive mutation and crossover operators for an evolutionary neural architecture search (NAS) algorithm.While NAS still proves too difficult a task for LMs to succeed at solely through prompting, we find that the combination of evolutionary prompt engineering with soft prompt-tuning, a method we term EvoPrompting, consistently finds diverse and high performing models. We first demonstrate that EvoPrompting is effective on the computationally efficient MNIST-1D dataset, where EvoPrompting produces convolutional architecture variants that outperform both those designed by human experts and naive few-shot prompting in terms of accuracy and model size. We then apply our method to searching for graph neural networks on the CLRS Algorithmic Reasoning Benchmark, where EvoPrompting is able to design *novel* architectures that outperform current state-of-the-art models on 21 out of 30 algorithmic reasoning tasks while maintaining similar model size. EvoPrompting is successful at designing accurate and efficient neural network architectures across a variety of machine learning tasks, while also being general enough for easy adaptation to other tasks beyond neural network design.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search asks how to design a network that performs well without relying entirely on manual architecture choices. This paper uses code-generating language models inside an evolutionary search process. The language model serves as an adaptive mechanism for modifying and combining candidate architectures, extending its role beyond producing a design from a single prompt.

EvoPrompting combines evolutionary prompt engineering with soft prompt-tuning. The authors find that prompting alone is insufficient for the architecture-search task they study, whereas this combined procedure consistently discovers diverse, high-performing networks. Its approach ties language-model generation to an ongoing search process, so architecture proposals can benefit from adaptation throughout the search.

On MNIST-1D, EvoPrompting produces convolutional variants that improve accuracy and model size relative to human-designed architectures and naive few-shot prompting. On the CLRS Algorithmic Reasoning Benchmark, it discovers graph-network architectures that outperform the stated leading models on 21 of 30 tasks with similar model size. These findings demonstrate successful search across the evaluated settings; the authors also describe the framework as adaptable to tasks beyond network design.
summary.tldr: EvoPrompting combines evolutionary search and soft prompt-tuning to make language models effective generators of accurate, efficient neural architectures.

title: EvoPrompting: Language Models for Code-Level Neural Architecture Search

abstract: Active Domain Adaptation (ADA) has emerged as an attractive technique for assisting domain adaptation by actively annotating a small subset of target samples. Most ADA methods focus on measuring the target representativeness beyond traditional active learning criteria to handle the domain shift problem, while leaving the uncertainty estimation to be performed by an uncalibrated deterministic model. In this work, we introduce a probabilistic framework that captures both data-level and prediction-level uncertainties beyond a point estimate. Specifically, we use variational inference to approximate the joint posterior distribution of latent representation and model prediction. The variational objective of labeled data can be formulated by a variational autoencoder and a latent diffusion classifier, and the objective of unlabeled data can be implemented in a knowledge distillation framework. We utilize adversarial learning to ensure an invariant latent space. The resulting diffusion classifier enables efficient sampling of all possible predictions for each individual to recover the predictive distribution. We then leverage a t-test-based criterion upon the sampling and select informative unlabeled target samples based on the p-value, which encodes both prediction variability and cross-category ambiguity. Experiments on both ADA and Source-Free ADA settings show that our method provides more calibrated predictions than previous ADA methods and achieves favorable performance on three domain adaptation datasets.

paragraphs: Active domain adaptation chooses a small set of examples from a target domain for annotation. That choice depends partly on knowing where predictions are uncertain. The paper addresses approaches that emphasize target representativeness while obtaining uncertainty from an uncalibrated deterministic model, replacing a single estimate with a probabilistic treatment of representations and predictions.

The method uses variational inference to approximate their joint posterior distribution. Labeled examples are handled through a variational autoencoder and latent diffusion classifier, while unlabeled examples enter through knowledge distillation. Adversarial learning encourages a domain-invariant latent space. Sampling from the diffusion classifier then provides a predictive distribution for each example.

To select examples for labeling, the authors apply a t-test-based criterion to these samples. Its p-value captures both variation in predictions and ambiguity between categories. Experiments in standard and source-free active domain adaptation show better calibration than earlier methods and favorable performance on three datasets. The findings support using richer uncertainty estimates to guide annotation decisions when adapting across domains.
summary.tldr: A diffusion-based probabilistic classifier improves uncertainty calibration and guides target-sample annotation for active domain adaptation.

title: Diffusion-Based Probabilistic Uncertainty Estimation for Active Domain Adaptation

abstract: Controllable scene synthesis aims to create interactive environments for numerous industrial use cases. Scene graphs provide a highly suitable interface to facilitate these applications by abstracting the scene context in a compact manner. Existing methods, reliant on retrieval from extensive databases or pre-trained shape embeddings, often overlook scene-object and object-object relationships, leading to inconsistent results due to their limited generation capacity. To address this issue, we present CommonScenes, a fully generative model that converts scene graphs into corresponding controllable 3D scenes, which are semantically realistic and conform to commonsense. Our pipeline consists of two branches, one predicting the overall scene layout via a variational auto-encoder and the other generating compatible shapes via latent diffusion, capturing global scene-object and local inter-object relationships in the scene graph while preserving shape diversity. The generated scenes can be manipulated by editing the input scene graph and sampling the noise in the diffusion model. Due to the lack of a scene graph dataset offering high-quality object-level meshes with relations, we also construct SG-FRONT, enriching the off-the-shelf indoor dataset 3D-FRONT with additional scene graph labels. Extensive experiments are conducted on SG-FRONT, where CommonScenes shows clear advantages over other methods regarding generation consistency, quality, and diversity. Codes and the dataset are available on the website.

paragraphs: CommonScenes generates controllable 3D indoor environments from scene graphs, which compactly describe objects and their relationships. The paper addresses inconsistencies that can arise when generation methods overlook how objects relate to the overall scene and to one another. Its aim is to produce diverse shapes that also fit coherently into a scene.

The model has two branches. A variational autoencoder predicts the scene layout, while a latent diffusion model generates compatible object shapes. Both global scene-object relationships and local relationships between objects guide generation. Users can change the resulting environment by editing the input graph or varying the noise used by the diffusion model.

The authors also construct SG-FRONT by adding scene graph annotations to 3D-FRONT, addressing the need for data that combines object-level meshes with relationships. Experiments on SG-FRONT show advantages over other methods in consistency, quality, and diversity. These findings support jointly considering scene structure and object generation when building environments that are both editable and semantically coherent.
summary.tldr: CommonScenes combines scene-layout prediction and shape diffusion to generate editable 3D interiors with improved consistency, quality, and diversity on SG-FRONT.

title: CommonScenes: Generating Commonsense 3D Indoor Scenes with Scene Graph Diffusion

abstract: Machine learning tools often rely on embedding text as vectors of real numbers.In this paper, we study how the semantic structure of language is encoded in the algebraic structure of such embeddings.Specifically, we look at a notion of "semantic independence" capturing the idea that, e.g., "eggplant" and "tomato" are independent given "vegetable". Although such examples are intuitive, it is difficult to formalize such a notion of semantic independence. The key observation here is that any sensible formalization should obey a set of so-called independence axioms, and thus any algebraic encoding of this structure should also obey these axioms. This leads us naturally to use partial orthogonality as the relevant algebraic structure. We develop theory and methods that allow us to demonstrate that partial orthogonality does indeed capture semantic independence.Complementary to this, we also introduce the concept of independence preserving embeddings where embeddings preserve the conditional independence structures of a distribution, and we prove the existence of such embeddings and approximations to them.

paragraphs: Text embeddings encode language as numerical vectors, but the semantic meaning of their algebraic relationships can be difficult to establish. This paper examines semantic independence: the intuition that concepts such as eggplant and tomato can be independent once the broader concept vegetable is given. The challenge is turning that intuition into a coherent mathematical relation.

The authors begin with independence axioms that a sensible formalization should satisfy. They argue that an algebraic representation of semantic independence should obey those same rules. This leads to partial orthogonality as the relevant structure, and they develop theory and methods demonstrating that it captures semantic independence.

The paper also introduces independence-preserving embeddings, which retain the conditional independence structure of a distribution. It proves that such embeddings and approximations exist. Together, these contributions connect semantic interpretation with formal constraints on vector geometry, while also establishing that embeddings can preserve specified probabilistic independence relationships. This provides a principled basis for studying meaning beyond informal interpretations of vector similarity.
summary.tldr: The paper connects semantic independence to partial orthogonality and proves the existence of embeddings that preserve conditional independence structures.

title: Uncovering Meanings of Embeddings via Partial Orthogonality

abstract: Co-occurrent visual patterns suggest that pixel relation modeling facilitates dense prediction tasks, which inspires the development of numerous context modeling paradigms, \emph{e.g.}, multi-scale-driven and similarity-driven context schemes. Despite the impressive results, these existing paradigms often suffer from inadequate or ineffective contextual information aggregation due to reliance on large amounts of predetermined priors. To alleviate the issues, we propose a novel \textbf{I}ntervention-\textbf{D}riven \textbf{R}elation \textbf{Net}work (\textbf{IDRNet}), which leverages a deletion diagnostics procedure to guide the modeling of contextual relations among different pixels. Specifically, we first group pixel-level representations into semantic-level representations with the guidance of pseudo labels and further improve the distinguishability of the grouped representations with a feature enhancement module. Next, a deletion diagnostics procedure is conducted to model relations of these semantic-level representations via perceiving the network outputs and the extracted relations are utilized to guide the semantic-level representations to interact with each other. Finally, the interacted representations are utilized to augment original pixel-level representations for final predictions. Extensive experiments are conducted to validate the effectiveness of IDRNet quantitatively and qualitatively. Notably, our intervention-driven context scheme brings consistent performance improvements to state-of-the-art segmentation frameworks and achieves competitive results on popular benchmark datasets, including ADE20K, COCO-Stuff, PASCAL-Context, LIP, and Cityscapes.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation benefits from context: relationships between different image regions can help determine each pixel’s label. Existing context mechanisms often rely on predetermined assumptions about scale or similarity, which can produce inadequate information aggregation. IDRNet instead uses deletion diagnostics to guide how contextual relationships are modeled.

The method first groups pixel representations into semantic-level representations using pseudo labels. A feature enhancement module makes these groups more distinguishable. It then examines network outputs through a deletion-based diagnostic procedure to infer relationships among the grouped representations. Those relationships guide how the groups exchange information, and the updated group representations enrich the original pixel features before final prediction.

This design makes the network’s response to interventions part of determining which contextual information should interact. Quantitative and qualitative experiments support the method’s effectiveness. The authors report consistent improvements when adding the context scheme to state-of-the-art segmentation frameworks, along with competitive results on ADE20K, COCO-Stuff, PASCAL-Context, LIP, and Cityscapes. The findings support intervention-guided context modeling as a useful addition to established segmentation systems.
summary.tldr: IDRNet uses deletion diagnostics to learn contextual relationships that improve pixel-level semantic segmentation.

title: IDRNet: Intervention-Driven Relation Network for Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Large-scale pre-training has shown great potential to enhance models on downstream tasks in vision and language. Developing similar techniques for scalp electroencephalogram (EEG) is suitable since unlabelled data is plentiful. Meanwhile, various sampling channel selections and inherent structural and spatial information bring challenges and avenues to improve existing pre-training strategies further. In order to break boundaries between different EEG resources and facilitate cross-dataset EEG pre-training, we propose to map all kinds of channel selections to a unified topology. We further introduce MMM, a pre-training framework with Multi-dimensional position encoding, Multi-level channel hierarchy, and Multi-stage pre-training strategy built on the unified topology to obtain topology-agnostic representations. Experiments demonstrate that our approach yields impressive improvements over previous state-of-the-art techniques on emotional recognition benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Scalp EEG offers plentiful unlabeled data for pre-training, but datasets can use different selections of recording channels. Those differences complicate learning a shared representation across resources. At the same time, the channels carry structural and spatial information that could help a model understand the recordings if that information is represented consistently.

The paper proposes mapping different channel selections onto a unified topology. It then builds the MMM pre-training framework on that shared organization. MMM combines multidimensional position encoding, a multilevel channel hierarchy, and a multistage training strategy. Together, these components aim to produce representations that are less tied to a particular channel arrangement while still using EEG geometry.

Experiments on emotion-recognition benchmark datasets report substantial improvements over previous state-of-the-art techniques. The approach therefore provides empirical support for coordinating channel structure before and during pre-training. Its central contribution is a route toward cross-dataset EEG learning in which differing channel selections can share a representation framework, with the demonstrated downstream benefit in emotion recognition.
summary.tldr: MMM maps different EEG channel selections to a shared topology and uses geometric pre-training to improve emotion recognition.

title: Learning Topology-Agnostic EEG Representations with Geometry-Aware Modeling

abstract: Conventional statistical wisdom established a well-understood relationship between model complexity and prediction error, typically presented as a _U-shaped curve_ reflecting a transition between under- and overfitting regimes. However, motivated by the success of overparametrized neural networks, recent influential work has suggested this theory to be generally incomplete, introducing an additional regime that exhibits a second descent in test error as the parameter count $p$ grows past sample size $n$ -- a phenomenon dubbed _double descent_. While most attention has naturally been given to the deep-learning setting, double descent was shown to emerge more generally across non-neural models: known cases include _linear regression, trees, and boosting_. In this work, we take a closer look at the evidence surrounding these more classical statistical machine learning methods and challenge the claim that observed cases of double descent truly extend the limits of a traditional U-shaped complexity-generalization curve therein. We show that once careful consideration is given to _what is being plotted_ on the x-axes of their double descent plots, it becomes apparent that there are implicitly multiple, distinct complexity axes along which the parameter count grows. We demonstrate that the second descent appears exactly (and _only_) when and where the transition between these underlying axes occurs, and that its location is thus _not_ inherently tied to the interpolation threshold $p=n$. We then gain further insight by adopting a classical nonparametric statistics perspective. We interpret the investigated methods as _smoothers_ and propose a generalized measure for the _effective_ number of parameters they use _on unseen examples_, using which we find that their apparent double descent curves do indeed fold back into more traditional convex shapes -- providing a resolution to the ostensible tension between double descent and traditional statistical intuition.

paragraphs: Double descent describes prediction error falling, rising, and then falling again as a model's parameter count increases. It appears to challenge the traditional U-shaped relationship between complexity and generalization. This paper reexamines that interpretation for classical methods, including linear regression, trees, and boosting, by asking whether parameter count consistently measures the same kind of complexity.

The authors find that the investigated plots combine multiple underlying complexity axes. Increasing the parameter count can move a method from one axis to another, and the second descent occurs precisely at these transitions in their analysis. Its position is therefore not inherently determined by the point where parameter count equals sample size.

To clarify the relationship, the paper treats these methods as smoothers and proposes a generalized measure of their effective parameter use on unseen examples. With this measure, the studied double-descent curves return to more traditional convex shapes. The contribution resolves the apparent conflict for the investigated classical methods; its stated analysis does not establish the same conclusion for every neural network.
summary.tldr: For the classical methods studied, double descent reflects changing complexity axes, and a revised effective-parameter measure restores traditional convex error curves.

title: A U-turn on Double Descent: Rethinking Parameter Counting in Statistical Learning

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, which lead to incorrect predictions. In black-box settings, transfer attacks can be conveniently used to generate adversarial examples. However, such examples tend to overfit the specific architecture and feature representations of the source model, resulting in poor attack performance against other target models. To overcome this drawback, we propose a novel model modification-based transfer attack: Blurred-Dilated method (BD) in this paper. In summary, BD works by reducing downsampling while introducing BlurPool and dilated convolutions in the source model. Then BD employs the modified source model to generate adversarial samples. We think that BD can more comprehensively preserve the feature information than the original source model. It thus enables more thorough destruction of the image features, which can improve the transferability of the generated adversarial samples. Extensive experiments on the ImageNet dataset show that adversarial examples generated by BD achieve significantly higher transferability than the state-of-the-art baselines. Besides, BD can be conveniently combined with existing black-box attack techniques to further improve their performance.
originalAbstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, which lead to incorrect predictions. In black-box settings, transfer attacks can be conveniently used to generate adversarial examples. However, such examples tend to overfit the specific architecture and feature representations of the source model, resulting in poor attack performance against other target models. To overcome this drawback, we propose a novel model modification-based transfer attack: Blurred-Dilated method (BD) in this paper. In summary, BD works by reducing downsampling while introducing BlurPool and dilated convolutions in the source model. Then BD employs the modified source model to generate adversarial samples. We think that BD can more comprehensively preserve the feature information than the original source model. It thus enables more thorough destruction of the image features, which can improve the transferability of the generated adversarial samples. Extensive experiments on the ImageNet dataset show that adversarial examples generated by BD achieve significantly higher transferability than the state-of-the-art baselines. Besides, BD can be conveniently combined with existing black-box attack techniques to further improve their performance.

paragraphs: An adversarial image created against one neural network may also fool another, enabling attacks when the target model is inaccessible. But this transfer often weakens because the image changes exploit details specific to the source network. The paper addresses that problem by changing the source model used to construct adversarial examples.

The Blurred-Dilated method reduces downsampling and introduces BlurPool and dilated convolutions into the source network. Adversarial samples are then generated using this modified model. The authors suggest that these changes preserve more feature information, allowing the attack to disrupt image features more thoroughly. That proposed explanation links the architectural modification to attacks that depend less on the original source model’s particular representations.

Experiments on ImageNet show significantly greater transferability than the state-of-the-art baselines considered. The method can also be combined with existing black-box attack techniques to improve their performance further. Its contribution is therefore a modification to the model used for attack generation that strengthens transfer in the reported evaluations, with feature preservation offered as the authors’ explanation for the improvement.
summary.tldr: Modifying the source network with reduced downsampling, BlurPool, and dilated convolutions improves adversarial attack transfer on ImageNet.

title: Blurred-Dilated Method for Adversarial Attacks

abstract: Neural network pruning and quantization techniques are almost as old as neural networks themselves. However, to date, only ad-hoc comparisons between the two have been published. In this paper, we set out to answer the question of which is better: neural network quantization or pruning? By answering this question, we hope to inform design decisions made on neural network hardware going forward. We provide an extensive comparison between the two techniques for compressing deep neural networks. First, we give an analytical comparison of expected quantization and pruning error for general data distributions.Then, we provide lower and upper bounds for the per-layer pruning and quantization error in trained networks and compare these to empirical error after optimization.Finally, we provide an extensive experimental comparison for training 8 large-scale models trained on 3 tasks and provide insights into the representations learned during fine-tuning with quantization and pruning in the loop.Our results show that in most cases quantization outperforms pruning. Only in some scenarios with a very high compression ratio, compression might be beneficial from an accuracy standpoint.

paragraphs: Pruning and quantization are established ways to compress neural networks, but comparisons between them have often been ad hoc. This paper builds a more systematic comparison intended to inform compression choices and future neural-network hardware design. It combines analytical error comparisons with experiments on trained networks rather than relying on only one type of evidence.

The analysis first compares expected pruning and quantization error for general data distributions. It then develops lower and upper error bounds for individual layers in trained networks and compares those bounds with empirical errors after optimization. This connects mathematical estimates of compression error to the behavior of networks whose parameters have been adjusted.

The experimental study covers eight large-scale models across three tasks and examines representations learned during fine-tuning with compression in the loop. Quantization performs better in most evaluated cases. The abstract also notes that compression might benefit accuracy in some very-high-compression scenarios. Overall, the findings provide a qualified empirical preference for quantization alongside analysis that helps ground the comparison.
summary.tldr: A combined theoretical and empirical comparison finds that quantization outperforms pruning in most studied cases.

title: Pruning vs Quantization: Which is Better?

abstract: In recent years, there has been a rapid development of spatio-temporal prediction techniques in response to the increasing demands of traffic management and travel planning. While advanced end-to-end models have achieved notable success in improving predictive performance, their integration and expansion pose significant challenges. This work aims to address these challenges by introducing a spatio-temporal pre-training framework that seamlessly integrates with downstream baselines and enhances their performance. The framework is built upon two key designs: (i) We propose a spatio-temporal mask autoencoder as a pre-training model for learning spatio-temporal dependencies. The model incorporates customized parameter learners and hierarchical spatial pattern encoding networks. These modules are specifically designed to capture spatio-temporal customized representations and intra- and inter-cluster region semantic relationships, which have often been neglected in existing approaches. (ii) We introduce an adaptive mask strategy as part of the pre-training mechanism. This strategy guides the mask autoencoder in learning robust spatio-temporal representations and facilitates the modeling of different relationships, ranging from intra-cluster to inter-cluster, in an easy-to-hard training manner. Extensive experiments conducted on representative benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method. We have made our model implementation publicly available at https://github.com/HKUDS/GPT-ST.

paragraphs: Spatio-temporal prediction requires learning how observations relate across both locations and time. GPT-ST introduces a pretraining framework intended to integrate with downstream prediction models and improve their performance. The motivation is to make learned representations reusable when advanced end-to-end models can be difficult to integrate and extend.

The pretraining model is a masked autoencoder designed around spatial and temporal dependencies. It includes customized parameter learners and a hierarchical spatial encoding network. Together, these components capture representations tailored to spatio-temporal patterns and relationships both within groups of regions and between those groups, which the authors identify as often neglected in existing approaches.

An adaptive masking strategy organizes training from easier relationships toward harder ones, spanning within-cluster and between-cluster structure. This gives the reconstruction task a progression intended to produce robust representations. Experiments on representative benchmarks support the framework's effectiveness. The contribution is the combination of structured representation learning and adaptive pretraining that can strengthen downstream baselines, rather than only a standalone forecasting architecture.
summary.tldr: GPT-ST combines hierarchical spatial encoding with adaptive masked pretraining to learn representations that improve downstream spatio-temporal prediction models.

title: GPT-ST: Generative Pre-Training of Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks

abstract: In this paper, we contribute to solving a threefold problem: outlier rejection, true model reasoning and parameter estimation with a unified optimization modeling. To this end, we first pose this task as a sparse subspace recovering problem, to search a maximum of independent bases under an over-embedded data space. Then we convert the objective into a continuous optimization paradigm that estimates sparse solutions for both bases and errors. Wherein a fast and robust solver is proposed to accurately estimate the sparse subspace parameters and error entries, which is implemented by a proximal approximation method under the alternating optimization framework with the ``optimal'' sub-gradient descent. Extensive experiments regarding known and unknown model fitting on synthetic and challenging real datasets have demonstrated the superiority of our method against the state-of-the-art. We also apply our method to multi-class multi-model fitting and loop closure detection, and achieve promising results both in accuracy and efficiency. Code is released at: https://github.com/StaRainJ/DSP.

paragraphs: The paper combines three related tasks: rejecting outliers, reasoning about the true model, and estimating its parameters. Treating these tasks together is intended to let a single optimization framework account for both the structure in the data and the errors that interfere with fitting it.

The authors first express the task as sparse subspace recovery in an over-embedded data space, searching for a maximum set of independent bases. They then reformulate it as continuous optimization that seeks sparse solutions for both the bases and the errors. This dual sparsity is the organizing idea: the optimization represents model structure and erroneous entries within the same formulation.

The proposed solver uses proximal approximation within alternating optimization, together with a subgradient descent procedure. Experiments on synthetic and challenging real datasets report advantages over state-of-the-art methods for fitting both known and unknown models. Applications to multi-class multi-model fitting and loop closure detection also yield promising accuracy and efficiency, supporting the framework’s usefulness across several related estimation problems.
summary.tldr: Dual sparsity pursuit jointly models structure and errors to unify outlier rejection, model reasoning, and parameter estimation.

title: Robust Model Reasoning and Fitting via Dual Sparsity Pursuit

abstract: Adversarial contrastive learning (ACL) does not require expensive data annotations but outputs a robust representation that withstands adversarial attacks and also generalizes to a wide range of downstream tasks. However, ACL needs tremendous running time to generate the adversarial variants of all training data, which limits its scalability to large datasets. To speed up ACL, this paper proposes a robustness-aware coreset selection (RCS) method. RCS does not require label information and searches for an informative subset that minimizes a representational divergence, which is the distance of the representation between natural data and their virtual adversarial variants. The vanilla solution of RCS via traversing all possible subsets is computationally prohibitive. Therefore, we theoretically transform RCS into a surrogate problem of submodular maximization, of which the greedy search is an efficient solution with an optimality guarantee for the original problem. Empirically, our comprehensive results corroborate that RCS can speed up ACL by a large margin without significantly hurting the robustness transferability. Notably, to the best of our knowledge, we are the first to conduct ACL efficiently on the large-scale ImageNet-1K dataset to obtain an effective robust representation via RCS. Our source code is at https://github.com/GodXuxilie/Efficient_ACL_via_RCS.

paragraphs: Adversarial contrastive learning builds representations without expensive annotations while aiming to withstand adversarial attacks and transfer to other tasks. Its computational burden comes from generating adversarial versions of all training examples. This paper asks whether a carefully selected subset can retain useful robustness while making the learning process substantially faster.

The proposed robustness-aware coreset selection method uses no labels. It searches for an informative subset that minimizes the distance between representations of natural data and their virtual adversarial variants. Exhaustively comparing subsets would be prohibitively expensive, so the authors transform the selection problem into a submodular maximization surrogate. This permits an efficient greedy search with a stated optimality guarantee for the original problem.

Experiments show large speedups without significantly harming the transferability of robustness. The authors also demonstrate efficient adversarial contrastive learning on ImageNet-1K, describing this as the first such result to their knowledge. The contribution connects subset selection directly to representation stability under perturbations, providing a route to scaling robust learning without requiring every training example to receive the same costly treatment.
summary.tldr: Robustness-aware subset selection speeds adversarial contrastive learning substantially while largely preserving the transferability of learned robustness.

title: Efficient Adversarial Contrastive Learning via Robustness-Aware Coreset Selection

abstract: LLMs are seeing growing use for applications which require large context windows, and with these large context windows KV cache activations surface as the dominant contributor to memory consumption during inference. Quantization is a promising approach for compressing KV cache activations; however, existing solutions fail to represent activations accurately in sub-4-bit precision. Our work, KVQuant, facilitates low precision KV cache quantization by incorporating several novel methods: (i) Per-Channel Key Quantization, where we adjust the dimension along which we quantize the Key activations to better match the distribution; (ii) Pre-RoPE Key Quantization, where we quantize Key activations before the rotary positional embedding to mitigate its impact on quantization; (iii) Non-Uniform KV Cache Quantization, where we derive per-layer sensitivity-weighted non-uniform datatypes that better represent the distributions; and (iv) Per-Vector Dense-and-Sparse Quantization, where we isolate outliers separately for each vector to minimize skews in quantization ranges. By applying our method to the LLaMA, Llama-2, Llama-3, and Mistral models, we achieve < 0.1 perplexity degradation with 3-bit quantization on both Wikitext-2 and C4, outperforming existing approaches. Our method enables serving LLaMA-7B with a context length of up to 1 million on a single A100-80GB GPU and up to 10 million on an 8-GPU system. We develop custom CUDA kernels for KVQuant, showing that we can achieve up to ~1.7x speedups, compared to baseline fp16 matrix-vector multiplications, for the LLaMA-7B model.

paragraphs: KVQuant addresses the memory consumed by cached key and value activations when language models process long contexts. Compressing this cache could support much longer inputs, but representing its values with fewer than four bits is difficult without losing accuracy. The method adapts quantization to the structure of these activations.

It quantizes keys by channel and before rotary positional embeddings, uses non-uniform representations tailored to each layer's sensitivity, and separates unusually large values within each vector. These choices address different sources of quantization error: mismatched grouping, positional transformations, uneven value distributions, and outliers that distort the range used for compression.

Across the listed LLaMA-family and Mistral models, three-bit quantization produces less than 0.1 perplexity degradation on Wikitext-2 and C4. The method enables serving LLaMA-7B with up to one million context tokens on one A100-80GB GPU and ten million on eight GPUs. Custom kernels also achieve up to approximately 1.7-fold speedups over baseline fp16 matrix-vector multiplication for LLaMA-7B.
summary.tldr: KVQuant compresses language-model KV caches to three bits with small reported perplexity changes, enabling substantially longer contexts on specified GPU systems.

title: KVQuant: Towards 10 Million Context Length LLM Inference with KV Cache Quantization

abstract: In this paper, we study the non-asymptotic sample complexity for the pure exploration problem in contextual bandits and tabular reinforcement learning (RL): identifying an $\epsilon$-optimal policy from a set of policies $\Pi$ with high probability. Existing work in bandits has shown that it is possible to identify the best policy by estimating only the *difference* between the behaviors of individual policies–which can have substantially lower variance than estimating the behavior of each policy directly—yet the best-known complexities in RL fail to take advantage of this, and instead estimate the behavior of each policy directly. Does it suffice to estimate only the differences in the behaviors of policies in RL? We answer this question positively for contextual bandits, but in the negative for tabular RL, showing a separation between contextual bandits and RL. However, inspired by this, we show that it *almost* suffices to estimate only the differences in RL: if we can estimate the behavior of a *single* reference policy, it suffices to only estimate how any other policy deviates from this reference policy. We develop an algorithm which instantiates this principle and obtains, to the best of our knowledge, the tightest known bound on the sample complexity of tabular RL.

paragraphs: The paper studies how many samples are needed to identify a policy that is within epsilon of optimal from a given policy set, with high probability. Its setting is pure exploration in contextual bandits and tabular reinforcement learning, where the central goal is reliable policy identification.

Previous bandit research shows that estimating differences between policies can have much lower variance than estimating each policy's behavior separately. The authors ask whether differences alone also suffice in reinforcement learning. They answer positively for contextual bandits but negatively for tabular RL, establishing a meaningful separation between the two settings.

The negative result still leaves a useful route forward. In tabular RL, estimating one reference policy's behavior is sufficient to make difference estimates for the other policies useful: each can be assessed through its deviation from that reference. The authors build an algorithm around this principle and report what they believe is the tightest known sample-complexity bound for tabular RL. The contribution identifies both the limit of a differences-only strategy and the additional reference information needed to recover its benefits.
summary.tldr: Policy differences alone do not suffice in tabular RL, but estimating one reference policy enables a difference-based algorithm with a strong sample-complexity bound.

title: Sample Complexity Reduction via Policy Difference Estimation in Tabular Reinforcement Learning

abstract: 3D generation methods have shown visually compelling results powered by diffusion image priors. However, they often fail to produce realistic geometric details, resulting in overly smooth surfaces or geometric details inaccurately baked in albedo maps. To address this, we introduce a new method that incorporates touch as an additional modality to improve the geometric details of generated 3D assets. We design a lightweight 3D texture field to synthesize visual and tactile textures, guided by 2D diffusion model priors on both visual and tactile domains. We condition the visual texture generation on high-resolution tactile normals and guide the patch-based tactile texture refinement with a customized TextureDreambooth. We further present a multi-part generation pipeline that enables us to synthesize different textures across various regions. To our knowledge, we are the first to leverage high-resolution tactile sensing to enhance geometric details for 3D generation tasks. We evaluate our method in both text-to-3D and image-to-3D settings. Our experiments demonstrate that our method provides customized and realistic fine geometric textures while maintaining accurate alignment between two modalities of vision and touch.

paragraphs: Image-guided 3D generation can produce convincing appearances while leaving the underlying surface too smooth. It can also encode apparent geometric detail in surface color instead of actual geometry. Tactile DreamFusion introduces touch information to help generated assets contain realistic fine surface structure as well as plausible visual appearance.

The method uses a lightweight 3D texture field guided by diffusion priors from both visual and tactile domains. High-resolution tactile normals condition visual texture generation, linking appearance to detailed surface orientation. A customized TextureDreambooth guides tactile refinement on local patches, and a multi-part pipeline allows different regions of an object to receive different textures.

The authors evaluate the approach for both text-to-3D and image-to-3D generation. Their experiments report realistic, customizable fine geometric textures while maintaining alignment between visual and tactile modalities. The significance is that touch contributes information about surface structure that visual generation alone may represent inadequately. The combined system aims to make the generated asset’s appearance and geometric texture agree, including when different regions require different surface treatments.
summary.tldr: Tactile DreamFusion combines visual and touch-based diffusion guidance to generate finer, mutually aligned surface geometry and appearance.

title: Tactile DreamFusion: Exploiting Tactile Sensing for 3D Generation

abstract: As large language models (LLMs) develop increasingly sophisticated capabilities and find applications in medical settings, it becomes important to assess their medical safety due to their far-reaching implications for personal and public health, patient safety, and human rights. However, there is little to no understanding of the notion of medical safety in the context of LLMs, let alone how to evaluate and improve it. To address this gap, we first define the notion of medical safety in LLMs based on the Principles of Medical Ethics set forth by the American Medical Association. We then leverage this understanding to introduce MedSafetyBench, the first benchmark dataset designed to measure the medical safety of LLMs. We demonstrate the utility of MedSafetyBench by using it to evaluate and improve the medical safety of LLMs. Our results show that publicly-available medical LLMs do not meet standards of medical safety and that fine-tuning them using MedSafetyBench improves their medical safety while preserving their medical performance. By introducing this new benchmark dataset, our work enables a systematic study of the state of medical safety in LLMs and motivates future work in this area, paving the way to mitigate the safety risks of LLMs in medicine. The benchmark dataset and code are available at https://github.com/AI4LIFE-GROUP/med-safety-bench.

paragraphs: As language models enter medical settings, assessing their capabilities also requires a clear account of medical safety. This paper addresses how to define, evaluate, and improve that safety. It grounds its definition in the American Medical Association’s Principles of Medical Ethics, connecting evaluation to an explicit ethical framework.

The authors introduce MedSafetyBench, a dataset designed around that definition, and use it to evaluate publicly available medical language models. Their results show that the evaluated models fall short of the medical safety standards being assessed. The benchmark turns a broad concern about harmful medical use into a target for systematic comparison and improvement.

The paper also uses MedSafetyBench for fine-tuning and reports improved medical safety while preserving medical performance. That result suggests the assessed safety behaviors can be improved without sacrificing the medical capabilities measured in the study. The contribution combines a definition, an evaluation resource, and an intervention, enabling research to examine safety explicitly alongside medical task performance rather than treating capability alone as sufficient evidence of safe behavior.
summary.tldr: MedSafetyBench evaluates medical language models against an ethics-based safety framework and improves measured safety through fine-tuning.

title: MedSafetyBench: Evaluating and Improving the Medical Safety of Large Language Models

abstract: As part of an ongoing worldwide effort to comprehend and monitor insect biodiversity, this paper presents the BIOSCAN-5M Insect dataset to the machine learning community and establish several benchmark tasks. BIOSCAN-5M is a comprehensive dataset containing multi-modal information for over 5 million insect specimens, and it significantly expands existing image-based biological datasets by including taxonomic labels, raw nucleotide barcode sequences, assigned barcode index numbers, geographical, and size information. We propose three benchmark experiments to demonstrate the impact of the multi-modal data types on the classification and clustering accuracy. First, we pretrain a masked language model on the DNA barcode sequences of the BIOSCAN-5M dataset, and demonstrate the impact of using this large reference library on species- and genus-level classification performance. Second, we propose a zero-shot transfer learning task applied to images and DNA barcodes to cluster feature embeddings obtained from self-supervised learning, to investigate whether meaningful clusters can be derived from these representation embeddings. Third, we benchmark multi-modality by performing contrastive learning on DNA barcodes, image data, and taxonomic information. This yields a general shared embedding space enabling taxonomic classification using multiple types of information and modalities. The code repository of the BIOSCAN-5M Insect dataset is available at https://github.com/bioscan-ml/BIOSCAN-5M.

paragraphs: BIOSCAN-5M brings together information about more than five million insect specimens to support biodiversity research. Alongside images, it includes taxonomic labels, DNA barcode sequences, assigned barcode index numbers, geographic information, and specimen sizes. This gives researchers several connected views of the same biological specimens instead of relying entirely on visual appearance.

The paper introduces three benchmark experiments. The first trains a masked language model on DNA barcode sequences and examines how this large reference collection affects classification at the species and genus levels. The second investigates whether representations learned through self-supervision support meaningful clustering in a zero-shot transfer task involving images and DNA barcodes.

The third experiment uses contrastive learning to connect DNA, images, and taxonomy within a shared representation space. That space supports taxonomic classification from multiple kinds of information. Together, the dataset and tasks provide a way to investigate how these modalities contribute to classification and clustering, and whether their learned representations capture biologically useful groupings.
summary.tldr: BIOSCAN-5M pairs information from over five million insects with benchmarks connecting images, DNA barcodes, and taxonomy.

title: BIOSCAN-5M: A Multimodal Dataset for Insect Biodiversity

abstract: Navigating the vast chemical space of druggable compounds is a formidable challenge in drug discovery, where generative models are increasingly employed to identify viable candidates. Conditional 3D structure-based drug design (3D-SBDD) models, which take into account complex three-dimensional interactions and molecular geometries, are particularly promising. Scaffold hopping is an efficient strategy that facilitates the identification of similar active compounds by strategically modifying the core structure of molecules, effectively narrowing the wide chemical space and enhancing the discovery of drug-like products. However, the practical application of 3D-SBDD generative models is hampered by their slow processing speeds. To address this bottleneck, we introduce TurboHopp, an accelerated pocket-conditioned 3D scaffold hopping model that merges the strategic effectiveness of traditional scaffold hopping with rapid generation capabilities of consistency models. This synergy not only enhances efficiency but also significantly boosts generation speeds, achieving up to 30 times faster inference speed as well as superior generation quality compared to existing diffusion-based models, establishing TurboHopp as a powerful tool in drug discovery. Supported by faster inference speed, we further optimize our model, using Reinforcement Learning for Consistency Models (RLCM), to output desirable molecules. We demonstrate the broad applicability of TurboHopp across multiple drug discovery scenarios, underscoring its potential in diverse molecular settings.The code is provided at https://github.com/orgw/TurboHopp

paragraphs: Scaffold hopping searches for related candidate molecules by changing their core structure. It narrows the enormous chemical search space while seeking compounds with useful activity. TurboHopp combines this strategy with three-dimensional generation conditioned on a binding pocket, addressing the slow processing of existing structure-based generative approaches.

The model uses consistency models to accelerate molecule generation while accounting for the pocket and molecular geometry. The authors report inference speeds up to thirty times faster than existing diffusion-based models, together with better generation quality. Faster generation is central to the approach because it reduces the time required to produce candidate molecular structures.

The paper then uses Reinforcement Learning for Consistency Models to further optimize generation toward desirable molecules. It demonstrates the approach across multiple drug-discovery scenarios, supporting its potential across different molecular settings. The contribution joins a focused search strategy with rapid generation and subsequent optimization: scaffold hopping defines the type of structural change being explored, while the generative model makes that exploration faster.
summary.tldr: TurboHopp uses consistency models for pocket-conditioned scaffold hopping, reporting up to thirtyfold faster inference and improved molecular generation quality.

title: TurboHopp: Accelerated Molecule Scaffold Hopping with Consistency Models

abstract: 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) has shown promising results in image rendering and surface reconstruction. However, its potential in volumetric reconstruction tasks, such as X-ray computed tomography, remains under-explored. This paper introduces R$^2$-Gaussian, the first 3DGS-based framework for sparse-view tomographic reconstruction. By carefully deriving X-ray rasterization functions, we discover a previously unknown \emph{integration bias} in the standard 3DGS formulation, which hampers accurate volume retrieval. To address this issue, we propose a novel rectification technique via refactoring the projection from 3D to 2D Gaussians. Our new method presents three key innovations: (1) introducing tailored Gaussian kernels, (2) extending rasterization to X-ray imaging, and (3) developing a CUDA-based differentiable voxelizer. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in accuracy and efficiency. Crucially, it delivers high-quality results in 4 minutes, which is 12$\times$ faster than NeRF-based methods and on par with traditional algorithms.

paragraphs: R²-Gaussian adapts 3D Gaussian splatting to sparse-view tomography, where a volume must be reconstructed from a limited collection of X-ray views. Although Gaussian splatting has shown promise for rendering images and reconstructing surfaces, recovering an entire volume poses a different challenge. The authors derive X-ray rasterization functions and identify an integration bias in the standard formulation that interferes with accurate volume recovery.

Their correction changes how three-dimensional Gaussians are projected into two dimensions. The framework combines Gaussian kernels tailored to the task, rasterization extended to X-ray imaging, and a CUDA-based differentiable voxelizer. These components connect the corrected Gaussian representation to volumetric reconstruction while supporting efficient computation.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data report better accuracy and efficiency than state-of-the-art approaches. The method produces high-quality reconstructions in four minutes, reported as 12 times faster than NeRF-based methods and comparable in speed to traditional algorithms. The key finding is that correcting the projection's integration behavior makes Gaussian splatting useful for fast reconstruction of volumetric information.
summary.tldr: R²-Gaussian corrects an integration bias in Gaussian splatting to deliver accurate sparse-view tomographic reconstructions in four minutes.

title: R$^2$-Gaussian: Rectifying Radiative Gaussian Splatting for Tomographic Reconstruction

abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved tremendous success in various applications, they are also susceptible to jailbreaking attacks. Several primary defense strategies have been proposed to protect LLMs from producing harmful information, mostly focusing on model fine-tuning or heuristical defense designs. However, how to achieve intrinsic robustness through prompt optimization remains an open problem. In this paper, motivated by adversarial training paradigms for achieving reliable robustness, we propose an approach named **Prompt Adversarial Tuning (PAT)** that trains a prompt control attached to the user prompt as a guard prefix. To achieve our defense goal whilst maintaining natural performance, we optimize the control prompt with both adversarial and benign prompts. Comprehensive experiments show that our method is effective against both grey-box and black-box attacks, reducing the success rate of advanced attacks to nearly 0, while maintaining the model's utility on the benign task and incurring only negligible computational overhead, charting a new perspective for future explorations in LLM security. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-ML/PAT.

paragraphs: Jailbreaking attacks try to make language models produce harmful responses despite their safeguards. Many defenses rely on changing model weights or manually designed rules. This paper investigates whether optimizing an added prompt can provide an effective defense while preserving the model’s ability to answer ordinary requests.

Prompt Adversarial Tuning, or PAT, learns a control prompt that is attached as a guard prefix to the user’s prompt. Its optimization uses both adversarial inputs and benign requests. Including both kinds of input makes the training objective address attack resistance alongside normal task performance, rather than measuring defensive behavior in isolation.

The reported experiments cover grey-box and black-box attacks. PAT reduces the success rates of advanced attacks to nearly zero in those evaluations, preserves utility on the benign task, and adds negligible computational overhead. The result supports prompt optimization as a practical direction for language-model defense. The empirical scope matters: nearly zero success on the evaluated attacks does not establish that every future jailbreak will fail.
summary.tldr: PAT learns a guard prefix from adversarial and benign prompts, sharply reducing evaluated jailbreak success while preserving ordinary task utility.

title: Fight Back Against Jailbreaking via Prompt Adversarial Tuning

abstract: Accurately restoring topology is both challenging and crucial in tubular structure extraction tasks, such as blood vessel segmentation and road network extraction. Diverging from traditional approaches based on pixel-level classification, our proposed method, named GraphMorph, focuses on branch-level features of tubular structures to achieve more topologically accurate predictions. GraphMorph comprises two main components: a Graph Decoder and a Morph Module. Utilizing multi-scale features extracted from an image patch by the segmentation network, the Graph Decoder facilitates the learning of branch-level features and generates a graph that accurately represents the tubular structure in this patch. The Morph Module processes two primary inputs: the graph and the centerline probability map, provided by the Graph Decoder and the segmentation network, respectively. Employing a novel SkeletonDijkstra algorithm, the Morph Module produces a centerline mask that aligns with the predicted graph. Furthermore, we observe that employing centerline masks predicted by GraphMorph significantly reduces false positives in the segmentation task, which is achieved by a simple yet effective post-processing strategy. The efficacy of our method in the centerline extraction and segmentation tasks has been substantiated through experimental evaluations across various datasets. Source code will be released soon.
