paragraphs: Extracting blood vessels or road networks requires recovering how branches connect, as well as identifying the pixels they occupy. GraphMorph approaches this through branch-level features. Its purpose is to produce predictions with more accurate topology by explicitly representing the tubular structure as a graph within each image patch.

A Graph Decoder takes features at multiple scales from a segmentation network and predicts that graph. A separate Morph Module then combines the graph with the network's centerline probability map. Using the proposed SkeletonDijkstra algorithm, it creates a centerline mask aligned with the predicted graph, linking the branch representation to an image-based output.

The authors also use GraphMorph's centerline masks in a simple post-processing strategy for segmentation. They observe a significant reduction in false positives, showing that the structural prediction can improve the broader segmentation result as well as centerline extraction. Evaluations across multiple datasets support both uses. The method's central contribution is a connection between learned branch structure and the final centerline mask.
summary.tldr: GraphMorph predicts branch graphs and converts them into centerline masks to improve tubular topology and reduce segmentation false positives.

title: GraphMorph: Tubular Structure Extraction by Morphing Predicted Graphs

abstract: Partial observability in environments poses significant challenges that impede the formation of effective policies in reinforcement learning. Prior research has shown that borrowing the complete state information can enhance sample efficiency. This strategy, however, frequently encounters unstable learning with high variance in practical applications due to the over-reliance on complete information. This paper introduces DCRL, a Dual Critic Reinforcement Learning framework designed to adaptively harness full-state information during training to reduce variance for optimized online performance. In particular, DCRL incorporates two distinct critics: an oracle critic with access to complete state information and a standard critic functioning within the partially observable context. It innovates a synergistic strategy to meld the strengths of the oracle critic for efficiency improvement and the standard critic for variance reduction, featuring a novel mechanism for seamless transition and weighting between them. We theoretically prove that DCRL mitigates the learning variance while maintaining unbiasedness. Extensive experimental analyses across the Box2D and Box3D environments have verified DCRL's superior performance. The source code is available in the supplementary.

paragraphs: An agent in a partially observable environment must learn from observations that omit some of the underlying state. Training can sometimes access complete state information, which can improve sample efficiency. However, the paper identifies a practical difficulty: relying too heavily on that complete information can produce high-variance updates and unstable learning.

Dual Critic Reinforcement Learning, or DCRL, uses two critics to manage this tension. An oracle critic receives the full state, while a standard critic operates with partial observations. The framework adaptively weights and transitions between their contributions. The intended division of labor is to use the oracle's information for efficiency while drawing on the standard critic to reduce variance.

The authors prove that DCRL reduces learning variance while retaining unbiasedness, and report superior performance in experiments across Box2D and Box3D environments. The approach therefore treats privileged training information as something to combine adaptively with the agent's restricted perspective. Full-state access during training is central to this setup; the framework is designed to improve online performance under partial observability.
summary.tldr: DCRL adaptively combines full-state and partially informed critics to reduce training variance while preserving unbiasedness.

title: Dual Critic Reinforcement Learning under Partial Observability

abstract: In the rapidly evolving domain of vision-based deep reinforcement learning (RL), a pivotal challenge is to achieve generalization capability to dynamic environmental changes reflected in visual observations.Our work delves into the intricacies of this problem, identifying two key issues that appear in previous approaches for visual RL generalization: (i) imbalanced saliency and (ii) observational overfitting.Imbalanced saliency is a phenomenon where an RL agent disproportionately identifies salient features across consecutive frames in a frame stack. Observational overfitting occurs when the agent focuses on certain background regions rather than task-relevant objects.To address these challenges, we present a simple yet effective framework for generalization in visual RL (SimGRL) under dynamic scene perturbations.First, to mitigate the imbalanced saliency problem, we introduce an architectural modification to the image encoder to stack frames at the feature level rather than the image level.Simultaneously, to alleviate the observational overfitting problem, we propose a novel technique called shifted random overlay augmentation, which is specifically designed to learn robust representations capable of effectively handling dynamic visual scenes.Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior generalization capability of SimGRL, achieving state-of-the-art performance in benchmarks including the DeepMind Control Suite.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent that acts from images can struggle when the scene changes visually. This paper identifies two problems in earlier approaches: the agent may assign uneven importance to consecutive frames, and it may rely on particular background regions instead of the objects relevant to its task. Both problems concern which visual information the agent learns to use.

The proposed framework, SimGRL, addresses these problems with two targeted changes. Its image encoder combines frames after extracting their features, rather than stacking the original images together. This modification is intended to reduce the uneven treatment of successive frames. The framework also introduces shifted random overlay augmentation, a training technique designed to reduce reliance on backgrounds under dynamic visual changes.

Experiments report stronger generalization and state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks including the DeepMind Control Suite. The findings support combining changes to temporal representation with visual augmentation: one addresses how information from different frames enters the model, while the other addresses sensitivity to distracting scene content.
summary.tldr: SimGRL improves visual reinforcement learning generalization by changing how frames are combined and augmenting scenes to reduce background dependence.

title: A Simple Framework for Generalization in Visual RL under Dynamic Scene Perturbations

abstract: Detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) samples is important for deploying machine learning models in safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving and robot-assisted surgery. Existing research has mainly focused on unimodal scenarios on image data. However, real-world applications are inherently multimodal, which makes it essential to leverage information from multiple modalities to enhance the efficacy of OOD detection. To establish a foundation for more realistic Multimodal OOD Detection, we introduce the first-of-its-kind benchmark, MultiOOD, characterized by diverse dataset sizes and varying modality combinations. We first evaluate existing unimodal OOD detection algorithms on MultiOOD, observing that the mere inclusion of additional modalities yields substantial improvements. This underscores the importance of utilizing multiple modalities for OOD detection. Based on the observation of Modality Prediction Discrepancy between in-distribution (ID) and OOD data, and its strong correlation with OOD performance, we propose the Agree-to-Disagree (A2D) algorithm to encourage such discrepancy during training. Moreover, we introduce a novel outlier synthesis method, NP-Mix, which explores broader feature spaces by leveraging the information from nearest neighbor classes and complements A2D to strengthen OOD detection performance. Extensive experiments on MultiOOD demonstrate that training with A2D and NP-Mix improves existing OOD detection algorithms by a large margin. To support accessibility and reproducibility, our source code and MultiOOD benchmark are available at https://github.com/donghao51/MultiOOD.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection identifies inputs that differ from the data a model is intended to handle. Much existing work focuses on images alone, while applications can combine several kinds of information. This paper introduces MultiOOD, a benchmark with varying dataset sizes and modality combinations, to support evaluation in that broader setting.

Testing existing unimodal detection algorithms on the benchmark shows substantial improvements from including additional modalities. The authors also observe a relationship between detection performance and disagreement among modality-specific predictions. They build on that observation with Agree-to-Disagree, a training algorithm that encourages the relevant prediction discrepancy.

A second component, NP-Mix, synthesizes outliers using information from nearest-neighbor classes to explore a broader feature space. It complements the disagreement-based training strategy. Experiments on MultiOOD show that combining A2D and NP-Mix improves existing detection algorithms by a large margin. The work therefore contributes both an evaluation resource and a training approach that uses relationships between modalities to strengthen detection of unfamiliar inputs.
summary.tldr: MultiOOD benchmarks multimodal outlier detection, while disagreement-based training and synthesized outliers substantially improve the evaluated detectors.

title: MultiOOD: Scaling Out-of-Distribution Detection for Multiple Modalities

abstract: Test-time adaptation aims to improve model robustness under distribution shifts by adapting models with access to unlabeled target samples. A primary cause of performance degradation under such shifts is the model’s reliance on features that lack a direct causal relationship with the prediction target. We introduce Test-time Adaptation by Causal Trimming (TACT), a method that identifies and removes non-causal components from representations for test distributions. TACT applies data augmentations that preserve causal features while varying non-causal ones. By analyzing the changes in the representations using Principal Component Analysis, TACT identifies the highest variance directions associated with non-causal features. It trims the representations by removing their projections on the identified directions, and uses the trimmed representations for the predictions. During adaptation, TACT continuously tracks and refines these directions to get a better estimate of non-causal features. We theoretically analyze the effectiveness of this approach and empirically validate TACT on real-world out-of-distribution benchmarks. TACT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin.

paragraphs: Models can fail when their deployment data differs from training data because they rely on features that lack a direct causal relationship with the target. Test-time Adaptation by Causal Trimming, or TACT, addresses this problem using unlabeled samples from the target distribution. It adapts predictions by removing representation components associated with non-causal variation.

TACT applies augmentations designed to preserve causal features while changing non-causal ones. It examines the resulting representation changes with Principal Component Analysis and identifies directions with the highest variance. Under this augmentation design, those directions are associated with non-causal features. The method removes representations' projections onto them and makes predictions using the trimmed representations.

As adaptation continues, TACT tracks and refines the selected directions to improve its estimate of non-causal variation. The authors theoretically analyze the approach and evaluate it on real-world out-of-distribution benchmarks, reporting consistent, significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The mechanism depends on augmentations that distinguish the unwanted variation from features that should remain useful for prediction.
summary.tldr: TACT uses causal-feature-preserving augmentations to identify and remove non-causal representation directions during test-time adaptation.

title: Test-Time Adaptation by Causal Trimming

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle with mathematical reasoning tasks requiring precise, verifiable computation. While Reinforcement Learning (RL) from outcome-based rewards enhances text-based reasoning, understanding how agents autonomously learn to leverage external tools like code execution remains crucial. We investigate RL from outcome-based rewards for Tool-Integrated Reasoning, ZeroTIR, training base LLMs to spontaneously generate and execute Python code for mathematical problems without supervised tool-use examples. Our central contribution is we demonstrate that as RL training progresses, key metrics scale predictably. Specifically, we observe strong positive correlations where increased training steps lead to increases in the spontaneous code execution frequency, the average response length, and, critically, the final task accuracy. This suggests a quantifiable relationship between computational effort invested in training and the emergence of effective, tool-augmented reasoning strategies. We implement a robust framework featuring a decoupled code execution environment and validate our findings across standard RL algorithms and frameworks. Experiments show ZeroTIR significantly surpasses non-tool ZeroRL baselines on challenging math benchmarks. Our findings provide a foundational understanding of how autonomous tool use is acquired and scales within Agent RL, offering a reproducible benchmark for future studies. Code is released at \href{https://github.com/yyht/openrlhf_async_pipline}{https://github.com/yyht/openrlhf\_async\_pipline}.

paragraphs: Mathematical problem solving often requires calculations that must be exact and checkable. This paper investigates whether language models can learn to use Python execution through reinforcement learning driven by final outcomes, without supervised examples demonstrating tool use. Its approach, ZeroTIR, trains base models to generate and execute code as part of solving mathematics problems.

The central finding concerns how behavior changes during training. Across the reported experiments, additional training steps correlate strongly with more frequent spontaneous code execution, longer average responses, and higher final accuracy. These observations suggest a measurable relationship between training effort and the development of useful tool-assisted reasoning. They describe observed scaling behavior rather than establishing that every additional step or code execution necessarily improves an answer.

The implementation separates code execution from the training framework and tests the findings across standard reinforcement-learning algorithms and frameworks. ZeroTIR substantially outperforms non-tool ZeroRL baselines on challenging mathematics benchmarks. Together, the results show that outcome rewards can support the acquisition of tool use and provide a reproducible framework for studying how that ability develops.
summary.tldr: ZeroTIR learns Python use from outcome rewards, with training progress correlated with more tool execution, longer responses, and better mathematics accuracy.

title: Agentic RL Scaling Law: Spontaneous Code Execution for Mathematical Problem Solving

abstract: Search-augmented LLMs often struggle with complex reasoning tasks due to ineffective multi-hop retrieval and limited reasoning ability. We propose AceSearcher, a cooperative self-play framework that trains a single large language model (LLM) to alternate between two roles: a decomposer that breaks down complex queries and a solver that integrates retrieved contexts for answer generation. AceSearcher couples supervised fine-tuning on a diverse mixture of search, reasoning, and decomposition tasks with reinforcement fine-tuning optimized for final answer accuracy, eliminating the need for intermediate annotations. Extensive experiments on three reasoning-intensive tasks across 10 datasets show that AceSearcher outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving an average exact match improvement of 7.6%. Remarkably, on document-level finance reasoning tasks, AceSearcher-32B matches the performance of the giant DeepSeek-V3 model using less than 5% of iits parameters. Even at smaller scales (1.5B and 8B), AceSearcher often surpasses existing search-augmented LLMs with up to 9× more parameters, highlighting its exceptional efficiency and effectiveness in tackling complex reasoning tasks.

paragraphs: Search can supply a language model with relevant information, but complex questions also require deciding what to retrieve and connecting evidence across steps. AceSearcher addresses these linked difficulties by training one model to alternate between two cooperating roles: decomposing a question into smaller queries and solving it using retrieved context.

Training begins with supervised examples covering search, reasoning, and decomposition. Reinforcement fine-tuning then rewards final answer accuracy, allowing the two roles to improve together without intermediate annotations for that stage. This connects the usefulness of question decomposition to the quality of the eventual answer, rather than evaluating the retrieval and reasoning processes only in isolation.

Across ten datasets spanning three reasoning-intensive tasks, AceSearcher reports an average exact match improvement of 7.6% over leading baselines. On document-level finance reasoning, its 32-billion-parameter version matches DeepSeek-V3 with less than 5% of its parameters. Smaller versions also often beat search-augmented models up to nine times larger, supporting the effectiveness of the cooperative training approach.
summary.tldr: AceSearcher trains one language model to cooperate with itself as a query decomposer and evidence-based solver, improving search-intensive reasoning.

title: AceSearcher: Bootstrapping Reasoning and Search for LLMs via Reinforced Self-Play

abstract: Deep neural networks trained with gradient descent exhibit varying rates of learning for different patterns. However, the complexity of fitting models to data makes direct elucidation of the dynamics of learned patterns challenging. To circumvent this, many works have opted to characterize phases of learning through summary statistics known as order parameters. In this work, we propose a unifying framework for constructing order parameters based on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK), in which the relationship with the data set is more transparent. In particular, we derive a local approximation of the NTK for a class of deep regression models (SIRENs) trained to reconstruct natural images. In so doing, we analytically connect three seemingly distinct phase transitions: the emergence of wave patterns in residuals (a novel observation), loss rate collapse, and NTK alignment. Our results provide a dynamical perspective on the observed biases of SIRENs, and deep image regression models more generally.

summary.tldr: An NTK-based analysis connects three changes in SIREN image reconstruction training, revealing a shared account of their learning dynamics.

title: A Closer Look at NTK Alignment: Linking Phase Transitions in Deep Image Regression

abstract: We take two key steps in automating the open-ended discovery of new mathematical theories, a grand challenge in artificial intelligence. First, we introduce Fermat, a reinforcement learning (RL) environment that models concept discovery and theorem-proving using a set of symbolic actions, opening up a range of RL problems relevant to theory discovery. Second, we explore a specific problem through Fermat: automatically scoring the interestingness of mathematical objects. We investigate evolutionary algorithms for synthesizing nontrivial interestingness measures. In particular, we introduce an LLM-based evolutionary algorithm that features function abstraction, leading to notable improvements in discovering elementary number theory and finite fields over hard-coded baselines. We open-source the \fermat environment at github.com/trishullab/Fermat.

paragraphs: Automating mathematical theory formation involves both developing concepts and proving theorems about them. An open-ended discovery system also needs a way to decide which mathematical objects deserve attention. This paper contributes an environment for studying that broader process and investigates how a system can learn measures of mathematical interestingness.

The environment, Fermat, represents concept discovery and theorem proving through symbolic actions. This makes those activities available as reinforcement-learning problems. Within Fermat, the authors examine evolutionary algorithms that synthesize nontrivial scoring measures, making the criteria for interestingness themselves objects of search rather than relying entirely on fixed, manually written scores.

Their proposed evolutionary algorithm uses a language model and includes function abstraction. It produces notable improvements over hard-coded baselines in discovery involving elementary number theory and finite fields. These results support learning useful discovery criteria in the studied mathematical settings. The open-source Fermat environment also provides a shared setting for investigating additional reinforcement-learning problems related to theory discovery.
summary.tldr: Fermat provides a symbolic mathematical discovery environment where an LLM-based evolutionary algorithm learns useful interestingness measures.

title: Learning Interestingness in Automated Mathematical Theory Formation

abstract: Geometric graph neural networks (GNNs) that respect E(3) symmetries have achieved strong performance on small molecule modeling, but they face scalability and expressiveness challenges when applied to large biomolecules such as RNA and proteins. These systems require models that can simultaneously capture fine-grained atomic interactions, long-range dependencies across spatially distant components, and biologically relevant hierarchical structure—such as atoms forming residues, which in turn form higher-order domains. Existing geometric GNNs, which typically operate exclusively in either Euclidean or Spherical Harmonics space, are limited in their ability to capture both the fine-scale atomic details and the long-range, symmetry-aware dependencies required for modeling the multi-scale structure of large biomolecules. We introduce DualEquiNet, a Dual-Space Hierarchical Equivariant Network that constructs complementary representations in both Euclidean and Spherical Harmonics spaces to capture local geometry and global symmetry-aware features. DualEquiNet employs bidirectional cross-space message passing and a novel Cross-Space Interaction Pooling mechanism to hierarchically aggregate atomic features into biologically meaningful units, such as residues, enabling efficient and expressive multi-scale modeling for large biomolecular systems. DualEquiNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple existing benchmarks for RNA property prediction and protein modeling, and outperforms prior methods on two newly introduced 3D structural benchmarks demonstrating its broad effectiveness across a range of large biomolecule modeling tasks.

The paper argues that geometric graph networks operating only in Euclidean space or only in spherical harmonics space have difficulty capturing all these scales efficiently and expressively.

DualEquiNet builds complementary representations in both spaces. Its Euclidean representation captures local geometry, while its spherical harmonics representation captures global features that respect spatial symmetries. Information passes in both directions between the spaces, allowing their different strengths to contribute to the same molecular model.

A cross-space pooling mechanism then combines atomic features into meaningful higher-level units such as residues. This hierarchy connects the dual representations to the molecule's biological structure. The authors report state-of-the-art results on multiple existing RNA prediction and protein modeling benchmarks, plus improvements over prior methods on two newly introduced 3D structural benchmarks. The findings support combining spatial representations and hierarchical aggregation for the evaluated large-biomolecule tasks.
summary.tldr: DualEquiNet combines two geometric representation spaces with biological hierarchy to improve large-biomolecule modeling.

title: DualEqui: A Dual-Space Hierarchical Equivariant Network for Large Biomolecules

abstract: We introduce H-SPLID, a novel algorithm for learning salient feature representations through the explicit decomposition of salient and non-salient features into separate spaces. We show that H-SPLID promotes learning low-dimensional, task-relevant features. We prove that the expected prediction deviation under input perturbations is upper-bounded by the dimension of the salient subspace and the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) between inputs and representations. This establishes a link between robustness and latent representation compression in terms of the dimensionality and information preserved. Empirical evaluations on image classification tasks show that models trained with H-SPLID primarily rely on salient input components, as indicated by reduced sensitivity to perturbations affecting non-salient features, such as image backgrounds.

paragraphs: A model can perform well while depending on irrelevant input details, such as a background correlated with the label. H-SPLID explicitly decomposes salient and nonsalient information into separate representation spaces, aiming to retain a compact set of task-relevant features.

The authors prove an upper bound on expected prediction deviation under input perturbations. The bound depends on the salient subspace’s dimension and the Hilbert–Schmidt Independence Criterion between inputs and representations, connecting robustness with both representation size and preserved information.

The theoretical and empirical results jointly motivate compression that is selective rather than indiscriminate: the objective is to preserve useful predictive content while limiting pathways through which irrelevant variation can change the prediction.
summary.tldr: H-SPLID separates salient and nonsalient features and links compressed representations to perturbation robustness.

title: H-SPLID: HSIC-based Saliency Preserving Latent Information Decomposition

abstract: Leveraging diffusion models, 3D LiDAR scene generation has achieved great success in both range-view and voxel-based representations. While recent voxel-based approaches can generate both geometric structures and semantic labels, existing range-view methods are limited to producing unlabeled LiDAR scenes. Relying on pretrained segmentation models to predict the semantic maps often results in suboptimal cross-modal consistency. To address this limitation while preserving the advantages of range-view representations, such as computational efficiency and simplified network design, we propose Spiral, a novel range-view LiDAR diffusion model that simultaneously generates depth, reflectance images, and semantic maps. Furthermore, we introduce novel semantic-aware metrics to evaluate the quality of the generated labeled range-view data. Experiments on SemanticKITTI and nuScenes datasets demonstrate that Spiral achieves state-of-the-art performance with the smallest parameter size, outperforming two-step methods that combine the best available generative and segmentation models. Additionally, we validate that Spiral’s generated range images can be effectively used for synthetic data augmentation in the downstream segmentation training, significantly reducing the labeling effort on LiDAR data.

paragraphs: Synthetic LiDAR scenes are more useful for understanding tasks when their geometry comes with matching semantic labels. Existing range-view generators produce unlabeled scenes, leaving a separate segmentation model to add labels afterward. Spiral addresses the inconsistency that can arise between those separately generated outputs while retaining the efficiency and simpler network design of range-view representations.

Spiral is a diffusion model that jointly generates depth, reflectance, and semantic maps. Bringing these outputs into one generation process makes their relationship part of the modeling task. The authors also introduce semantic-aware evaluation metrics, so assessment considers the quality of labeled range-view data rather than geometry alone.

On SemanticKITTI and nuScenes, Spiral reports state-of-the-art performance with the smallest parameter count among the compared methods. It outperforms two-stage systems assembled from leading generation and segmentation models. The generated range images also improve downstream segmentation training through synthetic augmentation, substantially reducing labeling effort. These findings connect joint generation to both output consistency and a practical use for synthetic labeled data.
summary.tldr: Spiral jointly generates LiDAR geometry, reflectance, and labels, producing useful synthetic training data with strong benchmark performance.

title: Spiral: Semantic-Aware Progressive LiDAR Scene Generation and Understanding

abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained Large Language Models (LLMs) for downstream tasks using First-Order (FO) optimizers presents significant computational challenges. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning~(PEFT) methods have been proposed to address these challenges by freezing most model parameters and training only a small subset. While PEFT is efficient, it may not outperform full fine-tuning when high task-specific performance is required. Zeroth-Order (ZO) methods offer an alternative for fine-tuning the entire pre-trained model by approximating gradients using only the forward pass, thus eliminating the computational burden of back-propagation, % in first-order methods, but they converge painfully slowly and are very sensitive to the choice of task prompts. We bridge these worlds with Bilevel‑ZOFO, a penalty‑based bilevel formulation that treats adapter parameters as a lower‑level learner coupled to an upper‑level ZO optimizer of the full backbone. This double-loop optimization strategy only requires the gradient of the PEFT model and the forward pass of the base model. We provide theoretical convergence guarantees for Bilevel ZOFO. Empirically, we demonstrate that Bilevel-ZOFO significantly outperforms existing ZO methods, achieves 2–4$\times$ faster training, and reduces sensitivity to prompts. Bilevel-ZOFO also outperforms FO PEFT methods while maintaining similar memory efficiency. Additionally, we show its strong potential for meta learning.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a large language model presents a trade-off between how much of the model can change and the resources needed to train it. Parameter-efficient methods update a small subset of parameters. Zeroth-order methods can update the full model using forward passes to approximate gradients, but the abstract identifies slow convergence and prompt sensitivity as problems.

Bilevel-ZOFO combines these approaches through two coupled optimization levels. An inner learner trains adapter parameters, while an outer zeroth-order optimizer updates the full backbone. A penalty-based formulation connects their objectives. This arrangement requires gradients for the parameter-efficient component and forward passes through the base model, bringing broader model adaptation together with economical gradient computation.

The paper provides convergence guarantees and reports stronger empirical performance than existing zeroth-order methods, with training two to four times faster and reduced prompt sensitivity. It also outperforms first-order parameter-efficient methods while using similar memory. The authors additionally demonstrate potential for meta-learning, extending the motivation beyond adaptation to a single downstream task.
summary.tldr: Bilevel-ZOFO couples gradient-trained adapters with forward-pass optimization of the full model to improve fine-tuning efficiency and performance.

title: Bilevel ZOFO: Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning and Meta-Training

abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) serves as a highly performant and efficient encoding of scene geometry, appearance, and semantics. Moreover, grounding language in 3D scenes has proven to be an effective strategy for 3D scene understanding. Current Language Gaussian Splatting line of work fall into three main groups: (i) per-scene optimization-based, (ii) per-scene optimization-free, and (iii) generalizable approach. However, most of them are evaluated only on rendered 2D views of a handful of scenes and viewpoints close to the training views, limiting ability and insight into holistic 3D understanding. To address this gap, we propose the first large-scale benchmark that systematically assesses these three groups of methods directly in 3D space, evaluating on 1060 scenes across three indoor datasets and one outdoor dataset. Benchmark results demonstrate a clear advantage of the generalizable paradigm, particularly in relaxing the scene-specific limitation, enabling fast feed-forward inference on novel scenes, and achieving superior segmentation performance. We further introduce SceneSplat-49K -- a carefully curated 3DGS dataset comprising of around 49K diverse indoor and outdoor scenes trained from multiple sources, with which we demonstrate generalizable approach could harness strong data priors. Our codes, benchmark, and datasets are available.

paragraphs: Language Gaussian Splatting connects language with three-dimensional scene representations that encode geometry, appearance, and semantics. Existing evaluations often inspect rendered images from only a few scenes and viewpoints near training views. SceneSplat++ broadens this assessment by evaluating methods directly in three-dimensional space.

The benchmark covers 1,060 scenes from three indoor datasets and one outdoor dataset. It compares three families of methods: approaches requiring per-scene optimization, approaches avoiding that optimization, and generalizable approaches. summary.tldr: SceneSplat++ evaluates language Gaussian Splatting directly in 3D and finds advantages for generalizable methods, supported by a roughly 49,000-scene dataset.

title: SceneSplat++: A Large Dataset and Comprehensive Benchmark for Language Gaussian Splatting

abstract: Modern reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms have found success by using powerful probabilistic models, such as transformers, energy-based models, and diffusion/flow-based models. To this end, RL researchers often choose to pay the price of accommodating these models into their algorithms -- diffusion models are expressive, but are computationally intensive due to their reliance on solving differential equations, while autoregressive transformer models are scalable but typically require learning discrete representations. Normalizing flows (NFs), by contrast, seem to provide an appealing alternative, as they enable likelihoods and sampling without solving differential equations or autoregressive architectures. However, their potential in RL has received limited attention, partly due to the prevailing belief that normalizing flows lack sufficient expressivity. We show that this is not the case. Building on recent work in NFs, we propose a single NF architecture which integrates seamlessly into RL algorithms, serving as a policy, Q-function, and occupancy measure. Our approach leads to much simpler algorithms, and achieves higher performance in imitation learning, offline, goal conditioned RL and unsupervised RL.

paragraphs: Powerful probabilistic models have improved reinforcement learning, but integrating them can complicate algorithms. Diffusion models require solving differential equations, while autoregressive Transformers commonly rely on learned discrete representations. This paper revisits normalizing flows, which support likelihood evaluation and sampling without those particular computational requirements.

The authors challenge the belief that normalizing flows are insufficiently expressive for reinforcement learning. Building on recent flow models, they propose one architecture that can fill several roles: a policy for choosing actions, a Q-function for evaluating them, and an occupancy measure for representing where behavior occurs. Using the architecture across these roles allows it to fit naturally into different reinforcement learning algorithms.

The reported results show simpler algorithms and higher performance in imitation learning, offline reinforcement learning, goal-conditioned learning, and unsupervised reinforcement learning. These findings support normalizing flows as capable models across the evaluated continuous-control settings. The broader contribution is architectural flexibility: the same model family can support several central components of decision learning while retaining convenient probability and sampling operations.
summary.tldr: A single normalizing-flow architecture supports policies, Q-functions, and occupancy measures, yielding simpler algorithms and improved results across several reinforcement learning settings.

title: Normalizing Flows are Capable Models for Continuous Control

abstract: The rapid progress of large language models (LLMs) has catalyzed the emergence of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that unify visual understanding and image generation within a single framework. However, most existing MLLMs rely on autoregressive (AR) architectures, which impose inherent limitations on future development, such as the raster-scan order in image generation and restricted reasoning abilities in causal context modeling. In this work, we challenge the dominance of AR-based approaches by introducing FUDOKI, a unified multimodal model purely based on discrete flow matching, as an alternative to conventional AR paradigms. By leveraging metric-induced probability paths with kinetic optimal velocities, our framework goes beyond the previous masking-based corruption process, enabling iterative refinement with self-correction capability and richer bidirectional context integration during generation. To mitigate the high cost of training from scratch, we initialize FUDOKI from pre-trained AR-based MLLMs and adaptively transition to the discrete flow matching paradigm. Experimental results show that FUDOKI achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art AR-based MLLMs across both visual understanding and image generation tasks, highlighting its potential as a foundation for next-generation unified multimodal models. Furthermore, we show that applying test-time scaling techniques to FUDOKI yields significant performance gains, further underscoring its promise for future enhancement through reinforcement learning.

Many use autoregressive prediction, whose sequential ordering constrains how context is incorporated and how images are generated. FUDOKI explores a unified model based entirely on discrete flow matching, providing an alternative way to perform both kinds of task.

These results establish discrete flow matching as a competitive basis for unified multimodal modeling in the reported evaluations. The authors see the gains as motivation for future reinforcement-learning improvements, rather than reporting those future improvements as an achieved result.
summary.tldr: FUDOKI unifies visual understanding and image generation through discrete flow matching, with competitive performance and gains from test-time scaling.

title: FUDOKI: Discrete Flow-based Unified Understanding and Generation via Kinetic-Optimal Velocities

abstract: Expensive communication cost is a common performance bottleneck in Federated Learning (FL), which makes it less appealing in real-world applications. Many communication-efficient FL methods focus on discarding a part of model updates mostly based on gradient magnitude. In this study, we find that recycling previous updates, rather than simply dropping them, more effectively reduces the communication cost while maintaining FL performance. We propose *FedLUAR*, a Layer-wise Update Aggregation with Recycling scheme for communication-efficient FL. We first define a useful metric that quantifies the extent to which the aggregated gradients influences the model parameter values in each layer. *FedLUAR* selects a few layers based on the metric and recycles their previous updates on the server side. Our extensive empirical study demonstrates that the update recycling scheme significantly reduces the communication cost while maintaining model accuracy. For example, our method achieves nearly the same AG News accuracy as FedAvg, while reducing the communication cost to just 17%.

paragraphs: Federated learning can spend substantial communication resources exchanging model updates. Many methods reduce this burden by discarding some updates, often using gradient magnitude to decide what to retain. This paper investigates a different use of the information already available to the server: reusing previous updates for selected layers.

The proposed FedLUAR method first measures how strongly aggregated gradients influence parameter values in each layer. It uses this layer-level metric to choose a small set of layers whose earlier updates will be recycled on the server. The decision therefore depends on the updates' influence on model parameters, and the server continues to use previously communicated information for those layers.

The empirical study finds that recycling can substantially reduce communication while maintaining model accuracy. On AG News, FedLUAR reaches nearly the same accuracy as FedAvg while using only 17% of its communication cost. That example illustrates the intended benefit: earlier updates can retain enough value to support continued learning without requiring equally frequent fresh communication for every layer.
summary.tldr: FedLUAR reuses earlier updates for selected model layers, reaching nearly FedAvg's AG News accuracy with 17% of its communication cost.

title: Layer-wise Update Aggregation with Recycling for Communication-Efficient Federated Learning

abstract: Brain-computer interfaces have shown great potential in motor and speech rehabilitation, but still suffer from low performance stability across days, mostly due to the instabilities in neural signals. These instabilities, partially caused by neuron deaths and electrode shifts, leading to channel-level variabilities among different recording days. Previous studies mostly focused on aligning multi-day neural signals of onto a low-dimensional latent manifold to reduce the variabilities, while faced with difficulties when neural signals exhibit significant drift. Here, we propose to learn a channel-level invariant neural representation to address the variabilities in channels across days. It contains a channel-rearrangement module to learn stable representations against electrode shifts, and a channel reconstruction module to handle the missing neurons. The proposed method achieved the state-of-the-art performance with cross-day decoding tasks over two months, on multiple benchmark BCI datasets. The proposed approach showed good generalization ability that can be incorporated to different neural networks.

Here, we propose to learn a channel-level invariant neural representation to address the variabilities in channels across days. It contains a channel-rearrangement module to learn stable representations against electrode shifts, and a channel reconstruction module to handle the missing neurons. The proposed method achieved the state-of-the-art performance with cross-day decoding tasks over two months, on multiple benchmark BCI datasets. The proposed approach showed good generalization ability that can be incorporated to different neural networks.

paragraphs: Brain-computer interfaces need to decode neural activity reliably across recording days. Their performance can drift because the recorded signals change, partly through neuron loss and electrode movement. These changes affect individual recording channels. Earlier approaches align recordings within a shared low-dimensional representation, but substantial signal drift can make that alignment difficult.

CRRL addresses variability directly at the channel level by learning representations intended to remain stable across days. Its channel-rearrangement module handles changes associated with electrode shifts. A separate channel-reconstruction module addresses missing neurons. Together, the modules target two concrete sources of recording instability rather than relying solely on alignment of the overall neural representation.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmark brain-computer-interface datasets for cross-day decoding tasks spanning two months. They also report good generalization and compatibility with different neural networks. These results support channel-level invariance as a useful design principle for more stable decoding. Its practical significance is that the representation addresses changes in the recording interface that would otherwise make the same decoding task harder on later days.
summary.tldr: CRRL learns stable channel-level neural representations to improve brain-computer-interface decoding across days despite electrode shifts and missing neurons.

title: CRRL: Learning Channel-invariant Neural Representations for High-performance Cross-day Decoding

abstract: Recent text-to-image systems face limitations in handling multimodal inputs and complex reasoning tasks. We introduce MindOmni, a unified multimodal large language model that addresses these challenges by incorporating reasoning generation through reinforcement learning. MindOmni leverages a three-phase training strategy: i) design of a unified vision language model with a decoder-only diffusion module, ii) supervised fine-tuning with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) instruction data, and iii) our proposed Reasoning Generation Policy Optimization (RGPO) algorithm, utilizing multimodal feedback to effectively guide policy updates. Experimental results demonstrate that MindOmni outperforms existing models, achieving impressive performance on both understanding and generation benchmarks, meanwhile showcasing advanced fine-grained reasoning generation capabilities, especially with mathematical reasoning instruction. All codes will be made public.

The paper proposes a unified vision-language model that incorporates reasoning into generation through reinforcement learning. Its aim is to bring understanding and generation into the same system, including situations where producing the requested output requires more detailed reasoning.

Training proceeds in three phases. First, the authors design the unified model with a decoder-only diffusion module. Next, they use supervised fine-tuning on chain-of-thought instruction data. Finally, Reasoning Generation Policy Optimization, or RGPO, uses multimodal feedback to guide policy updates. This sequence combines an integrated architecture, explicit reasoning-oriented supervision, and feedback-driven refinement.

The reported experiments show that MindOmni outperforms existing models on both understanding and generation benchmarks. The authors also highlight fine-grained reasoning generation, especially under mathematical reasoning instructions. These findings support the combined training approach as a way to improve generation that depends on reasoning, while demonstrating gains across the two capabilities the architecture is intended to unify.
summary.tldr: MindOmni combines reasoning supervision and multimodal reinforcement learning to improve unified visual understanding and generation.

title: MindOmni: Unleashing Reasoning Generation in Vision Language Models with RGPO

abstract: Recently, the powerful text-to-image capabilities of GPT-4o have led to growing appreciation for native multimodal large language models. However, its multimodal capabilities remain confined to images and text. Yet beyond images, the ability to understand and generate 3D content is equally crucial. To address this gap, we propose ShapeLLM-Omni—a native 3D large language model capable of understanding and generating 3D assets and text in any sequence. First, we train a 3D vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQVAE), which maps 3D objects into a discrete latent space to achieve efficient and accurate shape representation and reconstruction. Building upon the 3D-aware discrete tokens, we innovatively construct a large-scale continuous training dataset named 3D-Alpaca, encompassing generation, comprehension, and editing, thus providing rich resources for future research and training. Finally, we perform instruction-based fine-tuning of the Qwen-2.5-vl-7B-Instruct model on the 3D-Alpaca dataset, equipping it with native 3D understanding and generation capabilities. Our work represents an effective step toward extending multimodal large language models with fundamental 3D intelligence, paving the way for future advances in 3D-native AI.

The dataset brings several forms of 3D interaction into a common training resource.

summary.tldr: ShapeLLM-Omni combines discrete 3D tokens, a new instruction dataset, and model fine-tuning to understand and generate text and 3D assets.

title: ShapeLLM-Omni: A Native Multimodal LLM for 3D Generation and Understanding

abstract: Decision-making models for individuals, particularly in high-stakes scenarios like vaccine uptake, often diverge from population optimal predictions. This gap arises from the uniqueness of the individual decision-making process, shaped by numerical attributes (e.g., cost, time) and linguistic influences (e.g., personal preferences and constraints). Developing upon Utility Theory and leveraging the textual-reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), this paper proposes an Adaptive Textual-symbolic Human-centric Reasoning framework (ATHENA) to address the optimal information integration. ATHENA uniquely integrates two stages: First, it discovers robust, group-level symbolic utility functions via LLM-augmented symbolic discovery; Second, it implements individual-level semantic adaptation, creating personalized semantic templates guided by the optimal utility to model personalized choices. Validated on real-world travel mode and vaccine choice tasks, ATHENA consistently outperforms utility-based, machine learning, and other LLM-based models, lifting F1 score by at least 6.5\% over the strongest cutting-edge models. Further, ablation studies confirm that both stages of ATHENA are critical and complementary, as removing either clearly degrades overall predictive performance. By organically integrating symbolic utility modeling and semantic adaptation, ATHENA provides a new scheme for modeling human-centric decisions. The project page can be found at https://yibozh.github.io/Athena.

paragraphs: Predicting an individual's choices requires combining numerical considerations, such as cost and time, with preferences and constraints expressed in language. A prediction suited to a population may miss this individual variation. ATHENA addresses the problem by joining symbolic utility modeling with language-based personalization.

The framework has two stages. First, language-model-assisted symbolic discovery identifies robust utility functions at the group level. Second, individual semantic adaptation builds personalized textual templates guided by those utility functions. This connects a structured account of trade-offs with the language that describes a particular person's situation and preferences.

Tests on real-world travel-mode and vaccine-choice tasks report improvements over utility-based, machine-learning, and other language-model approaches. The abstract states an F1 improvement of at least 6.5% over the strongest competing models. Removing either stage reduces predictive performance, supporting their complementary roles. The findings concern modeling observed choices: they show the benefit of combining shared utility structure with individual semantic context when predicting decisions.
summary.tldr: ATHENA combines group-level symbolic utility functions with individual language-based adaptation to improve personalized choice prediction.

title: Personalized Decision Modeling: Utility Optimization or Textualized-Symbolic Reasoning

abstract: Adapter-based training has emerged as a key mechanism for extending the capabilities of powerful foundation image generators, enabling personalized and stylized text-to-image synthesis. These adapters are typically trained to capture a specific target attribute, such as subject identity, using single-image reconstruction objectives. However, because the input image inevitably contains a mixture of visual factors, adapters are prone to entangle the target attribute with incidental ones, such as pose, expression, and lighting. This spurious correlation problem limits generalization and obstructs the model's ability to adhere to the input text prompt. In this work, we uncover a simple yet effective solution: provide the very shortcuts we wish to eliminate during adapter training. In Shortcut-Rerouted Adapter Training, confounding factors are routed through auxiliary modules, such as ControlNet or LoRA, eliminating the incentive for the adapter to internalize them. The auxiliary modules are then removed during inference. When applied to tasks like facial and full-body identity injection, our approach improves generation quality, diversity, and prompt adherence. These results point to a general design principle in the era of large models: when seeking disentangled representations, the most effective path may be to establish shortcuts for what should NOT be learned.

paragraphs: An image-generation adapter may be trained to preserve a person’s identity, but its training image also contains pose, expression, and lighting. A reconstruction objective can encourage the adapter to learn those incidental properties together with identity. This entanglement makes it harder to generate varied images or follow text prompts that request different visual conditions.

Shortcut-Rerouted Adapter Training supplies auxiliary modules with the confounding factors during training. Modules such as ControlNet or LoRA provide an alternative route for reconstructing those properties, removing the incentive for the target adapter to absorb them. The auxiliary modules are removed at inference, leaving the trained adapter responsible for the intended attribute.

Applied to facial and full-body identity injection, the method improves generation quality, diversity, and prompt adherence. Its broader insight is about distributing learning responsibilities: explicitly providing a route for incidental information can help a specialized component avoid entangling that information with its target. The paper presents this as a potentially useful design principle for learning disentangled representations.
summary.tldr: Routing incidental visual factors through temporary auxiliary modules helps image adapters learn their intended attribute more cleanly.

title: Preventing Shortcuts in Adapter Training via Providing the Shortcuts

abstract: Model-Heterogeneous Federated Learning (Hetero-FL) has attracted growing attention for its ability to aggregate knowledge from heterogeneous models while keeping private data locally. To better aggregate knowledge from clients, ensemble distillation, as a widely used and effective technique, is often employed after global aggregation to enhance the performance of the global model. However, simply combining Hetero-FL and ensemble distillation does not always yield promising results and can make the training process unstable. The reason is that existing methods primarily focus on logit distillation, which, while being model-agnostic with softmax predictions, fails to compensate for the knowledge bias arising from heterogeneous models. To tackle this challenge, we propose a stable and efficient Feature Distillation for model-heterogeneous Federated learning, dubbed FedFD, that can incorporate aligned feature information via orthogonal projection to integrate knowledge from heterogeneous models better. Specifically, a new feature-based ensemble federated knowledge distillation paradigm is proposed. The global model on the server needs to maintain a projection layer for each client-side model architecture to align the features separately. Orthogonal techniques are employed to re-parameterize the projection layer to mitigate knowledge bias from heterogeneous models and thus maximize the distilled knowledge. Extensive experiments show that FedFD achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Federated learning can combine knowledge from clients while keeping their private data local. When clients use different model architectures, however, their knowledge is represented differently. The authors argue that distilling only output predictions does not adequately compensate for the resulting knowledge bias, and that combining heterogeneous federated learning with conventional ensemble distillation can make training unstable.

FedFD transfers internal feature information through a feature-based ensemble distillation procedure. The server’s global model maintains a separate projection layer for each client architecture, allowing features from different kinds of models to be aligned. Orthogonal reparameterization of these projections is used to mitigate architecture-related knowledge bias and improve how much useful information is distilled.

The central idea is to make heterogeneous internal representations compatible before using them to teach the global model. Extensive experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art comparison methods. These findings support the proposed aligned feature-distillation approach in the evaluated settings, while the architecture-specific projection layers explain how the method accommodates differences among client models.
summary.tldr: FedFD aligns client features through orthogonal projections to improve knowledge distillation across heterogeneous federated models.

title: Feature Distillation is the Better Choice for Model-Heterogeneous Federated Learning

abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has stimulated interest in multi-agent collaboration for addressing complex medical tasks. However, the practical advantages of multi-agent collaboration approaches remain insufficiently understood. Existing evaluations often lack generalizability, failing to cover diverse tasks reflective of real-world clinical practice, and frequently omit rigorous comparisons against both single-LLM-based and established conventional methods. To address this critical gap, we introduce MedAgentBoard, a comprehensive benchmark for the systematic evaluation of multi-agent collaboration, single-LLM, and conventional approaches. MedAgentBoard encompasses four diverse medical task categories: (1) medical (visual) question answering, (2) lay summary generation, (3) structured Electronic Health Record (EHR) predictive modeling, and (4) clinical workflow automation, across text, medical images, and structured EHR data. Our extensive experiments reveal a nuanced landscape: while multi-agent collaboration demonstrates benefits in specific scenarios, such as enhancing task completeness in clinical workflow automation, it does not consistently outperform advanced single LLMs (e.g., in textual medical QA) or, critically, specialized conventional methods that generally maintain better performance in tasks like medical VQA and EHR-based prediction. MedAgentBoard offers a vital resource and actionable insights, emphasizing the necessity of a task-specific, evidence-based approach to selecting and developing AI solutions in medicine. It underscores that the inherent complexity and overhead of multi-agent collaboration must be carefully weighed against tangible performance gains. All code, datasets, detailed prompts, and experimental results are open-sourced at [this link](https://medagentboard.netlify.app/).

summary.tldr: MedAgentBoard finds that multi-agent medical AI helps in some scenarios but does not consistently outperform single models or specialized conventional methods.

title: MedAgentBoard: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Collaboration with Conventional Methods for Diverse Medical Tasks

abstract: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have advanced GUI navigation agents, current approaches face limitations in cross-domain generalization and effective history utilization. We present a reasoning-enhanced framework that systematically integrates structured reasoning, action prediction, and history summarization. The structured reasoning component generates coherent Chain-of-Thought analyses combining progress estimation and decision reasoning, which inform both immediate action predictions and compact history summaries for future steps. Based on this framework, we train a GUI agent, GUI-Rise, through supervised fine-tuning on pseudo-labeled trajectories and reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). This framework employs specialized rewards, including a history-aware objective, directly linking summary quality to subsequent action performance. Comprehensive evaluations on standard benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art results under identical training data conditions, with particularly strong performance in out-of-domain scenarios. These findings validate our framework's ability to maintain robust reasoning and generalization across diverse GUI navigation tasks.

GUI-Rise addresses difficulties in using that history effectively and transferring navigation skills across domains. Its framework connects structured reasoning, action prediction, and history summarization so that the same assessment can support both current and future decisions.

The reasoning component estimates progress and develops the rationale for the next action. It also informs a compact summary that can be used at later steps. Training combines supervised fine-tuning on trajectories with automatically generated labels and reinforcement learning through Group Relative Policy Optimization. Specialized rewards include a history-aware objective that links the quality of summaries to performance on subsequent actions.

Under identical training-data conditions, evaluations on standard benchmarks report state-of-the-art results, with especially strong performance outside the training domain. These findings support the proposed connection between reasoning and memory: summaries are trained for their usefulness to later navigation. The reported generalization results indicate that this integrated approach helps across the diverse interface tasks evaluated.
summary.tldr: GUI-Rise links structured reasoning, action prediction, and useful history summaries to improve interface navigation, especially in evaluated out-of-domain settings.

title: GUI-Rise: Structured Reasoning and History Summarization for GUI Navigation

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are now integral across various domains and have demonstrated impressive performance. Progress, however, rests on the premise that benchmark scores are both accurate and reproducible. We demonstrate that the reproducibility of LLM performance is fragile: changing system configuration, such as evaluation batch size, GPU count, and GPU version, can introduce significant differences in the generated responses. This issue is especially pronounced in reasoning models, where minor rounding differences in early tokens can cascade into divergent chains of thought, ultimately affecting accuracy. For instance, under bfloat16 precision with greedy decoding, a reasoning model like DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B can exhibit up to 9\% variation in accuracy and 9,000 tokens difference in response length due to differences in GPU count, type, and evaluation batch size. We trace the root cause of this variability to the non-associative nature of floating-point arithmetic under limited numerical precision. This work presents the first systematic investigation into how numerical precision affects reproducibility in LLM inference. Through carefully controlled experiments across various hardware, software, and precision settings, we quantify when and how model outputs diverge. Our analysis reveals that floating-point precision—while critical for reproducibility—is often neglected in evaluation practices. Inspired by this, we develop a lightweight inference pipeline, dubbed LayerCast, that stores weights in 16-bit precision but performs all computations in FP32, balancing memory efficiency with numerical stability. Code is available at https://github.com/nanomaoli/llm_reproducibility.

This paper investigates the numerical origin of that instability. In limited-precision arithmetic, regrouping operations can change their rounded results, allowing seemingly incidental system configurations to affect generated responses.

The effect is especially consequential for reasoning models, where a small difference in an early token can lead to a different subsequent reasoning sequence. For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B under bfloat16 precision, the authors report up to 9% variation in accuracy and differences of 9,000 response tokens across configurations. summary.tldr: Limited-precision arithmetic can destabilize LLM evaluations across system configurations; LayerCast combines 16-bit weight storage with FP32 computation to improve stability.

title: Understanding and Mitigating Numerical Sources of Nondeterminism in LLM Inference

abstract: While large language models (LLMs) show considerable promise across various fields, they have notable limitations in handling multi-document question answering (Multi-doc QA) tasks. The first challenge is long-range dependency modeling, where LLMs struggle to focus on key information in long texts, which weakens important semantic connections. Second, most LLMs suffer from the ''lost-in-the-middle'' issue, where they have difficulty processing information in the middle of long inputs. Current solutions either truncate global dependencies or demand costly finetuning, ultimately lacking a universal and simple solution for these challenges. To resolve these limitations, we propose Dual-Stage Adaptive Sharpening (DSAS) containing two modules. (i) The Contextual Gate Weighting (CGW) module alleviates ''lost-in-the-middle'' by assessing paragraph relevance through layer-wise attention tracking and position-aware weighting. (ii) The Reciprocal Attention Suppression (RAS) module enhances focus on critical paragraphs by suppressing information exchange between key and irrelevant texts, thus mitigating the limitations in long-range dependency modeling. Extensive experiments on four benchmarks demonstrate DSAS's efficacy across mainstream LLMs (Llama, Qwen, Mistral, and Deepseek), with an average F1-score improvement of 4.2% in Multi-doc QA tasks on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct. Ablation studies confirm the essential contributions of both the CGW and RAS modules. In addition, detailed discussions in the Appendix further validate the robustness and scalability of DSAS.

paragraphs: Answering questions across several documents requires a language model to connect relevant information over long inputs. Two difficulties motivate DSAS: important connections can weaken with distance, and information near the middle of the input can receive insufficient attention. The paper proposes two cooperating attention adjustments to help models concentrate on the paragraphs that matter.

Contextual Gate Weighting tracks attention across layers to assess paragraph relevance, then incorporates paragraph position into its weighting. This targets the tendency to overlook the middle of an input. Reciprocal Attention Suppression reduces information exchange between important paragraphs and irrelevant text. Its purpose is to keep distracting material from interfering with the relationships needed to answer the question.

Together, the results suggest that addressing positional neglect and distracting attention can improve multi-document question answering through complementary changes.
summary.tldr: DSAS improves multi-document question answering by reweighting relevant paragraphs and suppressing distracting attention.

title: DSAS: A Universal Plug-and-Play Framework for Attention Optimization in Multi-Document Question Answering

abstract: Recently, machine learning algorithms have successfully entered large-scale real-world industrial applications (e.g. search engines and email spam filters). Here, the CPU cost during test-time must be budgeted and accounted for. In this paper, we address the challenge of balancing test-time cost and the classifier accuracy in a principled fashion. The test-time cost of a classifier is often dominated by the computation required for feature extraction-which can vary drastically across features. We incorporate this extraction time by constructing a tree of classifiers, through which test inputs traverse along individual paths. Each path extracts different features and is optimized for a specific sub-partition of the input space. By only computing features for inputs that benefit from them the most, our cost-sensitive tree of classifiers can match the high accuracies of the current state-of-the-art at a small fraction of the computational cost.

paragraphs: In large-scale applications, a classifier must fit within a prediction-time computing budget as well as make accurate decisions. The paper focuses on feature extraction, which often dominates this cost. Different features can require very different amounts of computation, so treating every input with the same feature set can make prediction unnecessarily expensive.

The proposed approach arranges classifiers in a tree. Each test input follows an individual path, and different paths extract different features. A path is optimized for a particular region of the input space, allowing the system to tailor its computation to the kinds of inputs reaching that path. Feature-extraction time is explicitly incorporated into this design.

The underlying idea is to compute features for the inputs that benefit from them most. The paper reports that this cost-sensitive tree can match the high accuracy of contemporary state-of-the-art methods at a small fraction of their computational cost. Its contribution is a principled way to balance prediction accuracy with the expense of obtaining the information needed for a decision.
summary.tldr: A tree of classifiers selectively computes features for each input, matching high accuracy at substantially lower prediction cost.

title: Cost-Sensitive Tree of Classifiers

abstract: We investigate the use of sparse coding and dictionary learning in the context of multitask and transfer learning. The central assumption of our learning method is that the tasks parameters are well approximated by sparse linear combinations of the atoms of a dictionary on a high or infinite dimensional space. This assumption, together with the large quantity of available data in the multitask and transfer learning settings, allows a principled choice of the dictionary. We provide bounds on the generalization error of this approach, for both settings. Numerical experiments on one synthetic and two real datasets show the advantage of our method over single task learning, a previous method based on orthogonal and dense representation of the tasks and a related method learning task grouping.

paragraphs: Learning related tasks together can provide more information than training each task independently. This paper studies sparse coding and dictionary learning as a way to organize that shared information in multitask and transfer learning. Its central assumption is that task parameters can be approximated well using sparse linear combinations of common dictionary atoms.

Each task therefore draws on only a small selection of components from a shared dictionary, even when the parameter space is high-dimensional or infinite-dimensional. The assumption, together with the quantity of data available across tasks, supports a principled choice of dictionary. Sharing occurs through reusable components while allowing tasks to use different combinations.

The authors derive generalization error bounds for both multitask and transfer learning. Experiments on one synthetic and two real datasets show advantages over independent task learning, an approach based on orthogonal dense task representations, and a related task-grouping method. These findings support sparse shared representations in the evaluated settings, while the theory explains the approach under its stated approximation assumption.
summary.tldr: A shared dictionary of sparsely combined components supports multitask and transfer learning with generalization bounds and empirical gains.

title: Sparse coding for multitask and transfer learning

abstract: In recent times, many real world applications have emerged that require estimates of class ratios in an unlabeled instance collection as opposed to labels of individual instances in the collection. In this paper we investigate the use of maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) for estimating such ratios. First, we theoretically analyze the MMD-based estimates. Our analysis establishes that, under some mild conditions, the estimate is statistically consistent. More importantly, it provides an upper bound on the error in the estimate in terms of intuitive geometric quantities like class separation and data spread. Next, we use the insights obtained from the theoretical analysis, to propose a novel convex formulation that automatically learns the kernel to be employed in the MMD-based estimation. We design an efficient cutting plane algorithm for solving this formulation. Finally, we empirically compare our estimator with several existing methods, and show significantly improved performance under varying datasets, class ratios, and training sizes.

paragraphs: Some applications need the proportion of examples belonging to each class in an unlabeled collection, rather than a separate predicted label for every example. This paper studies class-ratio estimation using maximum mean discrepancy, or MMD, in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The kernel determines the representation in which distribution differences are assessed.

The authors prove that the resulting estimates are statistically consistent under stated mild conditions. They also bound estimation error using geometric quantities, including how separated the classes are and how broadly the data are spread. This makes the analysis useful for understanding which aspects of the representation affect ratio estimation.

Those theoretical insights motivate a convex formulation that automatically learns the kernel used by the estimator. An efficient cutting-plane algorithm solves that formulation. Experiments across different datasets, class proportions, and training sizes report significantly improved performance over several existing methods. The paper thus connects a conditional consistency result and interpretable error bound to a practical procedure for choosing the estimator's representation.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes MMD-based class-ratio estimation and uses its error geometry to learn a more effective kernel.

title: Maximum Mean Discrepancy for Class Ratio Estimation: Convergence Bounds and Kernel Selection

abstract: Automatic synthesis of realistic images from text would be interesting and useful, but current AI systems are still far from this goal. However, in recent years generic and powerful recurrent neural network architectures have been developed to learn discriminative text feature representations. Meanwhile, deep convolutional generative adversarial networks (GANs) have begun to generate highly compelling images of specific categories such as faces, album covers, room interiors and flowers. In this work, we develop a novel deep architecture and GAN formulation to effectively bridge these advances in text and image modeling, translating visual concepts from characters to pixels. We demonstrate the capability of our model to generate plausible images of birds and flowers from detailed text descriptions.

We demonstrate the capability of our model to generate plausible images of birds and flowers from detailed text descriptions.

paragraphs: This paper studies generating images from detailed text descriptions. The task requires connecting two different kinds of representation: language expressing visual concepts and pixels depicting them. The authors build on progress in recurrent networks that learn discriminative text features and convolutional generative adversarial networks that produce compelling images within particular categories.

Their contribution is a deep architecture and adversarial formulation that brings these text and image modeling capabilities together. The text representation supplies information about the visual concepts to be generated. This makes the description part of the image-generation problem, linking what the language expresses to the content of the resulting image.

The demonstrated outcome is the generation of plausible bird and flower images from detailed descriptions. This is a concrete demonstration of the proposed bridge between language and image synthesis, with the evidence centered on those categories. The abstract frames fully realistic automatic text-to-image generation as a broader goal still beyond the systems it discusses, while showing progress through these specific generated-image examples.
summary.tldr: A text-conditioned adversarial architecture generates plausible bird and flower images from detailed descriptions.

title: Generative Adversarial Text to Image Synthesis

abstract: The problem of finding overlapping communities in networks has gained much attention recently. Optimization-based approaches use non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) or variants, but the global optimum cannot be provably attained in general. Model-based approaches, such as the popular mixed-membership stochastic blockmodel or MMSB (Airoldi et al., 2008), use parameters for each node to specify the overlapping communities, but standard inference techniques cannot guarantee consistency. We link the two approaches, by (a) establishing sufficient conditions for the symmetric NMF optimization to have a unique solution under MMSB, and (b) proposing a computationally efficient algorithm called GeoNMF that is provably optimal and hence consistent for a broad parameter regime. We demonstrate its accuracy on both simulated and real-world datasets.
