paragraphs: Finding overlapping network communities means allowing a node to participate in more than one group. Two approaches are nonnegative matrix factorization and probabilistic mixed-membership models. Each has a theoretical difficulty: general factorization methods cannot promise a global optimum, while standard inference for mixed-membership stochastic blockmodels does not guarantee consistency.

This paper connects the approaches by studying symmetric nonnegative matrix factorization under the mixed-membership stochastic blockmodel. It establishes sufficient conditions for the factorization problem to have a unique solution. Those conditions identify a setting in which the optimization formulation has a well-defined answer; they do not establish uniqueness for every network or parameter choice.

The authors introduce GeoNMF, a computationally efficient algorithm that is provably optimal and consequently consistent over a broad parameter regime. Simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate its accuracy. The main contribution is a bridge between an optimization procedure and a statistical model, allowing stronger recovery guarantees within the identified regime while retaining an efficient computational approach.
summary.tldr: GeoNMF links symmetric matrix factorization to mixed-membership community models, with optimality and consistency guarantees over a broad parameter regime.

title: On Mixed Memberships and Symmetric Nonnegative Matrix Factorizations

abstract: We introduce autoregressive implicit quantile networks (AIQN), a fundamentally different approach to generative modeling than those commonly used, that implicitly captures the distribution using quantile regression. AIQN is able to achieve superior perceptual quality and improvements in evaluation metrics, without incurring a loss of sample diversity. The method can be applied to many existing models and architectures. In this work we extend the PixelCNN model with AIQN and demonstrate results on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet using Inception scores, FID, non-cherry-picked samples, and inpainting results. We consistently observe that AIQN yields a highly stable algorithm that improves perceptual quality while maintaining a highly diverse distribution.

We consistently observe that AIQN yields a highly stable algorithm that improves perceptual quality while maintaining a highly diverse distribution.

paragraphs: Generative models need to produce convincing outputs while preserving the variety present in the distribution they learn. This paper introduces autoregressive implicit quantile networks, or AIQN, which capture a distribution through quantile regression. The central change is the way the model represents and learns that distribution, offering a different approach to generative modeling.

The method is designed to fit into many existing models and architectures. The authors demonstrate it by extending PixelCNN and evaluating image generation on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. Their evaluation combines Inception scores and FID with samples that were not selectively chosen and image inpainting results. These provide several perspectives on the resulting images rather than relying on a single assessment.

Across the reported observations, AIQN improves perceptual quality and evaluation metrics while retaining sample diversity. The authors also consistently observe stable algorithmic behavior. The significance is that the reported quality gains do not come with a corresponding loss of variety: the learned distribution continues to support a diverse collection of outputs.
summary.tldr: AIQN uses quantile regression for generative modeling and improves reported image quality while maintaining diversity and stable learning.

title: Autoregressive Quantile Networks for Generative Modeling

abstract: Deep latent variable models, trained using variational autoencoders or generative adversarial networks, are now a key technique for representation learning of continuous structures. However, applying similar methods to discrete structures, such as text sequences or discretized images, has proven to be more challenging. In this work, we propose a more flexible method for training deep latent variable models of discrete structures. Our approach is based on the recently proposed Wasserstein Autoencoder (WAE) which formalizes adversarial autoencoders as an optimal transport problem. We first extend this framework to model discrete sequences, and then further explore different learned priors targeting a controllable representation. Unlike many other latent variable generative models for text, this adversarially regularized autoencoder (ARAE) allows us to generate fluent textual outputs as well as perform manipulations in the latent space to induce change in the output space. Finally we show that the latent representation can be trained to perform unaligned textual style transfer, giving improvements both in automatic measures and human evaluation.

paragraphs: Learning a latent representation is useful when it supports both generating data and changing meaningful properties of the generated output. This paper addresses that goal for discrete structures, particularly text sequences, where applying approaches developed for continuous data has been more challenging.

The proposed adversarially regularized autoencoder extends the Wasserstein Autoencoder framework to discrete sequences. That framework describes adversarial autoencoders through an optimal transport formulation. The authors also investigate learned priors aimed at making the representation controllable. Together, these choices connect how the model organizes its latent space with the kinds of outputs it can produce.

The resulting model generates fluent text and supports latent-space manipulations that induce changes in the output. The authors further train the representation for unaligned textual style transfer, enabling style changes without aligned source-and-target text examples. They report improvements in both automatic measures and human evaluation. These findings support the representation’s usefulness for controlled text generation, beyond producing text alone.
summary.tldr: An adversarially regularized autoencoder learns controllable text representations that support fluent generation and unaligned style transfer.

title: Adversarially Regularized Autoencoders

abstract: While humor is often thought to be beyond the reach of Natural Language Processing, we show that several aspects of single-word humor correlate with simple linear directions in Word Embeddings. In particular: (a) the word vectors capture multiple aspects discussed in humor theories from various disciplines; (b) each individual’s sense of humor can be represented by a vector, which can predict differences in people’s senses of humor on new, unrated, words; and (c) upon clustering humor ratings of multiple demographic groups, different humor preferences emerge across the different groups. Humor ratings are taken from the work of Engelthaler and Hills (2017) as well as from an original crowdsourcing study of 120,000 words. Our dataset further includes annotations for the theoretically-motivated humor features we identify.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether word embeddings contain information about why individual words seem funny. Its scope is single-word humor, and its main finding is that several aspects of such humor correlate with simple linear directions in the vector representations. This makes some humor-related patterns accessible through relatively simple operations on embeddings.

The authors find that the vectors capture multiple features discussed in humor theories from different disciplines. They also represent an individual's humor preferences with a vector that can predict differences in reactions to new, unrated words. Clustering ratings from demographic groups reveals differing humor preferences across those groups.

The study draws on an existing collection of humor ratings and an original crowdsourcing study covering 120,000 words. Its dataset also includes annotations for the theoretically motivated humor features identified by the authors. Together, the results connect embedding structure with both shared humor features and variation between people. The claims concern correlations and predictive patterns in word ratings, rather than a general explanation of all forms of humor.
summary.tldr: Simple directions in word embeddings correlate with single-word humor and help predict differences in individual humor preferences.

title: Humor in Word Embeddings: Cockamamie Gobbledegook for Nincompoops

abstract: Planning has been very successful for control tasks with known environment dynamics. To leverage planning in unknown environments, the agent needs to learn the dynamics from interactions with the world. However, learning dynamics models that are accurate enough for planning has been a long-standing challenge, especially in image-based domains. We propose the Deep Planning Network (PlaNet), a purely model-based agent that learns the environment dynamics from images and chooses actions through fast online planning in latent space. To achieve high performance, the dynamics model must accurately predict the rewards ahead for multiple time steps. We approach this using a latent dynamics model with both deterministic and stochastic transition components. Moreover, we propose a multi-step variational inference objective that we name latent overshooting. Using only pixel observations, our agent solves continuous control tasks with contact dynamics, partial observability, and sparse rewards, which exceed the difficulty of tasks that were previously solved by planning with learned models. PlaNet uses substantially fewer episodes and reaches final performance close to and sometimes higher than strong model-free algorithms.

paragraphs: Planning in an unfamiliar environment requires a useful model of how actions affect what happens next. Learning such a model from images is particularly challenging because action selection needs accurate predictions of rewards several steps ahead. This paper introduces PlaNet, a purely model-based agent that learns dynamics from images and plans online in a latent representation.

Its dynamics model combines deterministic and stochastic transition components. The authors also introduce latent overshooting, a variational inference objective that operates over multiple steps. These choices address the need for predictions that remain useful beyond the immediate next transition, where planning depends on consequences that unfold over time.

Using only pixel observations, PlaNet solves continuous-control tasks involving contact dynamics, partial observability, and sparse rewards. The authors describe these tasks as more difficult than those previously solved by planning with learned models. PlaNet requires substantially fewer episodes than strong model-free algorithms while reaching final performance that is close to, and sometimes higher than, theirs. The comparison therefore supports improved experience efficiency without claiming uniformly superior final performance.
summary.tldr: PlaNet learns latent dynamics from images and plans with them, solving challenging control tasks with substantially fewer episodes than strong model-free methods.

title: Learning Latent Dynamics for Planning from Pixels

abstract: We propose a novel procedure which adds "content-addressability" to any given unconditional implicit model e.g., a generative adversarial network (GAN). The procedure allows users to control the generative process by specifying a set (arbitrary size) of desired examples based on which similar samples are generated from the model. The proposed approach, based on kernel mean matching, is applicable to any generative models which transform latent vectors to samples, and does not require retraining of the model. Experiments on various high-dimensional image generation problems (CelebA-HQ, LSUN bedroom, bridge, tower) show that our approach is able to generate images which are consistent with the input set, while retaining the image quality of the original model. To our knowledge, this is the first work that attempts to construct, at test time, a content-addressable generative model from a trained marginal model.

paragraphs: An unconditional generator can produce samples without offering a direct way to request content resembling particular examples. This paper adds that capability after training. A user supplies a set of desired examples, and the procedure guides generation toward samples consistent with that set. The input set can contain an arbitrary number of examples.

The approach uses kernel mean matching and applies to generative models that map latent vectors into samples, including GANs. It does not require retraining the original model. This makes the contribution a way of controlling an existing generative process at test time, using example content as the request rather than requiring a newly trained conditional generator.

Experiments cover several high-dimensional image-generation problems, including faces, bedrooms, bridges, and towers. The authors report images consistent with the supplied example sets while retaining the original generator's image quality. These results support the possibility of adding example-driven control to trained unconditional models. The broad applicability claim concerns the latent-vector-to-sample interface; the reported empirical evidence concerns the image tasks studied.
summary.tldr: Kernel mean matching lets users steer a trained unconditional generator with example sets, without retraining it.

title: Kernel Mean Matching for Content Addressability of GANs

abstract: A recent trend in algorithm design consists of augmenting classic data structures with machine learning models, which are better suited to reveal and exploit patterns and trends in the input data so to achieve outstanding practical improvements in space occupancy and time efficiency. This is especially known in the context of indexing data structures where, despite few attempts in evaluating their asymptotic efficiency, theoretical results are yet missing in showing that learned indexes are provably better than classic indexes, such as B+ trees and their variants. In this paper, we present the first mathematically-grounded answer to this open problem. We obtain this result by discovering and exploiting a link between the original problem and a mean exit time problem over a proper stochastic process which, we show, is related to the space and time occupancy of those learned indexes. Our general result is then specialised to five well-known distributions: Uniform, Lognormal, Pareto, Exponential, and Gamma; and it is corroborated in precision and robustness by a large set of experiments.

paragraphs: Learned indexes augment data structures with machine-learning models that exploit patterns in the stored data. They have shown substantial practical benefits in space use and time efficiency. This paper addresses the theoretical question behind those results: how to mathematically explain advantages over classical indexes such as B+ trees and their variants.

The authors connect the indexing problem to a mean exit time problem for a suitable stochastic process. They show that this process is related to the space and time requirements of the learned indexes. This connection supplies a mathematical route for analyzing the observed efficiency rather than relying solely on measurements from implementations.

The general result is specialized to five distributions: Uniform, Lognormal, Pareto, Exponential, and Gamma. A large experimental study supports the precision and robustness of the analysis. The paper’s contribution is a theoretically grounded account of learned-index effectiveness, linking properties of the input distribution to index resource requirements and checking that account empirically across the distributions considered.
summary.tldr: A connection to stochastic mean exit times provides a mathematical explanation of learned-index efficiency, supported by analysis of five distributions and experiments.

title: Why Are Learned Indexes So Effective?

abstract: We develop two new stochastic Gauss-Newton algorithms for solving a class of non-convex stochastic compositional optimization problems frequently arising in practice. We consider both the expectation and finite-sum settings under standard assumptions, and use both classical stochastic and SARAH estimators for approximating function values and Jacobians. In the expectation case, we establish $\BigO{\varepsilon^{-2}}$ iteration-complexity to achieve a stationary point in expectation and estimate the total number of stochastic oracle calls for both function value and its Jacobian, where $\varepsilon$ is a desired accuracy. In the finite sum case, we also estimate $\BigO{\varepsilon^{-2}}$ iteration-complexity and the total oracle calls with high probability. To our best knowledge, this is the first time such global stochastic oracle complexity is established for stochastic Gauss-Newton methods. Finally, we illustrate our theoretical results via two numerical examples on both synthetic and real datasets.

paragraphs: This paper develops two stochastic Gauss–Newton algorithms for a class of nonconvex problems whose objectives involve composed functions. It considers both objectives defined through expectations and those expressed as finite sums. Under standard assumptions, the methods approximate function values and Jacobians using classical stochastic estimators and SARAH estimators.

For the expectation setting, the authors establish an iteration complexity of order one over epsilon squared for reaching a stationary point in expectation, where epsilon specifies the desired accuracy. They also account for the total stochastic oracle calls needed to obtain function values and Jacobians. For finite sums, they provide the same order of iteration complexity and oracle-call estimates with high probability.

The distinction between iterations and oracle calls matters because each update requires information that has a computational cost. The authors identify their result as, to their knowledge, the first global stochastic oracle complexity analysis for these methods. Two numerical examples using synthetic and real datasets illustrate the theory. The convergence target is stationarity in a nonconvex problem.
summary.tldr: Two stochastic Gauss–Newton methods receive iteration and oracle-complexity guarantees for reaching stationarity in nonconvex compositional optimization.

title: Stochastic Gauss-Newton Algorithms for Nonconvex Compositional Optimization

abstract: Recent empirical works show that large deep neural networks are often highly redundant and one can find much smaller subnetworks without a significant drop of accuracy. However, most existing methods of network pruning are empirical and heuristic, leaving it open whether good subnetworks provably exist, how to find them efficiently, and if network pruning can be provably better than direct training using gradient descent. We answer these problems positively by proposing a simple greedy selection approach for finding good subnetworks, which starts from an empty network and greedily adds important neurons from the large network. This differs from the existing methods based on backward elimination, which remove redundant neurons from the large network. Theoretically, applying the greedy selection strategy on sufficiently large {pre-trained} networks guarantees to find small subnetworks with lower loss than networks directly trained with gradient descent. Our results also apply to pruning randomly weighted networks. Practically, we improve prior arts of network pruning on learning compact neural architectures on ImageNet, including ResNet, MobilenetV2/V3, and ProxylessNet. Our theory and empirical results on MobileNet suggest that we should fine-tune the pruned subnetworks to leverage the information from the large model, instead of re-training from new random initialization as suggested in \citet{liu2018rethinking}.
originalAbstract: Recent empirical works show that large deep neural networks are often highly redundant and one can find much smaller subnetworks without a significant drop of accuracy. However, most existing methods of network pruning are empirical and heuristic, leaving it open whether good subnetworks provably exist, how to find them efficiently, and if network pruning can be provably better than direct training using gradient descent. We answer these problems positively by proposing a simple greedy selection approach for finding good subnetworks, which starts from an empty network and greedily adds important neurons from the large network. This differs from the existing methods based on backward elimination, which remove redundant neurons from the large network. Theoretically, applying the greedy selection strategy on sufficiently large {pre-trained} networks guarantees to find small subnetworks with lower loss than networks directly trained with gradient descent. Our results also apply to pruning randomly weighted networks. Practically, we improve prior arts of network pruning on learning compact neural architectures on ImageNet, including ResNet, MobilenetV2/V3, and ProxylessNet. Our theory and empirical results on MobileNet suggest that we should fine-tune the pruned subnetworks to leverage the information from the large model, instead of re-training from new random initialization as suggested in \citet{liu2018rethinking}.

paragraphs: Large neural networks can contain much smaller subnetworks that retain strong predictive performance. This paper investigates whether such subnetworks can be shown to exist and found efficiently. Its pruning method starts with an empty network and repeatedly adds important neurons from a larger network, building the compact model through greedy forward selection.

The theoretical result depends on starting from a sufficiently large pretrained network. Under that condition, the selection strategy is guaranteed to find small subnetworks with lower loss than networks trained directly using gradient descent. The authors also extend their results to pruning networks with random weights. These statements give theoretical support to a process often approached through empirical pruning rules.

Experiments improve prior pruning results for compact ImageNet architectures, including ResNet, MobileNetV2/V3, and ProxylessNet. The theory and MobileNet experiments also support fine-tuning the selected subnetwork so that it retains information from the larger model. This recommendation concerns how to use the extracted network, alongside the paper’s contribution to how that network is selected.
summary.tldr: Greedily adding neurons yields compact subnetworks with conditional theoretical guarantees and improved reported pruning results.

title: Good Subnetworks Provably Exist: Pruning via Greedy Forward Selection

abstract: We introduce Phasic Policy Gradient (PPG), a reinforcement learning framework which modifies traditional on-policy actor-critic methods by separating policy and value function training into distinct phases. In prior methods, one must choose between using a shared network or separate networks to represent the policy and value function. Using separate networks avoids interference between objectives, while using a shared network allows useful features to be shared. PPG is able to achieve the best of both worlds by splitting optimization into two phases, one that advances training and one that distills features. PPG also enables the value function to be more aggressively optimized with a higher level of sample reuse. Compared to PPO, we find that PPG significantly improves sample efficiency on the challenging Procgen Benchmark.

paragraphs: Actor-critic reinforcement learning trains a policy alongside a value function. Using one network for both lets them share useful features, but their training objectives can interfere. Separate networks avoid that interference while giving up direct feature sharing. Phasic Policy Gradient addresses this design tension by organizing policy and value learning into distinct training phases.

One phase advances training, while another distills features. This separation is intended to retain the benefits of shared representations without continuously mixing the two optimization objectives. The framework also allows more aggressive value-function optimization through greater reuse of samples. The training schedule therefore changes both how the objectives interact and how extensively data support value learning.

Compared with PPO, the authors find a significant improvement in sample efficiency on the Procgen Benchmark. This result indicates that the proposed organization of training can make better use of experience in that evaluation. The paper’s contribution is a phased actor-critic framework that treats feature sharing and objective interference as issues that can be addressed through the optimization process.
summary.tldr: Phasic Policy Gradient separates policy and value training while sharing learned features, improving sample efficiency over PPO on Procgen.

title: Phasic Policy Gradient

abstract: A key problem in program synthesis is searching over the large space of possible programs. Human programmers might decide the high-level structure of the desired program before thinking about the details; motivated by this intuition, we consider two-level search for program synthesis, in which the synthesizer first generates a plan, a sequence of symbols that describes the desired program at a high level, before generating the program. We propose to learn representations of programs that can act as plans to organize such a two-level search. Discrete latent codes are appealing for this purpose, and can be learned by applying recent work on discrete autoencoders. Based on these insights, we introduce the Latent Programmer (LP), a program synthesis method that first predicts a discrete latent code from input/output examples, and then generates the program in the target language. We evaluate the LP on two domains, demonstrating that it yields an improvement in accuracy, especially on longer programs for which search is most difficult.

paragraphs: Program synthesis must search a large space of possible programs to find one matching a specification. The paper takes inspiration from programmers who choose an overall structure before working out details. It proposes organizing synthesis into two levels: first predict a high-level plan, then generate a program guided by that plan.

The plans are learned representations expressed as sequences of discrete symbols. Discrete autoencoders provide a way to learn these latent codes from programs. Latent Programmer first predicts a code from input/output examples and then generates the program in the target language. This gives the search an intermediate representation between observed examples and complete program text.

The authors evaluate the method in two domains and report improved accuracy, particularly for longer programs, where search is especially difficult. The results support using learned plans to organize program generation. The central contribution is the two-level search structure: a compact representation captures a program’s broad organization before the synthesizer commits to the details of its implementation.
summary.tldr: Latent Programmer predicts a discrete program plan before generating code, improving synthesis accuracy especially for longer programs.

title: Latent Programmer: Discrete Latent Codes for Program Synthesis

abstract: Recent observations have advanced our understanding of the neural network optimization landscape, revealing the existence of (1) paths of high accuracy containing diverse solutions and (2) wider minima offering improved performance. Previous methods observing diverse paths require multiple training runs. In contrast we aim to leverage both property (1) and (2) with a single method and in a single training run. With a similar computational cost as training one model, we learn lines, curves, and simplexes of high-accuracy neural networks. These neural network subspaces contain diverse solutions that can be ensembled, approaching the ensemble performance of independently trained networks without the training cost. Moreover, using the subspace midpoint boosts accuracy, calibration, and robustness to label noise, outperforming Stochastic Weight Averaging.

paragraphs: Neural network training can uncover regions containing multiple accurate but diverse solutions. Earlier methods for finding paths through such solutions required several training runs. This paper develops a single-run method that learns entire lines, curves, and simplexes of high-accuracy networks, at computational cost similar to training one model.

The learned subspace provides multiple solutions that can be combined into an ensemble. Reported ensemble performance approaches that of independently trained networks without requiring their separate training runs. The significance is that useful predictive diversity can be obtained within one training procedure, making a family of models available from a shared optimization process.

The subspace also offers a useful individual model at its midpoint. The authors report improvements in accuracy, calibration, and robustness to noisy labels, outperforming Stochastic Weight Averaging. These results connect two properties of the optimization landscape: diverse accurate solutions and wider minima associated with better performance. The method aims to benefit from both within the same training run.
summary.tldr: One training run learns a subspace of accurate networks, enabling useful ensembles and improved midpoint models at roughly single-model training cost.

title: Learning Neural Network Subspaces

abstract: Despite the recent success of graph neural networks (GNN), common architectures often exhibit significant limitations, including sensitivity to oversmoothing, long-range dependencies, and spurious edges, e.g., as can occur as a result of graph heterophily or adversarial attacks. To at least partially address these issues within a simple transparent framework, we consider a new family of GNN layers designed to mimic and integrate the update rules of two classical iterative algorithms, namely, proximal gradient descent and iterative reweighted least squares (IRLS). The former defines an extensible base GNN architecture that is immune to oversmoothing while nonetheless capturing long-range dependencies by allowing arbitrary propagation steps. In contrast, the latter produces a novel attention mechanism that is explicitly anchored to an underlying end-to-end energy function, contributing stability with respect to edge uncertainty. When combined we obtain an extremely simple yet robust model that we evaluate across disparate scenarios including standardized benchmarks, adversarially-perturbated graphs, graphs with heterophily, and graphs involving long-range dependencies. In doing so, we compare against SOTA GNN approaches that have been explicitly designed for the respective task, achieving competitive or superior node classification accuracy. Our code is available at https://github.com/FFTYYY/TWIRLS. And for an extended version of this work, please see https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.06064.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can struggle when repeated propagation makes node representations too similar, when relevant information lies far away, or when edges provide misleading information. This paper builds layers from classical optimization algorithms to address these issues within a transparent framework. The two starting points are proximal gradient descent and iterative reweighted least squares.

Proximal gradient descent supplies the update rules for a base architecture that the authors describe as immune to oversmoothing while allowing arbitrarily many propagation steps. Iterative reweighted least squares supplies an attention mechanism tied explicitly to an underlying end-to-end energy function. That connection contributes stability when graph edges are uncertain, rather than leaving attention disconnected from the optimization objective.

The combined model is evaluated on standard benchmarks, adversarially modified graphs, graphs with heterophily, and tasks involving long-range dependencies. Against leading methods tailored to those settings, it achieves competitive or better node-classification accuracy. The findings support using optimization-derived updates to combine long-range propagation and resistance to unreliable edges in a relatively simple architecture.
summary.tldr: Graph layers derived from two classical optimization algorithms combine long-range propagation with attention designed for uncertain edges.

title: Graph Neural Networks Inspired by Classical Iterative Algorithms

abstract: Recent investigations in noise contrastive estimation suggest, both empirically as well as theoretically, that while having more “negative samples” in the contrastive loss improves downstream classification performance initially, beyond a threshold, it hurts downstream performance due to a “collision-coverage” trade-off. But is such a phenomenon inherent in contrastive learning? We show in a simple theoretical setting, where positive pairs are generated by sampling from the underlying latent class (introduced by Saunshi et al. (ICML 2019)), that the downstream performance of the representation optimizing the (population) contrastive loss in fact does not degrade with the number of negative samples. Along the way, we give a structural characterization of the optimal representation in our framework, for noise contrastive estimation. We also provide empirical support for our theoretical results on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning uses positive pairs and negative samples to learn representations for later tasks such as classification. Previous investigations suggested that adding negatives helps initially but eventually hurts because of a collision-coverage tradeoff. This paper asks whether that deterioration is an inherent property of the contrastive objective.

The authors analyze a simplified setting in which positive pairs come from the same underlying latent class. Their result concerns the representation that optimizes the population contrastive loss, meaning the objective defined over the underlying distribution. Within this framework, increasing the number of negative samples does not degrade downstream performance. They also characterize the structure of an optimal representation for noise contrastive estimation.

The finding challenges the necessity of the proposed tradeoff without claiming that every practical training run improves with more negatives. Its theoretical scope is the specified latent-class model and the population optimum. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 provide supporting evidence. Together, the analysis and experiments show why observed degradation should not automatically be treated as an unavoidable consequence of adding negative samples.
summary.tldr: In a latent-class population model, optimal contrastive representations do not suffer worse downstream performance when the number of negatives increases.

title: Do More Negative Samples Necessarily Hurt In Contrastive Learning?

abstract: Relative entropy coding (REC) algorithms encode a sample from a target distribution Q using a proposal distribution P, such that the expected codelength is O(KL[Q || P]). REC can be seamlessly integrated with existing learned compression models since, unlike entropy coding, it does not assume discrete Q or P, and does not require quantisation. However, general REC algorithms require an intractable $\Omega$(exp(KL[Q || P])) runtime. We introduce AS* and AD* coding, two REC algorithms based on A* sampling. We prove that, for continuous distributions over the reals, if the density ratio is unimodal, AS* has O(D$\infty$[Q || P]) expected runtime, where D$\infty$[Q || P] is the Renyi $\infty$-divergence. We provide experimental evidence that AD* also has O(D$\infty$[Q || P]) expected runtime. We prove that AS* and AD* achieve an expected codelength of O(KL[Q || P]). Further, we introduce DAD*, an approximate algorithm based on AD* which retains its favourable runtime and has bias similar to that of alternative methods. Focusing on VAEs, we propose the IsoKL VAE (IKVAE), which can be used with DAD* to further improve compression efficiency. We evaluate A* coding with (IK)VAEs on MNIST, showing that it can losslessly compress images near the theoretically optimal limit.

paragraphs: Relative entropy coding encodes a sample from a target distribution using a proposal distribution, with expected message length governed by their KL divergence. It works with continuous distributions without quantization, making it compatible with learned compression models. However, general algorithms can require runtime exponential in that divergence, creating a major computational obstacle.

The paper introduces AS* and AD*, based on A* sampling, and proves that both achieve expected code lengths of order KL divergence. For continuous distributions on the real line with a unimodal density ratio, AS* has proven expected runtime of order Rényi infinity-divergence. The corresponding runtime behavior for AD* is supported experimentally rather than proved in the abstract.

An approximate variant, DAD*, retains favorable runtime with bias similar to alternative methods. The authors also introduce IsoKL VAEs to improve compression efficiency when combined with DAD*. Experiments using these models on MNIST show lossless image compression near the theoretical optimum. The results distinguish exact coding guarantees, conditional runtime theory, and empirical evidence for practical compression.
summary.tldr: A* sampling yields relative entropy coding methods with compact messages, conditional runtime guarantees, and promising lossless image compression results.

title: Fast Relative Entropy Coding with A* coding

abstract: Learning to play optimally against any mixture over a diverse set of strategies is of important practical interests in competitive games. In this paper, we propose simplex-NeuPL that satisfies two desiderata simultaneously: i) learning a population of strategically diverse basis policies, represented by a single conditional network; ii) using the same network, learn best-responses to any mixture over the simplex of basis policies. We show that the resulting conditional policies incorporate prior information about their opponents effectively, enabling near optimal returns against arbitrary mixture policies in a game with tractable best-responses. We verify that such policies behave Bayes-optimally under uncertainty and offer insights in using this flexibility at test time. Finally, we offer evidence that learning best-responses to any mixture policies is an effective auxiliary task for strategic exploration, which, by itself, can lead to more performant populations.

paragraphs: Competitive play can require responding to uncertainty about which strategy an opponent will use. Simplex-NeuPL tackles this by learning both a diverse population of basis policies and responses to mixtures of those policies. A mixture specifies probabilities over the basis strategies, allowing the learner to represent uncertainty about its opponent in a structured way.

Both capabilities are represented by the same conditional neural network. The network learns strategically different policies while also learning best responses throughout the simplex of mixture weights. This links population learning with opponent-conditioned decision making, so information about likely opposing strategies can directly influence the policy used to play.

In a game where best responses are tractable, the authors find near-optimal returns against arbitrary mixture policies and verify Bayes-optimal behavior under uncertainty. They also provide evidence that learning responses to mixtures serves as a useful auxiliary task for strategic exploration and can improve the population itself. The findings support both exploiting opponent information at test time and using mixture-response training to develop stronger strategies.
summary.tldr: Simplex-NeuPL uses one conditional network to learn diverse strategies and responses to mixtures, with evidence of near-optimal opponent-aware play.

title: Simplex Neural Population Learning: Any-Mixture Bayes-Optimality in Symmetric Zero-sum Games

abstract: We study the problem of designing an adaptive strategy for querying a noisy zeroth-order-oracle to efficiently learn about the optimizer of an unknown function $f$. To make the problem tractable, we assume that $f$ lies in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) associated with a known kernel $K$, with its norm bounded by $M<\infty$. Prior results, working in a minimax framework , have characterized the worst-case (over all functions in the problem class) limits on regret achievable by any algorithm, and have constructed algorithms with matching (modulo polylogarithmic factors) worst-case performance for the Matern family of kernels. These results suffer from two drawbacks. First, the minimax lower bound gives limited information about the limits of regret achievable by commonly used algorithms on a specific problem instance $f$. Second, the existing upper bound analysis fails to adapt to easier problem instances within the function class. Our work takes steps to address both these issues. First, we derive instance-dependent regret lower bounds for algorithms with uniformly (over the function class) vanishing normalized cumulative regret. Our result, valid for several practically relevant kernelized bandits algorithms, such as, GP-UCB, GP-TS and SupKernelUCB, identifies a fundamental complexity measure associated with every problem instance. We then address the second issue, by proposing a new minimax near-optimal algorithm that also adapts to easier problem instances.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to choose noisy function evaluations adaptively when searching for an unknown function’s optimizer. It assumes the function belongs to the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of a known kernel and has a bounded norm. These restrictions make it possible to analyze what an algorithm can learn from its queries.

Earlier worst-case analyses characterize the hardest functions in a class, but reveal less about a particular function or the benefits of easier instances. The authors derive instance-dependent regret lower bounds for algorithms whose normalized cumulative regret vanishes uniformly over the class. The result applies to several established kernelized-bandit algorithms and identifies a complexity measure associated with each individual instance.

The paper then proposes an algorithm that remains near-optimal in the minimax sense while adapting to easier instances. This joins two goals: retaining strong protection against difficult functions and exploiting favorable structure when it is present. The contribution is a more differentiated account of learning difficulty than a single worst-case rate can provide.
summary.tldr: Instance-dependent lower bounds and an adaptive algorithm distinguish easier kernelized-bandit problems while retaining near-optimal worst-case performance.

title: Instance Dependent Regret Analysis of Kernelized Bandits

abstract: We show how probabilistic numerics can be used to convert an initial value problem into a Gauss–Markov process parametrised by the dynamics of the initial value problem. Consequently, the often difficult problem of parameter estimation in ordinary differential equations is reduced to hyper-parameter estimation in Gauss–Markov regression, which tends to be considerably easier. The method’s relation and benefits in comparison to classical numerical integration and gradient matching approaches is elucidated. In particular, the method can, in contrast to gradient matching, handle partial observations, and has certain routes for escaping local optima not available to classical numerical integration. Experimental results demonstrate that the method is on par or moderately better than competing approaches.

paragraphs: Estimating the parameters of an ordinary differential equation means finding dynamics that explain observed behavior from an initial state. This can be a difficult optimization problem. Fenrir uses probabilistic numerics to represent the initial value problem as a Gauss–Markov process whose parameters encode the original dynamics, giving the estimation problem a different mathematical form.

With this construction, estimating differential-equation parameters becomes hyperparameter estimation in a regression model. The authors argue that this transformed problem tends to be considerably easier. The dynamics still shape the model, so the regression formulation incorporates the governing equations rather than treating observations as unrelated samples to be fitted independently.

The paper compares this approach with classical numerical integration and gradient matching. It can handle partial observations, unlike the gradient-matching approach discussed, and offers certain ways to escape local optima that classical integration does not provide. Experiments place its performance on par with or moderately above competing approaches. The reported benefit is a useful reformulation with specific capabilities, rather than uniformly dramatic empirical gains.
summary.tldr: Fenrir converts differential-equation parameter estimation into Gauss–Markov regression, supporting partial observations and competitive empirical performance.

title: Fenrir: Physics-Enhanced Regression for Initial Value Problems

abstract: Designing efficient general-purpose contextual bandit algorithms that work with large—or even infinite—action spaces would facilitate application to important scenarios such as information retrieval, recommendation systems, and continuous control. While obtaining standard regret guarantees can be hopeless, alternative regret notions have been proposed to tackle the large action setting. We propose a smooth regret notion for contextual bandits, which dominates previously proposed alternatives. We design a statistically and computationally efficient algorithm—for the proposed smooth regret—that works with general function approximation under standard supervised oracles. We also present an adaptive algorithm that automatically adapts to any smoothness level. Our algorithms can be used to recover the previous minimax/Pareto optimal guarantees under the standard regret, e.g., in bandit problems with multiple best arms and Lipschitz/H{ö}lder bandits. We conduct large-scale empirical evaluations demonstrating the efficacy of our proposed algorithms.

paragraphs: Learning to choose among a vast or continuous set of actions creates difficulties for contextual bandits. Standard regret, which evaluates the cost of imperfect decisions, can be too demanding to guarantee efficiently in this setting. The paper develops an alternative evaluation criterion intended to support useful learning guarantees for such action spaces.

The proposed smooth regret notion dominates earlier alternatives. For this criterion, the authors give an algorithm that is efficient in both data use and computation while accommodating general function approximation through standard supervised learning oracles. They also introduce an adaptive algorithm that automatically adjusts to any smoothness level, extending the approach beyond a single fixed level.

The framework can recover previously established minimax or Pareto-optimal standard-regret guarantees in settings including multiple best actions and Lipschitz or Hölder bandits. Thus, the alternative criterion also connects to familiar guarantees in structured cases. Large-scale experiments support the algorithms' efficacy, complementing the theoretical account of when broad action spaces can be handled efficiently.
summary.tldr: Smooth regret enables efficient contextual bandit algorithms for continuous actions, including an algorithm that adapts automatically to smoothness.

title: Contextual Bandits with Smooth Regret: Efficient Learning in Continuous Action Spaces

abstract: Maximizing a monotone submodular function under cardinality constraint $k$ is a core problem in machine learning and database with many basic applications, including video and data summarization, recommendation systems, feature extraction, exemplar clustering, and coverage problems. We study this classic problem in the fully dynamic model where a stream of insertions and deletions of elements of an underlying ground set is given and the goal is to maintain an approximate solution using a fast update time. A recent paper at NeurIPS’20 by Lattanzi, Mitrovic, Norouzi-Fard, Tarnawski, Zadimoghaddam claims to obtain a dynamic algorithm for this problem with a $(\frac{1}{2} -\epsilon)$ approximation ratio and a query complexity bounded by $\mathrm{poly}(\log(n),\log(k),\epsilon^{-1})$. However, as we explain in this paper, the analysis has some important gaps. Having a dynamic algorithm for the problem with polylogarithmic update time is even more important in light of a recent result by Chen and Peng at STOC’22 who show a matching lower bound for the problem – any randomized algorithm with a $\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon$ approximation ratio must have an amortized query complexity that is polynomial in $n$. In this paper, we develop a simpler algorithm for the problem that maintains a $(\frac{1}{2}-\epsilon)$-approximate solution for submodular maximization under cardinality constraint $k$ using a polylogarithmic amortized update time.
originalAbstract: Maximizing a monotone submodular function under cardinality constraint $k$ is a core problem in machine learning and database with many basic applications, including video and data summarization, recommendation systems, feature extraction, exemplar clustering, and coverage problems. We study this classic problem in the fully dynamic model where a stream of insertions and deletions of elements of an underlying ground set is given and the goal is to maintain an approximate solution using a fast update time. A recent paper at NeurIPS’20 by Lattanzi, Mitrovic, Norouzi-Fard, Tarnawski, Zadimoghaddam claims to obtain a dynamic algorithm for this problem with a $(\frac{1}{2} -\epsilon)$ approximation ratio and a query complexity bounded by $\mathrm{poly}(\log(n),\log(k),\epsilon^{-1})$. However, as we explain in this paper, the analysis has some important gaps. Having a dynamic algorithm for the problem with polylogarithmic update time is even more important in light of a recent result by Chen and Peng at STOC’22 who show a matching lower bound for the problem – any randomized algorithm with a $\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon$ approximation ratio must have an amortized query complexity that is polynomial in $n$. In this paper, we develop a simpler algorithm for the problem that maintains a $(\frac{1}{2}-\epsilon)$-approximate solution for submodular maximization under cardinality constraint $k$ using a polylogarithmic amortized update time.

paragraphs: Many selection problems ask for at most k items that collectively provide high value, with diminishing returns as more items are added. This is monotone submodular maximization under a cardinality constraint. The paper studies its fully dynamic version: available items can arrive or disappear, and the selected collection must remain useful as the underlying set changes.

The authors develop a simpler algorithm that maintains a solution worth at least a one-half-minus-epsilon fraction of the optimum. Its amortized update time is polylogarithmic, meaning the cost averaged across updates grows as powers of logarithms rather than as a polynomial in the number of available items. This makes rapid maintenance the central contribution.

The paper also identifies important gaps in an earlier analysis claiming a similar result. Its guarantee matters because a cited lower bound places a barrier just above one-half: randomized algorithms achieving one-half-plus-epsilon approximation require polynomial amortized query complexity. The new algorithm establishes an efficient guarantee on the attainable side of that stated tradeoff between approximation quality and update cost.
summary.tldr: A simpler dynamic algorithm maintains a one-half-minus-epsilon approximation for constrained submodular maximization with polylogarithmic amortized update time.

title: Dynamic Constrained Submodular Optimization with Polylogarithmic Update Time

abstract: Recent neural network-based wave functions have achieved state-of-the-art accuracies in modeling ab-initio ground-state potential energy surface. However, these networks can only solve different spatial arrangements of the same set of atoms. To overcome this limitation, we present Graph-learned orbital embeddings (Globe), a neural network-based reparametrization method that can adapt neural wave functions to different molecules. Globe learns representations of local electronic structures that generalize across molecules via spatial message passing by connecting molecular orbitals to covalent bonds. Further, we propose a size-consistent wave function Ansatz, the Molecular orbital network (Moon), tailored to jointly solve Schrödinger equations of different molecules. In our experiments, we find Moon converging in 4.5 times fewer steps to similar accuracy as previous methods or to lower energies given the same time. Further, our analysis shows that Moon’s energy estimate scales additively with increased system sizes, unlike previous work where we observe divergence. In both computational chemistry and machine learning, we are the first to demonstrate that a single wave function can solve the Schrödinger equation of molecules with different atoms jointly.

paragraphs: Neural wave functions have achieved high accuracy in modeling ground-state potential energy surfaces, but the methods discussed here are restricted to different arrangements of the same atoms. This paper seeks to share a wave-function model across different molecules, extending generalization beyond changes in molecular geometry.

The authors introduce Graph-learned orbital embeddings, or Globe, to reparameterize neural wave functions for different molecules. Globe connects molecular orbitals to covalent bonds and uses spatial message passing to learn transferable representations of local electronic structure. They also propose the Molecular orbital network, or Moon, a size-consistent wave-function form designed to solve Schrödinger equations for multiple molecules jointly.

Its energy estimates also scale additively as system size increases, unlike the divergence observed in prior work. The authors report the first demonstration of a single wave function jointly solving molecules containing different atoms, combining cross-molecule learning with physically relevant scaling behavior.
summary.tldr: Globe and Moon enable shared neural wave functions across different molecules, with faster experimental convergence and additive energy scaling.

title: Generalizing Neural Wave Functions

abstract: While it has long been empirically observed that adversarial robustness may be at odds with standard accuracy and may have further disparate impacts on different classes, it remains an open question to what extent such observations hold and how the class imbalance plays a role within. In this paper, we attempt to understand this question of accuracy disparity by taking a closer look at linear classifiers under a Gaussian mixture model. We decompose the impact of adversarial robustness into two parts: an inherent effect that will degrade the standard accuracy on all classes due to the robustness constraint, and the other caused by the class imbalance ratio, which will increase the accuracy disparity compared to standard training. Furthermore, we also show that such effects extend beyond the Gaussian mixture model, by generalizing our data model to the general family of stable distributions. More specifically, we demonstrate that while the constraint of adversarial robustness consistently degrades the standard accuracy in the balanced class setting, the class imbalance ratio plays a fundamentally different role in accuracy disparity compared to the Gaussian case, due to the heavy tail of the stable distribution. We additionally perform experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets to corroborate our theoretical findings. Our empirical results also suggest that the implications may extend to nonlinear models over real-world datasets. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/Accuracy-Disparity/AT-on-AD.

paragraphs: Adversarial robustness can reduce ordinary prediction accuracy and affect classes unequally. This paper investigates how much of that disparity comes from the robustness requirement and how much comes from class imbalance. It begins with linear classifiers under a Gaussian mixture data model, providing a structured setting for separating the effects.

In that setting, the authors identify an inherent robustness effect that reduces standard accuracy across all classes and an imbalance-related effect that increases accuracy disparity relative to standard training. They then extend the analysis to stable distributions. In the balanced setting, the robustness constraint still degrades standard accuracy, but heavy tails change how class imbalance influences the disparity.

This distinction matters because an explanation derived from Gaussian data does not describe the imbalance effect identically across the broader distribution family. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets corroborate the theoretical findings. Additional empirical results suggest that the implications may extend to nonlinear models on real-world data, while the stated formal analysis centers on the specified classifier and distribution settings.
summary.tldr: The paper separates robustness-induced accuracy loss from class-imbalance effects and shows that distribution tails change how imbalance affects accuracy disparity.

title: Understanding the Impact of Adversarial Robustness on Accuracy Disparity

abstract: Modern hierarchical vision transformers have added several vision-specific components in the pursuit of supervised classification performance. While these components lead to effective accuracies and attractive FLOP counts, the added complexity actually makes these transformers slower than their vanilla ViT counterparts. In this paper, we argue that this additional bulk is unnecessary. By pretraining with a strong visual pretext task (MAE), we can strip out all the bells-and-whistles from a state-of-the-art multi-stage vision transformer without losing accuracy. In the process, we create Hiera, an extremely simple hierarchical vision transformer that is more accurate than previous models while being significantly faster both at inference and during training. We evaluate Hiera on a variety of tasks for image and video recognition. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/hiera.

paragraphs: Hierarchical vision transformers have accumulated specialized components intended to improve supervised image classification. These additions can deliver good accuracy and appealing arithmetic-operation counts while still making execution slower than a simpler vision transformer. The paper investigates whether strong pretraining can remove the need for that architectural complexity.

Starting from a state-of-the-art multi-stage vision transformer, the authors use MAE, a strong visual pretraining task, and remove the specialized additions without losing accuracy. The resulting architecture, Hiera, retains a hierarchical structure while simplifying the network. The argument therefore connects architectural simplicity to the capabilities supplied through pretraining.

The authors report that Hiera is more accurate than previous models and significantly faster during both training and inference. They evaluate it across image- and video-recognition tasks. These findings support the usefulness of the simplified design in the tested settings and highlight why operation counts alone do not settle practical efficiency: the complexity of the operations and architecture also affects observed execution speed.
summary.tldr: Hiera combines strong MAE pretraining with a simplified hierarchical transformer to improve accuracy and training and inference speed.

title: Hiera: A Hierarchical Vision Transformer without the Bells-and-Whistles

abstract: GNNs rely on the exchange of messages to distribute information along the edges of the graph. This approach makes the efficiency of architectures highly dependent on the specific structure of the input graph. Certain graph topologies lead to inefficient information propagation, resulting in a phenomenon known as over-squashing. While the majority of existing methods address over-squashing by rewiring the input graph, our novel approach involves constructing a graph directly from features using Delaunay Triangulation. We posit that the topological properties of the resulting graph prove advantageous for mitigate oversmoothing and over-squashing. Our extensive experimentation demonstrates that our method consistently outperforms established graph rewiring methods.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks distribute information by passing messages along edges. Their ability to propagate useful information therefore depends on the graph’s structure, not just the neural architecture. Some structures create bottlenecks that squeeze information together, a problem called over-squashing. The paper also targets over-smoothing, another difficulty in learning useful graph representations.

Many approaches address propagation problems by rewiring the supplied graph. This work instead constructs a graph directly from the input features using Delaunay triangulation. The change makes feature-based graph construction the central intervention. The authors propose that the resulting graph’s topological properties are advantageous for mitigating both over-squashing and over-smoothing.

Across extensive experiments, the method consistently outperforms the established graph-rewiring methods evaluated. These results support treating graph construction itself as a way to improve information flow. The abstract presents the beneficial topology as the authors’ explanation and the comparative gains as experimental findings. Its main contribution is thus an alternative to repairing an existing graph: build a feature-derived graph whose structure is intended to better support message passing.
summary.tldr: Constructing a graph from features with Delaunay triangulation outperforms evaluated rewiring methods while targeting message-passing bottlenecks.

title: Delaunay Graph: Addressing Over-Squashing and Over-Smoothing Using Delaunay Triangulation

abstract: We propose TopDis (Topological Disentanglement), a method for learning disentangled representations via adding a multi-scale topological loss term. Disentanglement is a crucial property of data representations substantial for the explainability and robustness of deep learning models and a step towards high-level cognition. The state-of-the-art methods are based on VAE and encourage the joint distribution of latent variables to be factorized. We take a different perspective on disentanglement by analyzing topological properties of data manifolds. In particular, we optimize the topological similarity for data manifolds traversals. To the best of our knowledge, our paper is the first one to propose a differentiable topological loss for disentanglement learning. Our experiments have shown that the proposed TopDis loss improves disentanglement scores such as MIG, FactorVAE score, SAP score, and DCI disentanglement score with respect to state-of-the-art results while preserving the reconstruction quality. Our method works in an unsupervised manner, permitting us to apply it to problems without labeled factors of variation. The TopDis loss works even when factors of variation are correlated. Additionally, we show how to use the proposed topological loss to find disentangled directions in a trained GAN.

paragraphs: Disentangled representations aim to separate different factors of variation in data. Many existing methods encourage latent variables to have a factorized joint distribution. This paper proposes TopDis, which instead uses the topological structure of data manifolds to guide how a representation separates those factors.

TopDis adds a differentiable loss that measures topological similarity across manifold traversals at multiple scales. This provides an additional training signal based on the structure encountered as a representation varies. The method is unsupervised, so it does not require labels identifying the underlying factors, and the authors report that the loss also works when those factors are correlated.

Experiments show improved MIG, FactorVAE, SAP, and DCI disentanglement scores relative to state-of-the-art results while maintaining reconstruction quality. The authors also demonstrate using the loss to identify disentangled directions in an already trained GAN. These results suggest that topological structure can help organize latent variation without requiring the usual emphasis on statistically independent factors.
summary.tldr: TopDis uses a differentiable multiscale topological loss to improve unsupervised disentanglement while preserving reconstruction quality, including with correlated factors.

title: Disentanglement Learning via Topology

abstract: We introduce a novel Pseudo-Negative Regularization (PNR) framework for effective continual self-supervised learning (CSSL). Our PNR leverages pseudo-negatives obtained through model-based augmentation in a way that newly learned representations may not contradict what has been learned in the past. Specifically, for the InfoNCE-based contrastive learning methods, we define symmetric pseudo-negatives obtained from current and previous models and use them in both main and regularization loss terms. Furthermore, we extend this idea to non-contrastive learning methods which do not inherently rely on negatives. For these methods, a pseudo-negative is defined as the output from the previous model for a differently augmented version of the anchor sample and is asymmetrically applied to the regularization term. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that our PNR framework achieves state-of-the-art performance in representation learning during CSSL by effectively balancing the trade-off between plasticity and stability.

paragraphs: Continual self-supervised learning must develop useful representations from new data while preserving what earlier learning established. The proposed Pseudo-Negative Regularization framework addresses this tension using pseudo-negatives produced through model-based augmentation. These supply training signals intended to reduce contradictions between newly learned representations and knowledge captured by an earlier model.

For contrastive methods based on InfoNCE, the framework defines symmetric pseudo-negatives using both current and previous models. It places them in the main learning loss as well as the regularization loss. The design therefore makes the relationship between old and new representations part of both current learning and the mechanism intended to preserve earlier knowledge.

The authors also adapt the idea to non-contrastive methods, which do not ordinarily use negatives. There, a pseudo-negative comes from the previous model’s output for a differently augmented version of the anchor, and enters the regularization term asymmetrically. Extensive experiments report state-of-the-art representation learning performance in continual self-supervised settings, supporting the framework’s ability to balance adaptation to new information with stability.
summary.tldr: Pseudo-Negative Regularization uses current and previous models to balance new learning with representation stability.

title: Regularizing with Pseudo-Negatives for Continual Self-Supervised Learning

abstract: The increasing size of large language models (LLMs) traditionally requires low-precision integer formats to meet strict latency and power demands. Yet recently, alternative formats such as Normal Float (NF4) have increased model accuracy at the cost of increased chip area. In this work, we first conduct a large-scale analysis of LLM weights and activations across 30 networks and conclude that most distributions follow a Student’s t-distribution. We then derive a new theoretically optimal format, Student Float (SF4), that improves over NF4 across modern LLMs, for example increasing the average accuracy on LLaMA2-7B by 0.76% across tasks. Using this format as a high-accuracy reference, we then propose augmenting E2M1 with two variants of supernormal support for higher model accuracy. Finally, we explore the quality and efficiency frontier across 11 datatypes by evaluating their model accuracy and hardware complexity. We discover a Pareto curve composed of INT4, E2M1, and E2M1 with supernormal support, which offers a continuous tradeoff between model accuracy and chip area. For example, E2M1 with supernormal support increases the accuracy of Phi-2 by up to 2.19% with 1.22% area overhead, enabling more LLM-based applications to be run at four bits. The supporting code is hosted at https://github.com/cornell-zhang/llm-datatypes.

paragraphs: Representing language-model numbers with four bits can help meet latency and power requirements, but the numerical format affects accuracy and hardware cost. The authors analyze weights and activations across 30 networks and find that most of their distributions follow Student’s t-distribution. They use that observation to guide the design of low-precision formats.

The resulting Student Float format, SF4, is derived as theoretically optimal under the distributional model. One example improves Phi-2 accuracy by up to 2.19% with 1.22% area overhead. The findings show why numerical-format choices should be assessed jointly for model quality and implementation cost.
summary.tldr: An analysis of LLM number distributions motivates four-bit formats with improved accuracy and measured tradeoffs in chip area.

title: Learning from Students: Applying t-Distributions to Explore Accurate and Efficient Formats for LLMs

abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more powerful and are deployed more autonomously, it will be increasingly important to prevent them from causing harmful outcomes. To do so, safety measures either aim at making LLMs try to avoid harmful outcomes or aim at preventing LLMs from causing harmful outcomes, even if they try to cause them. In this paper, we focus on this second layer of defense. We develop and evaluate pipelines of safety techniques (protocols) that try to ensure safety despite intentional subversion - an approach we call AI control. We investigate a setting in which we want to solve a sequence of programming problems without ever submitting subtly wrong code, using access to a powerful but untrusted model (in our case, GPT-4), access to a less powerful trusted model (in our case, GPT-3.5), and limited access to high-quality trusted labor. We investigate a range of protocols and red-team them by exploring strategies that the untrusted model could use to subvert them. We find that using the trusted model to edit untrusted-model code or using the untrusted model as a monitor substantially improves on simple baselines.

paragraphs: AI control focuses on preventing harmful outcomes even when a model deliberately tries to cause them. This paper studies that additional layer of defense by designing and testing protocols around an untrusted model. The question is whether a system can benefit from powerful capabilities while resisting attempts to misuse them.

The evaluation setting involves solving a sequence of programming problems without submitting subtly incorrect code. The system has access to a stronger, untrusted GPT-4 model, a weaker, trusted GPT-3.5 model, and a limited amount of high-quality trusted labor. The authors examine multiple protocols and red-team them by developing strategies through which the untrusted model could undermine their safeguards.

Two approaches substantially improve on simple baselines: having the trusted model edit code produced by the untrusted model, and using the untrusted model as a monitor. These findings concern the evaluated programming setup and adversarial strategies. They show that the organization of checking and editing can materially improve safety even when the stronger model itself is not assumed trustworthy.
summary.tldr: Red-teamed programming protocols improve safety by structuring how trusted and untrusted models edit or monitor code.

title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion

abstract: Although deep learning models have taken on commercial and political relevance, key aspects of their training and operation remain poorly understood. This has sparked interest in science of deep learning projects, many of which require large amounts of time, money, and electricity. But how much of this research really needs to occur at scale? In this paper, we introduce MNIST-1D: a minimalist, procedurally generated, low-memory, and low-compute alternative to classic deep learning benchmarks. Although the dimensionality of MNIST-1D is only 40 and its default training set size only 4000, MNIST-1D can be used to study inductive biases of different deep architectures, find lottery tickets, observe deep double descent, metalearn an activation function, and demonstrate guillotine regularization in self-supervised learning. All these experiments can be conducted on a GPU or often even on a CPU within minutes, allowing for fast prototyping, educational use cases, and cutting-edge research on a low budget.

paragraphs: Studying deep learning can require substantial computation, even when the goal is to understand a basic training phenomenon. MNIST-1D is a small, procedurally generated benchmark intended to make such investigations faster and cheaper. Its examples have only 40 dimensions, and the default training set contains 4,000 examples.

Despite that small scale, the authors show that the benchmark supports several distinct investigations. These include comparing architectural inductive biases, finding lottery tickets, observing deep double descent, learning an activation function through meta-learning, and demonstrating guillotine regularization in self-supervised learning. The value is that a compact problem still exhibits a range of behaviors researchers want to study.

The reported experiments run within minutes on a GPU and often on a CPU. That makes repeated experimentation accessible for prototyping, teaching, and research with limited resources. The paper's contribution is a concrete demonstration that several substantive deep-learning questions can be explored at small scale, reducing the cost of investigating those particular phenomena.
summary.tldr: MNIST-1D makes several deep-learning phenomena practical to study within minutes using a tiny, procedurally generated dataset.

title: Scaling Down Deep Learning with MNIST-1D

abstract: Optimal transport (OT) and the related Wasserstein metric ($W$) are powerful and ubiquitous tools for comparing distributions. However, computing pairwise Wasserstein distances rapidly becomes intractable as cohort size grows. An attractive alternative would be to find an embedding space in which pairwise Euclidean distances map to OT distances, akin to standard multidimensional scaling (MDS). We present Wasserstein Wormhole, a transformer-based autoencoder that embeds empirical distributions into a latent space wherein Euclidean distances approximate OT distances. Extending MDS theory, we show that our objective function implies a bound on the error incurred when embedding non-Euclidean distances. Empirically, distances between Wormhole embeddings closely match Wasserstein distances, enabling linear time computation of OT distances. Along with an encoder that maps distributions to embeddings, Wasserstein Wormhole includes a decoder that maps embeddings back to distributions, allowing for operations in the embedding space to generalize to OT spaces, such as Wasserstein barycenter estimation and OT interpolation. By lending scalability and interpretability to OT approaches, Wasserstein Wormhole unlocks new avenues for data analysis in the fields of computational geometry and single-cell biology.
