paragraphs: Streaming video systems must keep processing new frames without letting memory or computation grow indefinitely. They also need to handle streams longer than the sequences used during training. This paper focuses on how key-value caches, which hold reusable internal information, are constructed when adapting pretrained offline video models to streaming use.

Decoupled Streaming Cache, or DSCache, maintains a cumulative cache for the past and builds a separate instant cache when needed. Constructing the instant cache independently of earlier caches is intended to preserve the information in recent inputs. A position-agnostic encoding strategy also allows cached information to support positions beyond the training length and avoids position overflow.

The mechanism requires no additional training. On streaming video question-answering benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art performance and an average accuracy improvement of 2.5% over earlier methods. The result highlights cache construction as a useful design choice alongside cache reuse: how new information enters memory matters when a model must continually interpret recent events while retaining past context.
summary.tldr: DSCache adapts offline video models to streaming without retraining by separating recent-input cache construction from accumulated past memory.

title: Decouple and Cache: KV Cache Construction for Streaming Video Understanding

abstract: We study optimal learning-rate selection in two-layer and three-layer linear neural networks trained to learn linear target functions. In particular, we derive the exact closed-form expressions for the gradients and test loss after one and two steps of gradient descent, enabling a precise characterization of early training dynamics. We characterize how learning rates should scale under the gradient approximation in the first two steps, and prove that performing updates with this approximation yields a tractable surrogate loss with a tight, small approximation error. This formulation enables the theoretical analysis of layer-wise learning rates and reveals a distinct early-training regime: test loss can be minimized by unequal learning rates at the initial step, while equal learning rates become optimal in subsequent steps. Our numerical experiments validate the theory and demonstrate the importance of balancing layer-wise learning rates early during training. The code is available at: TDCSZ327/Layer-Balancing.

paragraphs: A learning rate controls how far a layer's parameters move during a training update. This paper investigates how those rates should differ across layers at the start of training. Its setting is deliberately specific: two-layer and three-layer linear neural networks learning linear target functions, where early optimization can be examined mathematically.

The authors derive exact formulas for gradients and test loss after one and two gradient-descent steps. They then analyze how learning rates should scale under a gradient approximation. Updates using that approximation produce a simpler surrogate loss, and the authors prove that its approximation error is small and tightly controlled. This makes the interaction between layer-specific rates tractable to study.

The analysis reveals a change within early training: unequal rates can minimize test loss at the initial step, while equal rates become optimal in subsequent steps in the studied formulation. Numerical experiments support the theory. The contribution is a precise account of why balancing rates may depend on training stage, grounded in this linear-network setting.
summary.tldr: An analysis of linear networks shows why unequal layer learning rates can help initially before equal rates become optimal in the studied early-training regime.

title: Balancing Learning Rates Across Layers: Exact Two-Step Dynamics and Optimal Scaling in Linear Neural Networks

abstract: Bayesian experimental design (BED) provides a principled framework for optimising data collection by choosing experiments that are maximally informative about unknown parameters. However, existing methods cannot deal with the joint challenge of (a) partially observable dynamical systems, where only noisy and incomplete observations are available, and (b) fully online inference, which updates posterior distributions and selects designs sequentially in a computationally efficient manner. Under partial observability, dynamical systems are naturally modeled as state-space models (SSMs), in which latent states mediate the link between parameters and data, making the likelihood—and thus information-theoretic objectives like the expected information gain (EIG)—intractable. We address these challenges by deriving new estimators of the EIG and its gradient that explicitly marginalise latent states, enabling scalable stochastic optimisation in nonlinear SSMs. Our approach leverages nested particle filters for efficient online state-parameter inference with convergence guarantees. Applications to realistic models, such as the susceptible–infectious–recovered (SIR) model and a moving source location task, show that our framework successfully handles both partial observability and online inference.

Applications to realistic models, such as the susceptible–infectious–recovered (SIR) model and a moving source location task, show that our framework successfully handles both partial observability and online inference.

paragraphs: Choosing the next experiment can be as important as interpreting the data already collected. Bayesian experimental design selects experiments for how much they are expected to reveal about unknown parameters. This paper addresses systems that evolve over time but are observed only through noisy, incomplete measurements, while requiring inference and experimental choices to update sequentially.

Such systems are represented by state-space models, where hidden states connect parameters to observations. Accounting for those states makes the likelihood, and therefore expected information gain, intractable. The authors derive estimators of expected information gain and its gradient that explicitly marginalize the hidden states. These estimators make stochastic optimization of experimental choices possible for nonlinear state-space models.

The approach uses nested particle filters to perform online inference about both states and parameters, with convergence guarantees. Applications include a susceptible–infectious–recovered model and a moving-source location task. The results demonstrate handling partial observability and online inference together. This combination matters because experimental decisions can adapt to incoming evidence while still accounting for uncertainty about what the system is doing internally.
summary.tldr: New information-gain estimators enable sequential Bayesian experiment selection for nonlinear systems with noisy, incomplete observations.

title: Online Bayesian Experimental Design for Partially Observed Dynamical Systems

abstract: This paper proposes a suite of rationality measures and associated theory for reinforcement learning agents, a property increasingly critical yet rarely explored. We define an action in deployment to be perfectly rational if it maximises the hidden true value function in the steepest direction. The expected value discrepancy of a policy’s actions against their rational counterparts, culminating over the trajectory in deployment, is defined to be expected rational risk; an empirical average version in training is also defined. Their difference, termed as rational risk gap, is decomposed into (1) an extrinsic component caused by environment shifts between training and deployment, and (2) an intrinsic one due to the algorithm’s generalisability in a dynamic environment. They are upper bounded by, respectively, (1) the $1$-Wasserstein distance between transition kernels and initial state distributions in training and deployment, and (2) the empirical Rademacher complexity of the value function class. Our theory suggests hypotheses on the benefits from regularisers (including layer normalisation, $\ell_2$ regularisation, and weight normalisation) and domain randomisation, as well as the harm from environment shifts. Experiments are in full agreement with these hypotheses. The code is available at https://github.com/EVIEHub/Rationality.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a specific mathematical account of rational behavior for reinforcement-learning agents. It defines a perfectly rational deployment action through the steepest direction of improvement in a hidden true value function. Expected rational risk accumulates the value discrepancy between an agent’s actions and their rational counterparts over the trajectory.

The authors also define an empirical training version of this risk. The difference between training and deployment risk is separated into an external component caused by environment changes and an internal component reflecting the algorithm’s generalization. In particular, the theory suggests benefits from layer normalization, l2 regularization, weight normalization, and domain randomization, alongside harm from environment changes. Experiments agree with those hypotheses. The contribution supplies measures and explanatory theory for this defined notion of rationality, linking deployment behavior to both learning complexity and environmental differences.
summary.tldr: The paper defines rational risk for reinforcement-learning agents and bounds its training-to-deployment gap through environment shift and model complexity.

title: Rationality Measurement and Theory for Reinforcement Learning Agents

abstract: We identify a new dimension for enhancing rollout diversity in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for LLMs. While GRPO relies on diverse rollouts, prevailing strategies primarily increase diversity by injecting more token-level randomness, which may introduce step-wise noise and leads to incoherent trajectories. We uncover that smaller models within the same model family inherently exhibit higher policy-level diversity, indicated by their superior pass@k relative to larger counterparts as sample counts increase. Unlike token-level noise, this diversity is temporally correlated, preserves logical consistency, and provides structured exploration signals for gradient estimation. We thus propose S2L-PO (Small-to-Large Policy Optimization), a framework that leverages fixed small models as natural explorers to train larger models. To balance exploration and exploitation, we design a progressive annealing strategy that transitions from offline small-model rollouts to the large learner’s own sampling. This shift elegantly avoids mid-training performance drops caused by the small model’s capacity limits, achieving faster convergence and unlocking a higher performance ceiling. S2L-PO improves accuracy on diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks (eg., +8.8% on AIME 24 using a 1.7B explorer to guide the 8B model) while reducing rollout compute. The code will be made available.

paragraphs: Group Relative Policy Optimization benefits from varied generated solutions, but adding randomness at each token can produce incoherent reasoning. This paper identifies another source of diversity: smaller models within the same family. As sample counts increase, their stronger pass@k indicates a useful variety of possible solution paths.

The authors characterize this as policy-level diversity that remains correlated across reasoning steps and preserves logical consistency. Their S2L-PO framework uses fixed small models to supply exploration for a larger learner. A progressive annealing strategy gradually shifts training from offline small-model rollouts toward samples generated by the larger model itself.

That transition addresses the smaller model’s capacity limits, which can otherwise cause performance drops partway through training. The authors report faster convergence, improved mathematical reasoning accuracy, and reduced rollout computation. One result is an 8.8% accuracy gain on AIME 24 when a 1.7-billion-parameter explorer guides an 8-billion-parameter learner. The findings support using coherent variation between policies as a training resource beyond token-level randomness.
summary.tldr: S2L-PO uses smaller models’ diverse reasoning paths to train larger models, then gradually shifts to the learner’s own samples.

title: Smaller Models are Natural Explorers for Policy-Level Diversity in GRPO

abstract: For denoising Spatially Resolved Transcriptomics (SRT) data, existing methods often construct spot and gene graphs to model inter-spot and inter-gene relationships, respectively. However, these methods often introduce spurious similarity biases among spots when constructing the spot graph and fail to capture nonlinear relationships among genes when constructing the gene graph. Moreover, ineffective graph fusion strategies further bottleneck denoising performance. To address these challenges, we propose SpaEF, which innovatively constructs spot and gene graphs with two Large Models (LMs) to inject prior knowledge for mitigating biases and capture nonlinear relationships, and then fuses them with the proposed element-wise graph autoencoder. As far as we know, SpaEF is the first SRT denoising method that utilizes pre-trained LMs to construct spot and gene graphs. Experiments on four real-world datasets with corresponding downstream tasks demonstrate that SpaEF not only outperforms SOTA denoising methods in accuracy but also exhibits strong robustness across tasks.

paragraphs: Denoising spatially resolved transcriptomics requires modeling relationships among measurement spots and among genes. Existing approaches often represent these relationships with two graphs. The paper identifies weaknesses in both: spot graphs can introduce misleading similarities, while gene graphs can fail to capture nonlinear relationships. Combining the graphs ineffectively creates another obstacle.

SpaEF uses two pretrained large models to construct the spot and gene graphs. Their prior knowledge is intended to reduce similarity biases and capture relationships that simpler graph construction misses. An element-wise graph autoencoder then fuses the two representations, making the integration step an explicit part of the denoising design.

Experiments on four real-world datasets and their associated downstream tasks report higher denoising accuracy than state-of-the-art methods and strong robustness across tasks. The authors also describe SpaEF, to their knowledge, as the first approach to use pretrained large models for constructing both graphs in this setting. The findings support improving graph construction and graph fusion together when extracting useful structure from noisy transcriptomics measurements.
summary.tldr: SpaEF uses pretrained large models to build spot and gene graphs, then fuses them to improve spatial transcriptomics denoising.

title: SpaEF: Spatially Resolved Transcriptomics Data Element-Wise Denoising Framework Powered by Large Models

abstract: Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) scales poorly in cooperative multi-agent domains because expansion must consider an exponentially large set of joint actions, severely limiting exploration under realistic search budgets. We propose NonZero, which keeps multi-agent MCTS tractable by running surrogate-guided selection over a low-dimensional nonlinear representation using an interaction-guided proposal rule, instead of directly exploring the full joint-action space. Our exploration uses an interaction score: single-agent deviations are ranked by predicted gain, while two-agent deviations are scored by a mixed-difference measure that reveals coordination benefits even when no single agent can improve alone. We formalize candidate proposal as a bandit problem over local deviations and derive a proposal rule, NonUCT, with a sublinear local-regret guarantee for reaching approximate graph-local optima without enumerating the joint-action space. Empirically, NonZero improves sample efficiency and final performance on MatGame, SMAC, and SMACv2 relative to strong model-based and model-free baselines under matched search budgets.

paragraphs: Cooperative multi-agent planning becomes difficult because combinations of agent actions grow exponentially. Monte Carlo Tree Search can spend its limited budget exploring this enormous space without finding useful coordination. NonZero makes selection more manageable through a low-dimensional nonlinear representation and a surrogate that guides candidate exploration.

Its proposal rule explicitly considers interactions. Changes by one agent are ranked by predicted benefit, while changes by two agents receive a mixed-difference score that can expose coordination benefits even when neither agent can improve alone. The authors formulate candidate selection as a bandit problem over local deviations and derive the NonUCT proposal rule.

NonUCT has a sublinear local-regret guarantee for reaching approximate graph-local optima without enumerating all joint actions. This guarantee concerns local search quality. Experiments on MatGame, SMAC, and SMACv2 show better sample efficiency and final performance than strong model-based and model-free baselines under matched search budgets. The findings support directing exploration toward interactions that individual action changes would miss.
summary.tldr: NonZero guides multi-agent tree search toward useful individual and paired action changes, improving exploration without enumerating joint actions.

title: NonZero: Interaction-Guided Exploration for Multi-Agent Monte Carlo Tree Search

abstract: Group counterfactual explanations find a set of counterfactual instances to explain a group of input instances contrastively. However, existing methods either (i) optimize counterfactuals only for a fixed group and do not generalize to new group members, (ii) strictly rely on strong model assumptions (e.g., linearity) for tractability and/or (iii) poorly control the counterfactual group geometry distortion. We instead learn an explicit optimal transport map that sends any group instance to its counterfactual without re-optimization, minimizing the group’s total transport cost. This enables generalization with fewer parameters, making it easier to interpret the common actionable recourse. For linear classifiers, we prove that functions representing group counterfactuals are derived via mathematical optimization, identifying the underlying convex optimization type (QP, QCQP, ...). Experiments show that they accurately generalize, preserve group geometry and incur only negligible additional transport cost compared to baseline methods. If model linearity cannot be exploited, our approach also significantly outperforms the baselines.

We instead learn an explicit optimal transport map that sends any group instance to its counterfactual without re-optimization, minimizing the group’s total transport cost. This enables generalization with fewer parameters, making it easier to interpret the common actionable recourse. paragraphs: Group counterfactual explanations describe how instances in a group could change to receive different model outcomes. Existing approaches can require fresh optimization for new members, depend strongly on classifier assumptions, or distort relationships within the group. This paper learns an explicit mapping from original instances to their counterfactual counterparts.

The mapping is formulated through optimal transport, minimizing the group’s total movement cost. Once learned, it can produce a counterfactual for a new group instance without solving the optimization again. Using fewer parameters also makes the shared actionable change easier to interpret. For linear classifiers, the authors derive the functions through mathematical optimization and identify the relevant convex problem types, including quadratic and quadratically constrained quadratic programs.

Experiments show accurate generalization to new instances, preservation of group geometry, and only negligible additional transport cost compared with baseline methods. When classifier linearity cannot be exploited, the approach also substantially outperforms the baselines. The contribution combines reusable counterfactual generation with explicit attention to the structure of the whole group, rather than treating each explanation as an unrelated individual adjustment.
summary.tldr: Learned optimal transport maps generate reusable group counterfactuals while preserving group geometry and keeping movement costs competitive.

title: Optimal Transport Group Counterfactual Explanations

abstract: Diffusion-based generative models increasingly rely on inference-time guidance, adding a drift term or reweighting mixture of experts, to improve sample quality on task-specific objectives. However, most existing techniques require repeated score or gradient evaluations, introducing bias, high computational overhead, or both. We introduce $\texttt{URGE}$, Unbiased Resampling via Girsanov Estimation, a derivative-free inference-time scaling algorithm that performs path-wise importance reweighting via a Girsanov change of measure. Instead of computing gradient-based particle weights in previous work, $\texttt{URGE}$ attaches a simple multiplicative weight to each simulated trajectory and periodically resamples. No score, no Hessian, and no PDE evaluation is required. We establish an equivalence between path-wise and particle-wise SMC: the Girsanov path weight admits a backward conditional expectation that recovers the previous particle-level weights, guaranteeing that both schemes produce the same unbiased terminal law. Empirically, $\texttt{URGE}$ outperforms existing inference-time guidance baselines on synthetic tests and diffusion-model benchmarks, achieving better generation quality, while being significantly simpler to implement and fully gradient-free.

paragraphs: Guiding diffusion generation toward a task objective often requires repeated derivative or score evaluations. URGE replaces this guidance-weight computation with a trajectory-based procedure. It assigns a multiplicative importance weight to each simulated path and periodically resamples trajectories, using a Girsanov change of measure to define those weights.

The method connects two ways of organizing sequential Monte Carlo: weighting entire paths and weighting particles at individual stages. The authors establish that a backward conditional expectation of the path weight recovers the earlier particle-level weights. Their equivalence result shows that both schemes produce the same unbiased terminal law, providing a theoretical basis for the simpler path-based construction.

The proposed weighting procedure requires no score, Hessian, or partial-differential-equation evaluation and is described as fully gradient-free. On synthetic tests and diffusion-model benchmarks, URGE produces better generation quality than the tested inference-time guidance baselines. The contribution combines that empirical improvement with a simpler implementation and a formal account of how its trajectory weights relate to particle-based guidance.
summary.tldr: URGE guides diffusion sampling through derivative-free trajectory weighting and resampling, with a theoretical link to unbiased particle-based schemes.

title: Simple Approximation and Derivative Free Inference-Time Scaling for Diffusion Models via Sequential Monte Carlo on Path Measures

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) hold great promise for healthcare applications, but fast-changing medical knowledge can quickly make their outputs outdated or inaccurate, limiting use in high-stakes settings. Model editing can update LLMs without full retraining, but parameter-based methods often break locality and are risky in medicine, making retrieval-based editing a better fit. However, applying model editing methods to the medical domain has two key challenges: (1) retrieval-based methods suffer from representation overlap within the medical knowledge space that causes inaccurate retrieval and reduces editing accuracy; (2) existing medical editing methods are restricted to single-sample edits, while batch-editing remains largely unexplored despite its importance for real-world applications. To address these challenges, we construct MedVersa, an expanded benchmark that evaluates single and batch edits across broader medical coverage under strict locality constraints. We then propose MedREK, a retrieval-based editing framework that integrates a shared query–key module for precise matching with an attention-based prompt encoder for informative guidance. Experiments across various medical benchmarks show that our MedREK consistently improves key metrics and provides the first validated solution for batch editing in medical LLMs.

paragraphs: Medical language models need knowledge updates as information changes. Editing through retrieval offers a way to supply updated knowledge without full retraining, but similar medical concepts can overlap in representation space and cause the wrong update to be retrieved. The paper also identifies batch editing as an underexplored requirement for applying multiple updates.

The authors introduce MedVersa, an expanded benchmark covering both individual and batch edits across a broader medical knowledge range. It imposes strict locality requirements, meaning an edit should preserve behavior outside its intended scope. Their MedREK framework combines a shared query-key module for more precise retrieval matching with an attention-based prompt encoder that supplies informative guidance to the model.

Across the evaluated medical benchmarks, MedREK consistently improves the reported key metrics. The authors also report the first validated solution for batch editing in medical language models. The contribution links retrieval accuracy with controlled update scope: selecting the relevant edit and presenting it effectively are both central to making knowledge changes while preserving unrelated behavior.
summary.tldr: MedREK improves retrieval-based medical knowledge editing through precise query-key matching and guided prompts, including support for batch edits.

title: MedREK: Retrieval-Based Editing for Medical LLMs with Key-Aware Prompts

abstract: Preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL) avoids explicit reward engineering by learning from pairwise human preference feedback. Existing offline PbRL methods typically follow a two-stage pipeline, first learning a reward or preference model from labeled preferences and then performing offline RL on unlabeled data. We revisit offline PbRL through the lens of reward-free representation learning (RFRL) from the zero-shot RL literature, and propose a new training framework that first learns latent successor-measure representations from reward-free offline data, followed by contrastive search and fine-tuning using preference data. Through extensive experiments and ablations, we show that our method achieves superior preference efficiency over offline PbRL baselines. This work is the first to connect RFRL with PbRL, highlighting its potential as a feedback-efficient solution. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/rl-bandits-lab/FB-PbRL.

paragraphs: Preference-based reinforcement learning uses comparisons between behaviors to avoid manually specifying a reward function. In the offline setting, a common workflow first learns a reward or preference model from labeled comparisons, then uses that model for reinforcement learning on existing data. This paper changes what is learned before preference feedback enters the process.

The proposed framework begins with reward-free offline data and learns latent successor-measure representations. These representations provide a foundation for subsequent adaptation to preferences. The method then uses preference data for contrastive search and fine-tuning, bringing human feedback into a representation that has already been learned without rewards.

Experiments and ablations report better preference efficiency than offline preference-based reinforcement-learning baselines. The result concerns how effectively the method uses labeled feedback, which is the central resource the framework seeks to economize. By connecting reward-free representation learning from zero-shot reinforcement learning with preference-based learning, the paper shows a route for preparing useful internal structure before spending preference labels on selecting and refining behavior.
summary.tldr: Learning representations from reward-free offline data before preference-based adaptation improves the reported efficiency of human feedback.

title: From Reward-Free Representations to Preferences: Rethinking Offline Preference-Based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) on chain-of-thought reasoning has become a standard part of language model post-training recipes. A common assumption is that the reasoning chains trained through RLVR reliably represent how a model gets to its answer. In this paper, we develop two metrics for critically examining this assumption: Causal Importance of Reasoning (CIR), which measures the cumulative effect of reasoning tokens on the final answer, and Sufficiency of Reasoning (SR), which measures whether a verifier can arrive at an unambiguous answer based on the reasoning alone. Through experiments with the Qwen2.5 model series and ReasoningGym tasks, we find that: (1) While RLVR does improve task accuracy, it does not reliably improve CIR or SR, calling the role of reasoning in model performance into question. (2) A small amount of SFT before RLVR can be a remedy for low CIR and SR. (3) CIR and SR can be improved even without SFT by applying auxiliary CIR/SR rewards on top of the outcome-based reward. This joint reward matches the accuracy of RLVR while also leading to causally important and sufficient reasoning. These results show that RLVR does not always lead models to rely on reasoning in the way that is commonly thought, but this issue can be remedied with simple modifications to the post-training procedure.

paragraphs: Rewarding a model for correct answers can improve accuracy without ensuring that its written reasoning explains how it reached those answers. This paper examines that distinction for reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards. It asks whether reasoning tokens affect the answer and whether the reasoning itself gives a verifier enough information to determine an unambiguous answer.

The authors introduce Causal Importance of Reasoning to measure the cumulative effect of reasoning tokens on the final answer. Sufficiency of Reasoning measures whether a verifier can recover an unambiguous answer from the reasoning alone. Experiments with Qwen2.5 models on ReasoningGym find that outcome-based reinforcement learning improves task accuracy but does not reliably improve either measure.

Two training modifications help in the reported experiments. A small amount of supervised fine-tuning before reinforcement learning can improve both properties. Alternatively, auxiliary rewards targeting the two measures improve reasoning without that supervised stage, while matching ordinary outcome-reward training accuracy. The findings show why answer correctness and the usefulness of a reasoning trace require separate assessment.
summary.tldr: Correct-answer rewards do not reliably make reasoning causally important or sufficient, but targeted training changes improve both in the studied settings.

title: Outcome Rewards Do Not Guarantee Verifiable or Causally Important Reasoning

abstract: Open-domain multimodal document retrieval aims to retrieve specific components (paragraphs, tables, or images) from large and interconnected document corpora. Existing graph-based retrieval approaches typically rely on a uniform similarity metric that overlooks hop-specific semantics, and their rigid pre-defined plans hinder dynamic error correction. These limitations suggest that a retriever should adapt its reasoning to the evolving context and recover intelligently from dead ends. To address these needs, we propose Failure is Feedback, which casts subgraph retrieval as a sequential decision process and introduces two key innovations. (i) We introduce a history-aware backtracking mechanism; unlike standard backtracking that simply reverts the state, our approach piggybacks on the context of failed traversals, leveraging insights from previous failures. (ii) We implement an economically-rational agentic workflow. Unlike conventional agents with static strategies, our orchestrator employs a cost-aware traversal method to dynamically manage the trade-off between retrieval accuracy and inference costs, escalating to intensive LLM-based reasoning only when the prior failure justifies the additional computational investment. The project page is available at failureisfeedback.github.io.

paragraphs: Finding a particular paragraph, table, or image across connected documents can require several retrieval steps. A single similarity measure may miss what matters at different stages of that search, while a fixed plan gives the retriever little room to recover when it takes an unhelpful path. This paper treats retrieval as a sequence of decisions that can change with context.

Its history-aware backtracking mechanism retains information from unsuccessful traversals. Returning to an earlier point therefore does not erase what the agent learned about the failed route. The context of previous failures informs subsequent decisions, making a dead end part of the evidence available for continuing the search.

The framework also makes computation a decision variable. A cost-aware orchestrator manages the trade-off between retrieval accuracy and inference expense, escalating to more intensive language-model reasoning when prior failure justifies it. The contribution described in the abstract is this combination of adaptive recovery and selective reasoning effort: the search can revise both where it goes and how much computation it spends.
summary.tldr: Failure is Feedback uses unsuccessful retrieval paths to guide backtracking and decide when more expensive reasoning is warranted.

abstract: We propose a fast iterative classification algorithm for Kernel Fisher Discriminant (KFD) using heterogeneous kernel models. In contrast with the standard KFD that requires the user to predefine a kernel function, we incorporate the task of choosing an appropriate kernel into the optimization problem to be solved. The choice of kernel is defined as a linear combination of kernels belonging to a potentially large family of different positive semidefinitekernels. The complexity of our algorithm does not increase significantly with respect to the number of kernels on thekernel family. Experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that generalization performance of the proposed algorithm is not significantly different from that achieved by the standard KFD in which the kernel parameters have been tuned using cross validation. We also present results on a real-life colon cancer dataset that demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Kernel Fisher Discriminant requires a choice of kernel function, which determines how the method represents similarities between examples. Choosing that function is ordinarily a separate decision made before fitting the classifier. This paper brings kernel choice into the learning problem itself, allowing the optimization to select a suitable combination while constructing the classifier.

The proposed method uses a linear combination drawn from a potentially large family of different positive semidefinite kernels. A fast iterative algorithm searches within this combined model. The computational claim is that increasing the number of available kernels does not significantly increase the algorithm's complexity, making a broad collection of candidates practical to consider.

On benchmark datasets, the reported generalization performance is not significantly different from standard Kernel Fisher Discriminant with kernel parameters tuned through cross-validation. The contribution is therefore an efficient way to incorporate kernel selection into training while maintaining comparable predictive performance. Results on a colon cancer dataset also demonstrate the method's efficiency.
summary.tldr: An iterative Kernel Fisher Discriminant method learns a combination of kernels and achieves performance comparable to cross-validation-tuned standard KFD.

title: A fast iterative algorithm for fisher discriminant using heterogeneous kernels

abstract: We show that linear value function approximation is equivalent to a form of linear model approximation. We derive a relationship between the model approximation error and the Bellman error, and show how this relationship can guide feature selection for model improvement and/or value function improvement. We also show how these results give insight into the behavior of existing feature-selection algorithms.
originalAbstract: We show that linear value function approximation is equivalent to a form of linear model approximation. We derive a relationship between the model approximation error and the Bellman error, and show how this relationship can guide feature selection for model improvement and/or value function improvement. We also show how these results give insight into the behavior of existing feature-selection algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper connects two ways of approximating a reinforcement learning problem: using a linear value function and using a linear approximation to the model. Its central result establishes that linear value-function approximation is equivalent to a particular form of linear model approximation. This gives a shared perspective on approaches that otherwise emphasize different objects.

The authors then derive a relationship between model approximation error and Bellman error. The relationship matters because it links the quality of the approximate model with an error measure associated with value-function learning. It provides a mathematical basis for reasoning about how a representation affects these two aspects of the learning problem.

The paper shows how this connection can guide feature selection for improving the model, the value function, or both. It also uses the results to explain the behavior of existing feature-selection algorithms. The contribution is an analytical foundation for choosing features: representation decisions can be examined through the relationship between model error and value-function error.
summary.tldr: An equivalence between linear value and model approximation links their errors and provides guidance for reinforcement learning feature selection.

title: An analysis of linear models, linear value-function approximation, and feature selection for reinforcement learning

abstract: We propose a novel Bayesian multiple instance learning algorithm. This algorithm automatically identifies the relevant feature subset, and utilizes inductive transfer when learning multiple (conceptually related) classifiers. Experimental results indicate that the proposed baseline MIL method is more accurate than previous MIL algorithms and selects a much smaller set of useful features. Inductive transfer further improves the accuracy of the classifier as compared to learning each task individually.
originalAbstract: We propose a novel Bayesian multiple instance learning algorithm. This algorithm automatically identifies the relevant feature subset, and utilizes inductive transfer when learning multiple (conceptually related) classifiers. Experimental results indicate that the proposed baseline MIL method is more accurate than previous MIL algorithms and selects a much smaller set of useful features. Inductive transfer further improves the accuracy of the classifier as compared to learning each task individually.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a Bayesian approach to multiple instance learning that combines classifier training with automatic feature selection. Instead of treating every available feature as equally useful throughout learning, the method identifies a relevant subset. Feature selection is therefore part of the learning algorithm, connecting the classifier it produces with a smaller collection of useful inputs.

The approach also supports learning several conceptually related classifiers through inductive transfer. In this setting, information from related learning tasks can help train an individual classifier. The paper treats this sharing as an additional capability of the Bayesian method, alongside its baseline ability to learn a classifier and identify relevant features.

The reported experiments distinguish the benefits of these two elements. The baseline method achieves higher accuracy than previous multiple instance learning algorithms while selecting substantially fewer useful features. Adding inductive transfer further improves accuracy compared with training each task separately. Together, these results support combining feature selection and learning across related tasks in the evaluated problems.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian multiple instance learning method selects fewer useful features and improves reported accuracy, with further gains from transferring information across related tasks.

title: Bayesian multiple instance learning: automatic feature selection and inductive transfer

abstract: We consider the problem of how to improve the efficiency of Multiple Kernel Learning (MKL). MKL is often regarded as a convex-concave optimization problem, which is convex on the kernel weights and concave on the SVM dual variables. In literature, the alternating approach is widely observed: (1) the minimization of the kernel weights is solved by complicated techniques, such as Semi-infinite Linear Programming, Gradient Descent, or Level method; (2) the maximization of SVM dual variables can be solved by standard SVM solvers. However, the minimization over kernel weights in these methods is usually dependent on its solving techniques or commercial softwares, which therefore limits the efficiency and applicability. In this paper, we formulate a closed-form solution for the optimization of kernel weights based on the equivalence between group-lasso and MKL. Although this equivalence is not our invention, our derived variant equivalence not only lead to an efficient algorithm for MKL, but also generalize this equivalence to that between Lp-MKL (p >=1 and denoting the Lp-norm of kernel weights) and group lasso, which does not appear in literature. Therefore, our proposed algorithm provides a unified solution for the whole family of Lp-MKL models. Experiments on multiple data sets show the promising performance of the proposed technique compared with other competitive methods.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning combines kernels by learning their weights alongside an SVM. Common approaches alternate between optimizing kernel weights and updating the SVM variables. The paper focuses on the kernel-weight step, whose dependence on complicated optimization techniques or commercial software can limit efficiency and applicability.

Using a connection between multiple kernel learning and group lasso, the authors derive a closed-form solution for optimizing the kernel weights. The basic equivalence was already known; their contribution is a variant that enables this efficient calculation. It simplifies a key part of the alternating procedure while retaining the connection to a structured regularization problem.

The paper also extends the equivalence to the family of Lp multiple-kernel-learning models for p at least one. This yields a unified algorithmic treatment across those choices of kernel-weight norm. Experiments on multiple datasets show promising performance compared with competitive methods. The work therefore contributes both a simpler weight-update mechanism and a broader formulation that applies across a family of kernel-learning models.
summary.tldr: A group-lasso equivalence yields closed-form kernel-weight updates and a unified algorithm for Lp multiple kernel learning.

title: Simple and Efficient Multiple Kernel Learning by Group Lasso

abstract: We study simultaneous learning and covering problems: submodular set cover problems that depend on the solution to an active (query) learning problem. The goal is to jointly minimize the cost of both learning and covering. We extend recent work in this setting to allow for a limited amount of adversarial noise. Certain noisy query learning problems are a special case of our problem. Crucial to our analysis is a lemma showing the logical OR of two submodular cover constraints can be reduced to a single submodular set cover constraint. Combined with known results, this new lemma allows for arbitrary monotone circuits of submodular cover constraints to be reduced to a single constraint. As an example practical application, we present a movie recommendation website that minimizes the total cost of learning what the user wants to watch and recommending a set of movies.

Crucial to our analysis is a lemma showing the logical OR of two submodular cover constraints can be reduced to a single submodular set cover constraint. Combined with known results, this new lemma allows for arbitrary monotone circuits of submodular cover constraints to be reduced to a single constraint. paragraphs: Some selection problems depend on information that must first be learned through queries. This paper studies that coupling through submodular set cover problems whose solution depends on an active-learning problem. The objective combines the cost of gathering information with the cost of completing the cover, so both activities are optimized together.

The authors extend this setting to tolerate a limited amount of adversarial noise. A key lemma shows that an either-or requirement involving two submodular cover constraints can be expressed as a single such constraint. Combined with existing results, this also handles arbitrary monotone circuits built from submodular cover constraints, allowing more complicated logical combinations to fit the same framework.

Certain noisy query-learning problems appear as special cases. The paper also presents a movie-recommendation website that minimizes the combined cost of discovering a user's preferences and recommending a collection of movies. This application illustrates why learning and selection belong in one objective: obtaining information is itself part of the cost of delivering recommendations.
summary.tldr: A joint learning-and-covering framework tolerates limited adversarial noise and reduces logical combinations of submodular cover constraints to one constraint.

title: Simultaneous Learning and Covering with Adversarial Noise

abstract: Portfolio allocation theory has been heavily influenced by a major contribution of Harry Markowitz in the early fifties: the mean-variance approach. While there has been a continuous line of works in on-line learning portfolios over the past decades, very few works have really tried to cope with Markowitz model. A major drawback of the mean-variance approach is that it is approximation-free only when stock returns obey a Gaussian distribution, an assumption known not to hold in real data. In this paper, we first alleviate this assumption, and rigorously lift the mean-variance model to a more general mean-divergence model in which stock returns are allowed to obey any exponential family of distributions. We then devise a general on-line learning algorithm in this setting. We prove for this algorithm the first lower bounds on the most relevant quantity to be optimized in the framework of Markowitz model: the certainty equivalents. Experiments on four real-world stock markets display its ability to track portfolios whose cumulated returns exceed those of the best stock by orders of magnitude.

paragraphs: The paper revisits portfolio allocation through the mean-variance framework associated with Markowitz. It identifies a restriction: the approach is approximation-free only for Gaussian stock returns, an assumption the abstract says does not hold in real data. The authors seek a broader mathematical setting that also supports online portfolio learning.

They generalize mean-variance allocation to a mean-divergence model, allowing returns from any exponential family of distributions. This relaxes the Gaussian restriction within a specified family of models. They then develop a general online learning algorithm and prove lower bounds on certainty equivalents, the optimization quantity emphasized in their treatment of the Markowitz framework.

Experiments on four real-world stock markets show the algorithm's ability to track portfolios whose cumulative returns exceed those of the best individual stock by orders of magnitude. This is an empirical tracking result, alongside theoretical bounds on a different stated quantity. The contribution combines a broader return-distribution model, an online algorithm, and analysis aligned with the framework's certainty-equivalent objective.
summary.tldr: A mean-divergence generalization of Markowitz allocation supports exponential-family returns and online portfolio learning with certainty-equivalent bounds.

title: On tracking portfolios with certainty equivalents on a generalization of Markowitz model: the Fool, the Wise and the Adaptive
